reads.perf: The group is +4.2% versus SPY over 1M but -5.1% over 3M and -8.7% over 6M. The bounce came from large-cap guidance raises at LIN, ECL and PPG and the 10Y pulling back from 5.36%, not broad participation (51% 1M breadth).
reads.risk: Beta of 0.45, a -10.2% max drawdown and a 0.83 Sharpe reflect contracted gas cash flows at LIN and APD. Rates are the main factor at -2.0% per +25bp on the 10Y. Credit distress sits at the 98th percentile since 2024 and IG spreads are ~12bp wider, a quiet build-up of risk.
reads.fund: TTM revenue grew 4.5% and earnings 7.6%, and quarterly revenue growth re-accelerated from -2.4% (2025-Q3) to +10.6% (2026-Q2), mostly on price rather than volume (LIN volume +2%). The 10.9% operating margin and 7.2% ROIC are middling.
reads.health: D/E is 0.88, the current ratio 1.43 and interest cover 5.5x. Net debt/EBITDA is steady near 2.6x and inventory days are down to 66 (-11% y/y), so there is no destock risk. Still, 36% of cap has stretched balance sheets (ECL, APD, IFF, LYB, ESI, WLK) facing ~5.86% high-grade corporate yields.
reads.val: Trailing P/E of 43.8x is inflated by APD's $2.9B charge and LIN's $425M restructuring. Forward is 20.5x, and 14.9x ex-top-three. The NTM-earnings reverse DCF implies 1.0% growth against 7.3% consensus, and the FCF version implies 4.9% against 3.4% revenue history: in line, not stretched.
reads.earn: The beat rate is 60% with a +2.9% median EPS surprise. Guidance went up at LIN, ECL, PPG and APD, while SHW only narrowed around $12 and AXTA missed. Breadth of -0.20 and a -0.1% median 30-day revision show the headline +24% is a CLMT artifact.
reads.cycle: Cycle: late cycle, pricing power moderate. Demand across the 49-company group is price-led rather than volume-led: TTM revenue grew 4.5%, but LIN volume was only 2%, ECL guides 1-2% volume against 5-6% pricing into H1 2027, and SHW Paint Stores volume rose only low single digits.

hist.read: The five episodes split, with three of five up at 3M, 6M and 12M, but the 12M median of +5.1% sits close to the team's +4% view. 1M looks soft, since only 1 of 5 was up, and, and all fell in the first month or three. The 6M base rate is weak (55% up versus 67% for all months), and in 3 of 5 episodes the industry lagged the S&P 500 at 12M, so I would not expect outperformance. is the closest in spirit, because it combines oil, a high multiple, a rate shock and a market dip, though is the best case if the shock fades. Weight these modestly, since the analogs differ on valuation, VIX and the oil shock, and they support caution and selectivity over a broad bullish call.

episodes.then: In January 2022 the Fed pivoted hawkishly, 10-year yields were rising fast and growth stocks sold off, with VIX in the mid-20s. Oil was rallying toward the Russia-Ukraine war, and specialty chemicals were well off their highs from input-cost and rate worries.
episodes.after: Over the next 12 months the industry fell 8.5% and the S&P 500 fell 7.2%. Russia invaded Ukraine, the Fed hiked aggressively, and the industry lost 11.7% over 6 months, with a worst drawdown of 20.2%. Chemical stocks lagged as rate-driven de-rating and an energy shock hit margins.
episodes.different: Today's S&P is down 2.6% over 6 months, whereas in 2022 it was up 3.3%, and today's 10Y near 4.84% is already high, so more of the rate shock may be priced. That cuts mildly in today's favor, but the 82nd-percentile multiple is a similar valuation risk.
episodes.lesson: Rate and energy shock plus a high multiple meant a deep de-rating.

episodes.then: In March 2025 tariff announcements and growth fears drove a sharp equity correction, with VIX in the low 20s and the dollar strong. Chemicals were weak and trading below their 200-day average, with a P/E percentile near 80.
episodes.after: The industry gained 12.9% over 12 months, though it lagged the S&P 500's 18.5%. It dipped 10.3% at worst in the first 6 months, then recovered, rising 7.5% over 6 months as the tariff scare faded. The market rally lifted chemicals, but only partly.
episodes.different: Today has a higher VIX (28 vs 22) and an oil shock with Brent near $98.61, which compounds input-cost risk. That cuts against today, since the 2025 rebound had no energy headwind.
episodes.lesson: A policy-driven dip recovered, with the industry lagging the market.

episodes.then: In June 2015 China growth worries, a stronger dollar and falling oil were building ahead of the August devaluation selloff. Industrials and chemicals were already soft.
episodes.after: The industry lost 18.3% over 3 months and 11.7% over 6, with a worst drawdown of 18.8%. After 12 months it was down 12.4% while the S&P 500 was up 2.6%. The August 2015 China scare and global manufacturing weakness hit cyclical chemicals harder than the broad market.
episodes.different: Oil was falling then and is surging now, and today's VIX is far higher. Today's oil shock is an inflation and cost risk rather than a demand-collapse signal, so the bad outcome would come from a different cause.
episodes.lesson: A dollar-strength and global-slowdown dip kept hurting cyclicals.

episodes.then: In March 2018 tariff and trade-war worries and a Facebook-led tech wobble shook markets after the February volatility spike. Oil was climbing and chemicals were below their highs after a strong 2017.
episodes.after: The industry gained 17.6% over 12 months against 10.7% for the S&P 500. It was up 6.1% over 6 months, and the worst drop was only 4.7%. Earnings held up and the dip proved shallow.
episodes.different: The valuation then was at the 59th percentile versus 82nd today, and the dollar was falling then versus rising now. Both cut against today's setup.
episodes.lesson: A cheaper-valuation dip with intact earnings rebounded.

episodes.then: In September 2023 yields were surging toward 5% on higher-for-longer Fed talk, oil was rallying, and equities were correcting. Chemicals were in a destocking slump and lagged the market.
episodes.after: The industry rose 12.6% over 12 months, but the S&P 500 rose 34.8%. After an initial 1M slide of 4.3%, it gained 9.5% over 3 months and 14.4% over 6 as yields peaked and rates fell. The worst drop was 7.4%.
episodes.different: The P/E percentile was 42nd then versus 82nd today, so there was much more room for re-rating. Today's 10Y near 4.84% is no longer a falling-yield tailwind in the same way, which cuts against today.
episodes.lesson: A yield peak helped, but the valuation was low.

episodes.then: In January 2022 the Fed was turning hawkish and a growth-stock selloff was under way, with Russia-Ukraine tensions building. Fertilizer prices were already elevated, and the Ukraine invasion the following month sent nitrogen and potash prices higher.
episodes.after: The industry rose 5.9% in 1M and 7% in 3M, probably helped by the fertilizer spike after the invasion. It then faded to -4.4% at 6M and -9.7% at 12M, with a worst drawdown of -27.3% in the first 6 months, as fertilizer prices normalized. The S&P 500 fell 7.6% over 3M and 7.2% over 12M, so the industry's 12M loss was not much worse than the market's.
episodes.different: Today the industry has already fallen 8.2% over 3M and sits 13.2% below its high, whereas then it was near its high. Valuation is also richer today (90th vs 80th percentile). This cuts toward a smaller further squeeze but a less supportive starting point.
episodes.lesson: Commodity spikes fade after the initial pop

episodes.then: In October 2018 equities sold off sharply on Fed tightening worries and trade-war fears, ahead of the December low. Agricultural inputs were weighed down by US-China tariffs and weak farm sentiment.
episodes.after: The industry kept slipping, with -1.8% at 1M, -3.3% at 3M, -3.9% at 6M and -8.8% at 12M, and a worst drawdown of -14.7%. The S&P 500 rebounded to +9.3% at 6M and +15.4% at 12M, so the industry badly lagged the recovery.
episodes.different: Oil is up 14.8% over 6M today versus roughly flat then, and the industry has a +8.7pp lead on the S&P 500 while it lagged then. This cuts toward more input-cost and inflation pressure, but also more momentum to lose.
episodes.lesson: Rich valuation plus a weak backdrop meant lagging the rebound

episodes.then: In March 2025 markets were wobbling over tariff policy and growth fears, with the S&P 500 in a correction and the dollar firm. Agricultural inputs were holding up relatively well.
episodes.after: The industry rallied strongly: +14.9% at 1M, +29.6% at 3M, +27.7% at 6M and +42.8% at 12M, with only an -8.3% worst drawdown. It beat the S&P 500, which gained 10.7% at 3M and 19.8% at 6M. I am not certain of the specific drivers.
episodes.different: Today's VIX is 28 versus 22, and the industry has fallen 8.2% over 3M, whereas it had gained 6.1% then. This cuts toward a weaker setup, because there is no recent momentum to build on.
episodes.lesson: Relative strength can persist after a correction

episodes.then: In February 2021 reflation was driving a commodity rally and Treasury yields were rising fast. Agricultural commodities were strengthening, and the industry traded at a rich valuation.
episodes.after: The industry gained 5.4% at 1M, 10.5% at 3M and 4.5% at 6M, then 18.3% at 12M, with a worst drawdown of -9.4%. The S&P 500 did better over the first 6M at +18.1%, and the 12M figures were close (+16.6% for the S&P).
episodes.different: Then the industry was 8.9% above its 200-day average and at the start of a commodity upcycle. Today it is only 1.6% above, after a sell-off and with the S&P 500 down 2.6% over 6M. This cuts toward lower odds of a smooth ride.

episodes.then: In May 2010 the euro-zone debt crisis and the flash crash hit stocks, the dollar surged and the VIX spiked. The industry was falling with the market, even though it was in the middle of a multi-year agricultural upcycle.

reads.perf: The cap-weighted group is -24.8% against SPY over 6M, and only 20% of names beat SPY over 1Y. The sell-off came from AI-capex funding fears after GOOG and META posted negative FCF, not from weaker revenue. RSI of 11 and a price 13% below the 200-day average mark an extreme oversold reading.
reads.risk: Beta of 1.40, alpha of -15.1% and a Sharpe of -0.14 reflect a high-duration group hit by rising rates and the funding scare. The measured sensitivities are -1.8% per +25bp on the 10Y and -7.4% per 2% high-yield sell-off, with credit distress at the 99th percentile.
reads.fund: Revenue is growing 21.7% at a 29.5% operating margin and 21.8% ROIC. FCF margin is just 6.7% (-1.1% after stock pay of 7.9% of revenue), because capex reached 39.3% of sales and conversion fell to 17% of net income.
reads.health: D/E is 0.28, the current ratio 2.45, interest cover 36.8x and net debt/EBITDA -0.46, so the leaders hold net cash. META's $15-25B bond issuance and NBIS's asset-backed debt are building leverage at the margin. Stretched balance sheets are about 1% of industry cap.
reads.val: P/E of 16.4x is at the 0th percentile of its 5-year range against a 26.6x median. NTM earnings imply 7.3% growth, close to the 7.2% next-FY consensus EPS growth, so the price matches consensus margin compression. The FCF reverse DCF (31%) is a real hurdle while capex is still rising.
reads.earn: The beat rate is a middling 55%, with a median EPS surprise of 4.1%. Cap-weighted revisions are +2.3% over 30 days, but breadth is -0.36 (119 up vs 253 down). GOOG is +4.0%, META -1.2% and BIDU -10.2%.
reads.cycle: Cycle: expansion, pricing power moderate. The industry is two companies: GOOG (67.2% of cap) and META (26.1%), so sector results are really an AI-infrastructure-versus-ad-engine story. TTM revenue growth is 21.5% with a 29.6% operating margin.

hist.read: The five episodes lean positive but are dispersed. The 1M outcomes were mixed (up in 2 of 5), 3M and 6M were up in 4 of 5, and 12M was up in 4 of 5. The base rates show a median of about +3.5% at 1M, +6% at 3M, +9.1% at 6M and +9.3% at 12M, but the industry beat the S&P 500 only 45% of the time at 6M and 35% at 12M. Weight should be modest because the sample is small, the outcomes range from -18% to +55.5%, and today's oil, dollar and VIX backdrop is more hostile than most episodes. Today most resembles, which shared the same drawdown, trend and 200-day readings, with a rough path but a modest recovery. is the main warning, since the worst drop within 6 months ranged from -6.2% to -26.9%…

episodes.then: October 2018 brought a sharp equity selloff as the Fed kept hiking, Treasury yields rose and trade tensions with China escalated. Internet names were hit by the tech rout and by regulatory and privacy worries, including the Facebook scandals.
episodes.after: The industry fell 1.3% in the first month, then recovered to +3.1% at 3M, +8.4% at 6M and +7.8% at 12M. The S&P 500 did better, at +9.3% at 6M and +15.4% at 12M, so the industry lagged. The worst drop within the next 6 months was -14%, which fits the late-2018 Christmas Eve low, though that is my recollection rather than a measured figure.
episodes.different: Today's valuation is far cheaper, at the 6th percentile against the 25th, and VIX is higher at 28 versus 21. Oil is up 14.8% rather than flat. The cheaper starting valuation cuts in favor of the industry, while the higher VIX and the oil shock cut against it.
episodes.lesson: Drawdowns can be volatile before they recover

episodes.then: In May 2012 the euro-area crisis flared again with Greek election fears and Spanish bank worries. Yields fell as investors sought safety, and the S&P 500 pulled back from its spring high. Internet stocks were weak after the Facebook IPO and ahead of the mobile-ad shift.
episodes.after: The industry slipped 0.5% in the first month, then gained 9.8% at 3M, 14.4% at 6M and 32.6% at 12M. That beat the S&P 500's +27.2% at 12M. The worst drop inside 6 months was -15.2%, so the path was rough even though the outcome was strong.
episodes.different: In 2012 yields were falling and oil was down 15.9%, a deflationary backdrop. Today yields and oil are rising, which is a tighter, inflationary backdrop and cuts against a repeat.
episodes.lesson: Deep lagging can mean-revert strongly

episodes.then: March 2025 saw a tech-led equity correction on tariff escalation and growth fears. The dollar was strong, and large-cap internet names fell with the AI-trade wobble. Oil and yields were drifting in a way similar to today.
episodes.after: This is the worst analog. The industry fell 12.5% in the first month and was down 6.4% at 3M, 12.1% at 6M and 18% at 12M. The S&P 500 meanwhile rose 10.7% at 3M and 19.8% at 6M. The worst drop within 6 months was -26.9%.
episodes.different: The P/E percentile then was 68th, versus 6th today, so valuation was not a cushion then but is now. That cuts in favor of today, though it is no guarantee given the same relative-weakness pattern.
episodes.lesson: Expensive laggards can keep lagging

episodes.then: June 2015 had Greece's debt crisis and Chinese equity volatility just before the August devaluation selloff. The dollar was strong and oil was weak. Internet leaders were holding up well, near their highs.
episodes.after: The industry jumped 14.8% in the first month, then +3.3% at 3M, +30.4% at 6M and +16.6% at 12M. The S&P 500 managed only +1.9% at 6M and +2.6% at 12M, so the industry beat it by a wide margin. The worst drop within 6 months was -14.6%.
episodes.different: The industry was near its highs then, only 6.5% below the 12-month high, and it is 20.3% below today. Today's setup is a real drawdown with weak momentum, not a minor dip. This is a weak match, and it cuts both ways.
episodes.lesson: Leadership can persist when the dip is shallow

episodes.then: February 2023 followed the 2022 bear market, when rate hikes and an ad slump crushed internet stocks. The market was rebounding amid hopes for a soft landing, and the AI boom was starting with ChatGPT.
episodes.after: The industry rose 12.2% in the first month, then +34.3% at 3M, +44.7% at 6M and +55.5% at 12M. The S&P 500 gained 30.2% at 12M. The worst drop within 6 months was only -6.2%, as the AI rally lifted the group.
episodes.different: The industry was 46.3% off its high then, a far deeper washout than today's 20.3%, and the S&P 500 was in recovery. Today the group is less washed out and faces a higher VIX, so a similar rebound is less likely.
episodes.lesson: Deep washouts rebound hardest

reads.perf: The group is -16.0% vs SPY over 1Y and -18.3% over 6M, with median-stock breadth of 20% over 3M. The lag reflects a 10-year that hit 5.344% on 1 Oct, which hurt bond-proxy valuations, and a -22% fall at TMUS, rather than weaker operations.
reads.risk: Beta of 0.06 hides strong rate sensitivity: -1.5% per +25bp on the 10-year and -2.7% per +5% in the dollar. Volatility is 18.4% over the year, with 20-day volatility now 35% and a max drawdown of -21.8%.
reads.fund: Revenue grows 1.5% while TTM earnings are down 24.4%, as interest costs and charges offset VZ's record 40.2% EBITDA margin. FCF margin of 14% and 115% FCF conversion show earnings quality is better than reported net income suggests.
reads.health: D/E is 1.56, interest cover 3.1x and net debt/EBITDA 2.91. AT&T rose to 3.13x after the EchoStar spectrum purchase and 70% of market cap sits in stretched balance sheets. VZ and AMX (1.21x) are the clean balance sheets.
reads.val: P/E of 13.4x (21st percentile of its 5-year range) and 8.6x forward, plus a 12.7% FCF yield, price FCF falling 11% a year. That is undemanding against VZ's FCF growth near 12%, but justified only if 5%+ long yields last.
reads.earn: Beat rate is 57% with a median EPS surprise of 3.8%. The big three raised guidance this quarter. Revisions are narrow, with breadth at -0.31, and the cap-weighted +21.3% is distorted by CHT's +492% artifact.
reads.cycle: Cycle: late cycle, pricing power moderate. US telecom is a low-growth, high-cash-yield group. TTM revenue growth is 1.5% and the cap-weighted dividend yield is 5.70%, but net income growth is -24.4% and the group lagged SPY by 16.0% over 1Y and 18.3% over 6M (computed metrics).

The groups beat the S&P 500 only 45%, 30% and 25% of the time at 1M, 3M and 6M, so relative returns are poor, and the five episodes split 3 up and 2 down. The winners had falling yields or oil, while the losers had rising yields, and today's rising yields and oil fit the losers more. The evidence supports a neutral stance with modest absolute upside from a washed-out group, but no relative edge, and I would give it moderate weight, since the five episodes are few and rate backdrops differ. is the closest match (rising yields, oil spike, lagging…

episodes.then: In February 2022 the Fed was preparing its first hike, Treasury yields were rising fast, and Russia invaded Ukraine at month-end, pushing oil sharply higher. Telecom was already lagging the market; I am not sure of the specific sector catalysts that month.
episodes.after: The industry gained 1.5% over 1 month while the S&P 500 rose 6%. It then slid, with 3M -1.5%, 6M -12.8% and 12M -18.5%, and the worst drop inside 6 months was -14.9%. The S&P 500 also fell (6M -7.1%, 12M -8.1%) as rate hikes drove the 2022 bear market, so the group did worse than the market.
episodes.different: Today oil is up much less (+14.8% vs +40.5%) and Treasuries have fallen less (-0.8% vs -3.9%), so the rate shock is milder. The industry is also further below its high (-32.1% vs -25.8%), which cuts both ways: there is more room to rebound, but the damage is already deeper.
episodes.lesson: Rate and oil shock with a lagging sector kept falling

episodes.then: In May 2012 the euro-area crisis flared again, with Greek election worries and a risk-off market, while Treasury yields fell toward record lows. Telecom was down sharply over the year; I am not certain of the specific sector drivers.
episodes.after: The industry rebounded, with 1M +7.4%, 3M +12.2%, 6M +3% and 12M +14.5%. It still had a worst drawdown of -14.4% inside 6 months, and it lagged the S&P 500 at 12M (+27.2%). Falling yields and a market recovery helped the group.
episodes.different: Then Treasuries had rallied (+5.6%), whereas today yields are rising (-0.8%) and oil has jumped. The tailwind from falling rates is missing, which cuts against a repeat.
episodes.lesson: Falling yields powered the rebound

episodes.then: In November 2022 inflation was starting to cool and the market rallied off its October low, but the Fed was still hiking and yields were elevated. Telecom was weak after a bad year; I am not sure of the sector-specific catalysts.
episodes.after: The industry fell 5.3% in 1M, then 3M -1.4%, 6M -7.1% and 12M -4.2%, with a worst drop of -10.4%. The S&P 500 meanwhile gained 5.8% over 6M and 14.4% over 12M, so the group lagged a recovering market.
episodes.different: Today the S&P 500 is only 5.7% below its high versus 13.7% then, and the VIX is higher (27 vs 21). Today's market stress is more recent and oil is rising rather than falling, which cuts toward more volatility.
episodes.lesson: Value traps lagged a recovering market

episodes.then: In October 2018 a sharp equity selloff hit as the Fed kept hiking and trade-war worries grew, with the dollar firm. Telecom was a weak, defensive-ish group; I am not sure of specific sector drivers.
episodes.after: The industry rose 2.3% in 1M, then 3M +0.6%, 6M +4.7% and 12M +10.5%. It still lagged the S&P 500, which gained 9.3% over 6M and 15.4% over 12M. The Fed pivot in early 2019 helped, though the worst 6M drop was -11.7%.
episodes.different: The industry was far less depressed then (-4.8% vs 200-day, versus -16.2% today), and oil was flat rather than up 14.8%. Today's deeper washout cuts toward a bigger rebound, but a stronger inflation impulse is a risk.
episodes.lesson: Mild selloff, modest lagging recovery

episodes.then: In December 2015 oil had collapsed, high yield was stressed, and the Fed was about to deliver its first hike in nearly a decade. Telecom had lagged the market for months; I am not sure of specific sector events.
episodes.after: The industry slipped 0.4% in 1M, then rallied: 3M +11.2%, 6M +15% and 12M +10.1%, with a worst drop of -6.6%. The S&P 500 was weaker over 1M (-6.7%) and returned 4% over 6M and 12% over 12M. Falling oil and lower yields in 2016 favored defensive income.
episodes.different: Oil was falling 44.7% then but is rising 14.8% now, and credit spreads were widening sharply (-7.9pp) versus roughly flat today. Rising oil and yields are a much less friendly backdrop for bond-like telecom.
episodes.lesson: Oil collapse and falling yields favored defensives

hist.read: The base rates lean positive but are not decisive. Over 1 month, the five episodes were up in 3 of 5 and the median was only +1%, so the near term is close to a coin flip. At 3, 6 and 12 months, 4 of 5 episodes were up and the medians were +7.5%, +10.1% and +24.5%, though only about half of those months beat the S&P 500. The spread is wide: fell 42.2% in six months, and even the winners saw worst drops of -8.3% to -20.6%. Today most resembles on the numbers, with oil up, a stretched dollar, a market correction and an industry down about 8.5% over three months, but today's VIX of 28 and yields near 5% argue for less confidence, and is the tail to respect. These are industry-level results, so…

episodes.then: In March 2025 the S&P 500 was in a tariff-driven correction, with growth fears building ahead of the April 2 'Liberation Day' announcement. Entertainment shares had fallen about 11.5% over three months, even though the industry had been outperforming the S&P 500 over six months.
episodes.after: The April tariff shock was followed by a sharp rebound. The industry returned +10.2% after 1 month, +35.1% after 3 months, +30.2% after 6 months and +24.6% after 12 months, against +10.7%, +19.8% and +18.5% for the S&P 500 over 3, 6 and 12 months. The worst drop along the way was -8.3%, so the dip was shallow and recovered quickly.
episodes.different: Today the industry has lagged the S&P 500 by 3.2pp over six months, whereas then it led by 7.6pp. VIX is higher at 28 against 22, and near-5% yields are a live constraint, so there is less of a clear shock-then-relief setup. This cuts against repeating the same outcome.
episodes.lesson: Washed-out sentiment can reverse fast

episodes.then: In May 2023 markets were digesting the regional-bank failures and the debt-ceiling standoff, while an AI-led rally kept the S&P 500 near its highs. The Hollywood writers' strike began that month, and the entertainment group was lagging the S&P 500.
episodes.after: The industry gained +7.2% after 1 month, +4% after 3 months and +6.8% after 6 months, trailing the S&P 500's +6.5%, +8.3% and +9.6% over the same horizons. It then caught up to +24.3% at 12 months against +28% for the S&P 500. The worst drop within six months was -16.2%, so holders had to sit through a deep drawdown (I am not certain of the exact driver) before the gain came.
episodes.different: The S&P 500 was only 1.5% below its high then, and VIX was 18. Today the market is 5.9% off its high with VIX at 28, which means more stress but also more already priced in.
episodes.lesson: Lagging groups can still gain, with drawdowns

episodes.then: In November 2021 the Fed was starting to taper amid rising inflation, and the Omicron variant appeared at the end of the month. Streaming and media shares had already rolled over, with the industry 20% below its 12-month high and 18.8pp behind the S&P 500 over six months.
episodes.after: This was the bad outcome. The industry returned -0.4% after 1 month, -19.4% after 3 months, -42.2% after 6 months and -45.8% after 12 months, with a worst drop of -48%. The S&P 500 fell only -3.5%, -9.5% and -9.2% over 3, 6 and 12 months. The 2022 rate-hike cycle and the streaming-growth reset drove the de-rating.
episodes.different: Today the industry's P/E sits at the 24th percentile, against the 46th then, and the industry is less stretched, trading only 3.2% below its 200-day average against 11.4% then. That makes a repeat of this collapse less likely, though higher yields and a high VIX are still present.
episodes.lesson: Expensive growth can de-rate brutally

episodes.then: In October 2018 equities sold off on Fed tightening and trade-war worries, with the Q4 slide still ahead. The industry was 6.7% down over three months, though it was still up 23% over twelve.
episodes.after: The industry returned -1.8% after 1 month and +4% after 3 months, then +17.2% after 6 months and +4.2% after 12 months. The S&P 500 gained +9.3% and +15.4% over 6 and 12 months. The worst drop within six months was -20.6%, consistent with the late-2018 low, and the Fed's shift toward patience helped the recovery.
episodes.different: The industry then had a 67th-percentile P/E, so valuation was a headwind, whereas today it is cheap at the 24th. Today's policy backdrop is less clearly easing, since yields are near 5%, which cuts against the same relief.
episodes.lesson: Drawdown first, relief after

episodes.then: In July 2012 the euro-area crisis was at a peak, just before Draghi's 'whatever it takes' pledge later that month. The industry was cheap at the 14th percentile of its own history and 10.3% below its 12-month high.
episodes.after: The industry returned +5.3% after 1 month, +8.9% after 3 months, +33.9% after 6 months and +80.3% after 12 months, against +11.2% and +26.9% for the S&P 500 over 6 and 12 months. The worst drop was only -6.7%. Cheap valuation plus easing macro fear produced the strongest result of the five.
episodes.different: Then, oil was falling and Treasuries were rallying (IEF +3.6%), which is a growth-scare backdrop that eased policy. Today oil is up 14.8% and Treasuries are falling, an inflationary backdrop that gives less room for policy relief.
episodes.lesson: Cheap plus fear paid off

hist.read: The base rates lean positive: median returns of +2.7% at 1M, +5.4% at 3M, +11.4% at 6M and +19.5% at 12M, with the industry up in 5 of 5 episodes at 3M and 6M and 4 of 5 at 12M. Beating the S&P 500 is closer to a coin flip at 3M and 6M (50% and 55%), and these are only five episodes, so I would give them moderate weight. The drawdowns were large in (-31.3%) and (-22.8%), so volatility could come first. Today differs from the best outcomes in rising yields and oil, a higher VIX and a lagging industry, which argues for staged entries. Today most resembles: a similar yield and dollar backdrop, S&P weakness and an industry 3M return of -3.2% versus -3.3%.

episodes.then: March 2025 was a tariff-driven selloff. Equities were correcting ahead of the April 'Liberation Day' announcement, growth fears were rising and the dollar had been strong. Retailers were hit by tariff and consumer worries.
episodes.after: The industry rose 13.8% in 1M, 15.8% in 3M and 13.2% in 6M after the April tariff lows and the subsequent rebound, then slipped to -1.8% at 12M. The S&P 500 was -0.9% at 1M but gained 10.7% at 3M, 19.8% at 6M and 18.5% at 12M. The worst drop within 6 months was only -5.6%.
episodes.different: Today's VIX is 28 against 22 then, and the industry is lagging the S&P 500 by 8.7pp rather than leading it. The valuation is also cheaper at the 8th percentile versus the 18th. This cuts both ways: more stress, but more room for a rebound.
episodes.lesson: Tariff-scare lows can reverse sharply

episodes.then: August 2015 was the China devaluation and flash-crash selloff, with the VIX spiking and oil falling. Markets feared a global slowdown while the Fed debated its first hike.
episodes.after: The industry fell 2.6% in 1M, then gained 16.1% at 3M, but only 1% at 6M, before reaching +21.9% at 12M. The S&P 500 returned -2.6% at 1M, +6.1% at 3M, +1.8% at 6M and +12.7% at 12M. The worst drop within 6 months was -31.3%, so the path was very rough, with a second leg down in early 2016.
episodes.different: The industry then was strongly outperforming the S&P 500 (+14.7pp) and oil was falling, while today it lags and oil is up 14.8%. The oil move today is an inflation headwind where lower oil then was a tailwind.
episodes.lesson: Rebounds can be interrupted by a retest

episodes.then: July 2010 followed the spring flash crash and the European debt scare, with fears of a double-dip recession. The Fed was heading toward QE2 and Treasury yields were falling.
episodes.after: The industry fell 0.5% in 1M, then rose 26.8% at 3M, 29.5% at 6M and 49.8% at 12M. The S&P 500 gained 7.9%, 17.1% and 19.6% over 3M, 6M and 12M. The worst drop within 6 months was only -6.1%, as QE2 expectations drove a broad recovery in consumer cyclicals.
episodes.different: Yields then were falling, with IEF +8%, and the Fed was easing. Today yields are rising (IEF -0.8%) and the dollar is strong, so there is no easing tailwind. This cuts against a repeat.
episodes.lesson: Policy easing fueled the rebound

episodes.then: October 2018 saw a sharp equity selloff on Fed tightening worries, trade-war tariffs and rising yields. The market slid toward its December low and retailers sold off hard.
episodes.after: The industry gained 4.3% at 1M, 1.1% at 3M, 17.3% at 6M and 8% at 12M. The S&P 500 gained 1.9%, 1.1%, 9.3% and 15.4%. The worst drop within 6 months was -22.8%, reflecting the December 2018 low before the Fed pivot rally in early 2019.
episodes.different: The valuation then sat at the 67th percentile, but today it is at the 8th. Today's cheapness gives a better cushion, although the VIX is higher at 28.
episodes.lesson: Deep dips can come before the rebound

episodes.then: October 2014 was a brief swoon, with oil starting to collapse and the dollar surging. The S&P 500 was at its high, so the weakness was specific to the industry and not part of a broad selloff.
episodes.after: The industry gained 5% at 1M, 3.3% at 3M, 14.2% at 6M and 32.8% at 12M. The S&P 500 gained 2.7%, 2.1%, 4.6% and 6.4%. The worst drop within 6 months was -14.9%. Cheap oil boosted consumers.
episodes.different: Then the VIX was 14 and the S&P 500 was at its high, with oil falling. Today there is broad market stress and oil is rising, which cuts against it.
episodes.lesson: Cheap valuations and falling oil helped retailers

supports: AMZN fundamentals are strong: Q3 revenue +12%, record 13.9% operating margin, AWS +39.3% and a $578B backlog.
Valuation has de-rated to 19.9x P/E versus a 32.4x 5Y median while TTM net income grew 32.5%, leaving room for a re-rating.
Defensive and growth pockets: ORLY comps +7.2% with pro above 10%, MELI revenue +50%, SE GMV +28%.
risks: Fed hike risk in December with CPI 3.7%, core PCE 3.10% and PPI 1.30% keeps long yields near 5% and multiples compressed.
AI-capex and AI-debt stress: AMZN's FCF margin is -0.3% with 2026 capex of about $220B, while the Nasdaq-100 is in correction.
The consumer is thinning: control-group sales +0.2%, payrolls 29K, wages 3.0% against 3.7% inflation, Michigan sentiment 48.0, and ORLY DIY transactions and AZO DIY are weak.

moves.label: US nonfarm payrolls
moves.move: Nonfarm payrolls fell to 29K from 133K (August revised down from 162K) against a 90K consensus.
moves.driver: Weak September labor demand; wages rose only 0.1% m/m. El-Erian said demand is 'flashing yellow'. Later JOLTS openings rose 333K and claims stayed near 194K.
moves.so_what: Cooler hiring weakens discretionary and low-income traffic (CASY, FIVE, TSCO) but reduces the odds of a December hike if it persists, which would help multiples.
moves.situation: US labor market firms while consumers remain cash-strapped

moves.label: US GDP growth
moves.move: Q3 GDP rose 3.4% annualised against 3.2% consensus and 2.2% in Q2.
moves.driver: Zacks called the economy 'heating up', alongside PCE inflation of 3.6% y/y and core PCE of 3.1%. Strong growth with high inflation raises December hike risk.
moves.so_what: Healthy nominal demand supports revenue, but it sustains the rate floor that weighs on the group's de-rated multiples.
moves.situation: US labor market firms while consumers remain cash-strapped

moves.label: US PPI
moves.move: PPI jumped to 1.30% from 0.50%, against 0.50% consensus.
moves.driver: No coverage of the release was found. The likely cause (estimate) is the Gulf energy shock, with Brent about $105 and diesel, freight and resin costs rising.
moves.so_what: Input-cost pressure hits goods retailers' gross margins (WSM, BBY, FIVE, DKS) before they can pass it through.
moves.situation: Iran war and Gulf energy shock

moves.label: VIX
moves.move: VIX rose 36.1% in a month to 20.83.
moves.driver: The AI capex and AI-debt sell-off: the Nasdaq-100 is about 10% below its 6 Oct record, fell 6.66% in October, and the biggest AI stocks lost about $5T. Blackstone's Gray warned on 3 Nov that lenders are over-exposed.
moves.so_what: AMZN's multiple and cap-weighted performance are directly exposed, though 21 is elevated rather than panic.
moves.situation: AI capex sell-off and AI-debt stress hit risk appetite and the data-center demand story

moves.label: US retail sales ex gas/autos
moves.move: Retail sales ex gas/autos rose 0.2% against 1.1% prior.
moves.driver: The headline beat came from gasoline, with Brent about $105-115 in the Iran war. Zacks stressed resilience, but the control group shows real demand slowing.
moves.so_what: Underlying discretionary volumes are fading, which favors non-discretionary auto parts (ORLY, AZO) over big-ticket and low-income formats.
moves.situation: Iran war and Gulf energy shock

moves.label: US import prices
moves.move: Import prices rose 1.1% against 0.8% consensus and 0.5% prior.
moves.driver: No article explained the release. The likely driver (estimate) is energy after the Hormuz disruption, plus tariffs and FX.
moves.so_what: Higher landed costs squeeze import-heavy retailers' margins and keep CPI and Fed hike pricing elevated.
moves.situation: Iran war and Gulf energy shock

moves.label: Conference Board confidence
moves.move: Conference Board confidence rose to 91.7 from 84.2 against an 81.0 consensus.
moves.driver: No news coverage of the move was found. It likely reflects labor-market weighting (claims near 194K, JOLTS 7.52M) versus Michigan's 48.0, which weights inflation.
moves.so_what: Job security supports spending intent, but the gap with Michigan means that demand is uneven and price-sensitive.
moves.situation: US labor market firms while consumers remain cash-strapped

moves.label: US retail sales MoM
moves.move: September retail sales rose 0.8% m/m against a 0.3% consensus, down from 1.3%.
moves.driver: Zacks said spending remained resilient, but the mix is fuel prices from the Iran war; ex-autos was +0.9% and ex-gas/autos only +0.2%.
moves.so_what: The headline overstates store demand, so retail volumes are weaker than nominal sales imply.
moves.situation: Iran war and Gulf energy shock

scenarios.outcome: The dollar is modestly softer but choppy, and the euro stays pressured by France. Translation is a small, uneven tailwind for PM, BTI, MDLZ, BUD, ABEV and DEO. EM-currency politics (BRL, MXN) decide who really benefits.

scenarios.name: Escalation
scenarios.trigger: The debasement trade extends: weak jobs data, a dovish Fed shift, or deficit worries from a divided Congress push the dollar index well below 100 (estimate), with gold and bitcoin…
scenarios.outcome: Broad dollar weakness lifts reported USD revenue and EPS for foreign-revenue staples by a few percent. Lower yields help dividend-yield names. Commodities priced in USD (cocoa, sugar, aluminum, oil) rise in USD terms.

scenarios.name: De-escalation
scenarios.trigger: Strategists' 'resilience' call is proven right: a December Fed hike, a hot October jobs report, or an Iran flare-up lifting oil and yields sends the dollar back above recent highs.
scenarios.outcome: Translation tailwinds fade and the euro stays near its 17-month low. Foreign-revenue names lose some relative advantage, while US-centric names and the dollar-exposed cost base are neutral to better.

reads.val: The industry ranks last of 20 peers on P/E, but ex-top-three it trades at 9.8x forward, so the premium sits almost entirely in TSLA. The reverse DCF on NTM earnings needs 20% annual growth for a decade, against 16.8% consensus and 90-day estimates down 3.4%.

hist.read: The base rates lean cautious: median 1M -1.8% (up 4 of 5 episodes), 3M -1.8%, 6M +3.8% and 12M -3%, with only a 5% chance of beating the S&P 500 over 12M. The episodes split into early bounces and deeper crashes, so expect big swings in both directions and worst drops of -16% to -70% within 6M. is the statistically closest, but matches today's rich valuation and high VIX better, and the 80th-percentile P/E argues against relying on a-style rebound. Together with the poor 12M record, this supports staying underweight the cap-weighted group and favoring earnings quality, but with a position size that allows for a sharp short-term bounce.

episodes.then: March 2025 was a tariff-scare correction. The S&P 500 was falling, and autos were hit by trade-war fears and the slump in Tesla shares amid the backlash over Musk's political role.
episodes.after: The group rebounded sharply from the washed-out level: +23.7% in 1M, +19.9% in 3M, +31.2% in 6M and +28.2% in 12M, against the S&P 500's +18.5% over 12M. The worst drop along the way was still -16.2% in the first 6 months. The rebound followed a very large prior drawdown (3M -26.5%).
episodes.different: Today the group is less oversold (3M -12.2% vs -26.5%, 200-day gap -9.4% vs -21.3%) but pricier (P/E 80th vs 68th percentile) and the VIX is higher. That leaves less rebound fuel and more valuation risk, which cuts against the bounce.
episodes.lesson: Deep washouts can snap back hard, but today's is shallower

episodes.then: November 2021 was the peak of the EV and growth-stock mania, just before the Fed turned hawkish on inflation and the Omicron variant appeared. Valuations were stretched and the VIX was elevated at 27.
episodes.after: This was the disaster path: -9% in 1M, -51.6% in 3M, -65.5% in 6M and -74.4% in 12M, with a worst drop of -69.5%. The S&P 500 fell only 9.2% over 12M, so the group lagged badly. The cause is likely the unwinding of long-duration growth and EV names as rates rose, but I am not certain of the details of this index.
episodes.different: Today's yields are already higher and the group is 22.5% below its high rather than 40.2%, so some of the excess has been wrung out. Valuation is still stretched, and the political risk is new.
episodes.lesson: Stretched valuation plus tightening is the worst combination

episodes.then: May 2012 brought the euro-zone crisis flare-up around Greece and a roughly 7% S&P 500 pullback. The US auto recovery was under way, but the group had sold off hard (3M -28.3%).
episodes.after: A 1M bounce of +16.5% faded: 3M -8%, 6M -8.6% and 12M +2.1%, while the S&P 500 rose 27.2% over 12M. The worst drop within 6M was -36.4%. The group missed the broad market's rally, and I am not sure of the specific company drivers.
episodes.different: Then, yields were falling and oil collapsed (-15.9%). Today yields are rising, oil is up and the dollar is strong, a tougher macro mix for a cyclical group.
episodes.lesson: Early bounce, then lagging the market

episodes.then: May 2023 followed the March regional-bank stress and came amid a debt-ceiling standoff and an AI-led, narrow market rally. Autos were far off their highs (12M -36.6%) with a low VIX of 18.
episodes.after: The group rallied +22.7% in 1M, +33% in 3M and +16.6% in 6M, then gave it back to -4% over 12M while the S&P 500 gained 28%. The worst drop in the first 6M was -26.3%. The gains came early and did not last.
episodes.different: Then, valuation was moderate (44th percentile) and the VIX calm. Today the group is expensive (80th percentile) with a VIX of 28, so there is less cushion.
episodes.lesson: Rallies were sharp but did not hold

episodes.then: August 2013 saw the Fed's taper talk push Treasury yields up, plus Syria tensions. The group had fallen sharply over 3M (-23.3%) while the S&P 500 was near highs with a low VIX of 17.
episodes.after: The group did little in 1M (+0.8%), then fell: 3M -28.2%, 6M -13.1% and 12M -73.9%, with a worst drop of -45.5%. The S&P 500 rose 25% over 12M. I am not sure what drove such a steep fall in this index.
episodes.different: Then, the market was calm and strong (S&P 500 6M +9%) and the group was roughly in line with it. Today the market is weaker and the industry trails it by 13pp, which means more systemic stress.
episodes.lesson: A weak start can be followed by a deep fall

hist.read: The five episodes split: and rebounded 20% or more over 6M, gained modestly, and and suffered early drops. Base rates lean positive at longer horizons, with 80% up at 6M, a median of +3.4% and 90% up at 12M. At 1M and 3M they are only mildly positive and the group has beaten the S&P 500 in only 35 to 45% of cases, so the edge is thin. Weight on this is moderate, because rising credit stress and VIX at 28 look more like, which also had an oil spike and a stronger dollar. Today most resembles, so I would expect a choppy 1M to 3M and a better 6M to 12M, without a clear call to outperform.

episodes.then: In February 2022 Russia invaded Ukraine, oil spiked, and the Fed was about to start hiking, so yields rose and growth stocks sold off. Restaurants were already lagging the S&P 500 on food and wage inflation worries.
episodes.after: The industry fell 1.7% in 1M, 10.7% in 3M and 7.4% in 6M, and was still down 2.9% at 12M. The S&P 500 bounced 6% in 1M but then fell 4.6% by 3M, 7.1% by 6M and 8.1% by 12M. The industry's worst drop in the 6 months after was 18.5%, as rate hikes and inflation weighed on markets.
episodes.different: Back then the industry's P/E was at the 75th percentile, versus 44th today, so there was more valuation risk then. Today's industry is already 26.7% below its high, versus 14.4% then, which cuts toward a bit less downside.
episodes.lesson: Inflation and rate shock hurt both industry and market

episodes.then: In October 2016 markets were calm ahead of the US election, and yields were starting to rise. Restaurants were in a soft patch of slowing same-store sales and were lagging the market.
episodes.after: The industry gained 7.3% in 1M, 6.3% in 3M and 20.1% in 6M, and was up 20.2% at 12M. It trailed the S&P 500, which gained 13.4% in 6M and 23.4% in 12M. The worst 6-month drop was only 3.9%, helped by the post-election reflation rally.
episodes.different: VIX was 17 then versus 28 now, and credit spreads were tightening, whereas today's credit stress is rising. That cuts against a repeat.
episodes.lesson: Calm macro let the laggard rebound

episodes.then: In June 2018 the Fed was tightening and trade-war tariffs were escalating, while oil had rallied strongly. Restaurants were lagging a market that was close to its highs.
episodes.after: The industry slipped 0.4% in 1M, then gained 5.5% in 3M and 3.8% in 6M, and was up 26.4% at 12M. The S&P 500 gained 3.7% in 1M and 7.7% in 3M but fell 6.9% in 6M, which covers the Q4 2018 selloff. The industry's worst drop in the 6 months after was 11.1%.
episodes.different: VIX was 16 then, versus 28 today, so the market was less stressed and the S&P 500 sat only 4.5% below its high. Today's higher volatility cuts toward a rougher path.
episodes.lesson: Defensive laggard held up in a later selloff

episodes.then: In October 2012 the economy was in a slow recovery, with the Fed running QE3 and the US election and fiscal cliff approaching. Restaurants lagged the market and traded at a very low point in their own valuation history (10th percentile).
episodes.after: The industry gained 2.5% in 1M, 10.8% in 3M and 20.2% in 6M, and was up 27.1% at 12M, matching the S&P 500 at 27.1%. The worst 6-month drop was only 5%. Easy money and a strengthening market lifted the group.
episodes.different: The 10th-percentile P/E was a deep valuation cushion, while today's is 44th. Yields were also falling then and oil was down, whereas both are rising now. That cuts against a repeat.
episodes.lesson: Cheap valuation plus easy money drove a rebound

episodes.then: In February 2020 the COVID-19 outbreak was spreading beyond China and the market was just starting to crack, with VIX at 40. Restaurants were already lagging and went on to be among the hardest hit by lockdowns.
episodes.after: The industry fell 25.1% in 1M and 13% in 3M, then was down 2.9% at 6M and up 8% at 12M. The S&P 500 fell 11.2% in 1M but was up 18.8% at 6M and 34% at 12M. The worst 6-month drop was 39.5%, as dine-in closures hit the group before stimulus and reopening.
episodes.different: Today has no pandemic shock, and the stress is milder, with VIX at 28 versus 40. The downside tail is therefore far smaller, though today's P/E is distorted by pandemic-era earnings.
episodes.lesson: A one-off shock, not a typical setup

reads.val: Trailing P/E of 18.3x is at the 14th percentile of five years but the 43rd on the long history. The reverse DCF's 6.5% FCF growth roughly matches 7.7% consensus EPS growth, so the market prices about consensus. The 10.5x forward P/E is distorted by TCOM's 1.6x;

hist.read: The five episodes are split: and rallied strongly, while, and ended lower at 12M. The base rates are only mildly positive, with medians of +0.6% at 1M, +6.4% at 3M, +4.6% at 6M and +11.3% at 12M. The middle ranges are very wide (6M -4.9% to +18.6%), and the industry beat the S&P 500 only 40-45% of the time. Taken together, they suggest modest upside at 3M, roughly coin-flip odds at 6M and 12M, and a real risk of a deeper drawdown (the worst 6M drops were -57% in and -29.6% in). Today most resembles by the code's ranking, but the industry setup of rising oil, a laggard sector and a deep drawdown also echoes. With so few episodes and real differences in each, I would give them modest weight.…

episodes.then: March 2025 was a tariff-driven risk-off month. Growth fears and policy uncertainty hit equities ahead of the April 2 'Liberation Day' announcement, and travel stocks sold off on worries about consumer and cross-border demand.
episodes.after: The S&P 500 fell sharply in early April, but the industry then rebounded strongly: +10% after 1M, +39% after 3M, +45.8% after 6M and +39.7% after 12M. The worst drop in the next 6 months was only -8.9%, and the S&P 500 also recovered, up 18.5% at 12M. This looks like a washout followed by relief as tariff fears eased and travel demand held up.
episodes.different: Today's VIX (28 vs 22) and oil gain (+14.8% vs +10.6%) are higher, and the industry is further below its 12-month high (-22% vs -17.6%) and lags the S&P 500 (-6.5pp vs +4.2pp). Today the industry is already the laggard, and that cuts both ways, since it could mean more room to rebound or a…
episodes.lesson: Washouts can reverse sharply when the shock fades

episodes.then: January 2022 was the Fed's hawkish pivot, with rate-hike expectations surging, growth stocks derating and Omicron still disrupting travel. Oil was climbing, and Russia invaded Ukraine the following month, pushing energy prices higher still.
episodes.after: The industry fell hard: -5% after 1M, -11.5% after 3M, -44.6% after 6M and -39% after 12M, with a worst drop of -57% in the next 6 months. The S&P 500 also fell, by -8.6% at 6M and -7.2% at 12M, so the industry fell much more. I'm not certain of the exact industry-specific drivers, but tightening policy, high oil and a growth-stock derating plausibly all contributed.
episodes.different: Today's industry valuation is lower (43rd percentile vs 77th), so there is less multiple compression to unwind. Today's yields are not rising as they were then (IEF -0.8% vs -3.9%), and the S&P 500 is falling (-2.6% vs +3.3%), so the macro picture is different. Both differences cut in favour of…
episodes.lesson: High oil plus a stretched sector can mean deep drawdowns

episodes.then: October 2018 was the start of the Q4 selloff, driven by Fed tightening, US-China trade war worries and a stronger dollar. The S&P 500 bottomed on Christmas Eve, and travel stocks were already lagging.
episodes.after: The industry went nowhere and then slipped: +2.4% after 1M, -0.2% after 3M, -1.7% after 6M and -9.2% after 12M. The worst drop in the next 6 months was -20%. The S&P 500 recovered strongly (+9.3% at 6M, +15.4% at 12M), so a market rebound did not rescue a laggard industry.
episodes.different: Oil was flat then (-0.1%) and is up sharply now (+14.8%), and the industry was cheap then (17th percentile) while today it is mid-range (43rd). Both differences cut against today.
episodes.lesson: A market rebound need not lift a laggard sector

episodes.then: August 2015 saw China's yuan devaluation and the August 24 flash crash, with the VIX spiking, global growth fears and oil near multi-year lows. The industry had held up better than the market going in.
episodes.after: The industry was choppy and ended flat to lower: -1.8% after 1M, +6.3% after 3M, -2.2% after 6M and -4% after 12M. The worst drop in the next 6 months was -29.6%, so the path was rough even though the S&P 500 ended up +12.7% at 12M. I'm not certain what drove the industry's later weakness.
episodes.different: The industry was a relative winner then (+9.8pp vs the S&P 500, only -8.2% from its high) and oil was falling. Today it is the reverse on both counts: the industry has been weak and oil is rising, which cuts against today.
episodes.lesson: Volatility spikes can still leave sectors in a choppy range

episodes.then: October 2012 came after the ECB's 'whatever it takes' turn and the Fed's QE3, ahead of the US election and the fiscal cliff. Oil was drifting lower and markets were recovering from the euro crisis scare.
episodes.after: The industry rallied strongly: +8.3% after 1M, +13.8% after 3M, +15.1% after 6M and +44.3% after 12M. The worst drop in the next 6 months was only -7.2%. Falling oil, easy policy and a recovering market backdrop all helped.
episodes.different: Falling oil (-19.9%) and easy central-bank policy then contrast with rising oil (+14.8%) and a higher VIX now. The industry was also much closer to its high then (-10.2% vs -22%). The macro tailwinds are absent today, which cuts against.
episodes.lesson: Easy policy and falling oil gave a strong tailwind

reads.risk: A beta of 0.64 understates exposure. The group moves -5.1% per +25bp on the 10-year and -2.4% per +10% in oil, so rates and the Iran war drive risk. Realised volatility is rising (33% over 20 days against 27% for the year), and the equal-weighted index's 2021 drawdown (-49%) remains unrecovered.

hist.read: Past analogs lean positive: the 20 closest months were up 65% at 1M, 80% at 3M and 6M, and 85% at 12M, with 6M medians near +9%. But the five episodes are mixed. was a clear failure (-13.8% at 6M), lagged at 1M and 3M, and saw drawdowns up to -16.2% along the way. The base rates also show the industry beating the S&P 500 only 40% of the time at 6M and 20% at 12M, so any rebound would be absolute rather than relative. Today most resembles, given the stress, the oil and dollar moves, and the deep industry lag, but the higher valuation and the Lowe's guidance cut justify modest weight, which fits the team's neutral-to-underweight stance into the HD/LOW reports.

episodes.then: In March 2025 US stocks were in a tariff-driven correction. Growth worries and policy uncertainty were rising ahead of the April tariff announcements, and housing-linked stocks were weak under high mortgage rates.
episodes.after: The industry rose 6.2% in 1M, 4.9% in 3M, 16.2% in 6M and 16.4% in 12M, trailing the S&P 500's 19.8% over 6M and 18.5% over 12M. The 6M worst drawdown was -9.5%, so the gain came after a bumpy stretch. The recovery fits the market rebounding from the tariff scare, though I'm not certain of every driver for this industry.
episodes.different: Today's VIX is 28 versus 22, the industry is 27.2% below its 12-month high versus 17.9%, and the P/E percentile is lower. That cuts both ways: deeper washout, but the industry is still falling.
episodes.lesson: Washed-out sector rebounded with the market

episodes.then: In October 2018 stocks sold off sharply on rising Treasury yields, Fed tightening worries and trade-war fears. Housing-related stocks were already weak as mortgage rates climbed.
episodes.after: The industry gained 1% in 1M, 2% in 3M, 9.7% in 6M and 21.2% in 12M, versus the S&P 500's 9.3% over 6M and 15.4% over 12M. The worst 6M drop was -16.2%, so the path was rough. The market bottomed in December 2018 and the Fed pivoted in early 2019, but I'm less sure of the sector-specific details.
episodes.different: Today's 2-year yield is falling, and oil is up 14.8% where it was flat then. The valuation percentile is higher today (60th vs 36th), which leaves less cheapness cushion.
episodes.lesson: Dips can come first, then a rebound

episodes.then: In February 2022 Russia invaded Ukraine, oil spiked and the Fed was about to start its hiking cycle. Growth stocks were already falling and housing-linked names were sliding on rising mortgage rates.
episodes.after: The industry fell 0.4% in 1M, 9% in 3M, 13.8% in 6M and 21.1% in 12M, versus the S&P 500's -7.1% over 6M and -8.1% over 12M. The worst 6M drop was -26.6%, the deepest of the five. Tightening and falling housing demand explain the weakness, though I'm unsure of specific company details.
episodes.different: Today the 2-year yield is falling rather than rising ahead of a hiking cycle, which is better for housing. The industry is also further below its 12-month high and its 200-day average, so some of the damage is already done.
episodes.lesson: Rate-hike shocks hit housing hardest

episodes.then: In October 2016 markets were calm ahead of the US election, and bond yields were beginning to rise. Home improvement stocks had lagged as housing worries and rate concerns weighed on the sector.
episodes.after: The industry rose 5.7% in 1M, 10.3% in 3M, 24.2% in 6M and 24% in 12M, versus the S&P 500's 13.4% over 6M and 23.4% over 12M. The worst 6M drop was only -3.6%. The post-election reflation rally and a solid housing market likely helped, though I'm not sure of the full details.
episodes.different: The VIX was 17 then versus 28 today, and the S&P 500 was only 2.5% below its high versus 5.9% now. Today's backdrop is more stressed, and the industry gap to the S&P 500 is smaller (-8.2pp vs -17.6pp).
episodes.lesson: Big laggards can snap back sharply

episodes.then: In February 2023 markets were digesting sticky inflation and the Fed's continued hikes, with banking stress arriving the next month. Housing-linked stocks were recovering from the 2022 slump but remained far below their highs.
episodes.after: The industry fell 5.2% in 1M and 3.4% in 3M, then gained 6.5% over 6M and 18.1% over 12M, versus the S&P 500's 14.2% over 6M and 30.2% over 12M. The worst 6M drop was -7.8%. The lag fits the bank scare and higher-for-longer rates, though I'm unsure of the precise sector drivers.
episodes.different: The industry P/E percentile was 19th then versus 60th today, so valuation support is weaker now. The dollar was weaker then, versus +4.6% today.
episodes.lesson: Slow start, later gains, lagged market

debates.q: Will the Democratic Congress deliver housing policy that moves turnover?
debates.bull: The sweep revived hopes for targeted affordability measures and lower borrowing costs, and housing stocks rallied 8% or more. Any turnover incentive would help the most rate-sensitive retailers most.
debates.bear: No measure has been proposed, and the early Democratic focus is on reining in AI. Legislation must still clear the rest of Washington, and the effect on closings and remodels would lag into 2027-28. Rates, set by the Fed, matter more.

hist.read: Four of the five episodes were positive at 12M, and the base rates are favorable: 80% up at 3M and 6M and 90% at 12M, against 61%, 70% and 81% for all months. But the group beat the S&P 500 only 30% of the time at 12M, and drawdowns of 6.5% to 10.1% occurred in four of the five episodes, so a dip is plausible within 1-3 months. Today's 97th-percentile P/E, VIX of 28 and a 15.8% drop from the high are less favorable than most of these analogs, so I would weight them modestly. Today most resembles (high VIX, equities weak, defensive rotation) and (tariff-style and rate stress), with as the cautionary case; this supports market weight without chasing.

episodes.then: March 2018 brought the first Trump tariff announcements on steel and aluminum and a Fed hike, and the S&P 500 had just had its February volatility shock. Oil was rising, and staples-type groups such as beverages were lagging as yields climbed.
episodes.after: The industry slipped 2.6% in 1M and 1.3% in 3M, with a worst drawdown of 8.1% in the first six months. It then recovered to +12.5% at 6M and +15.9% at 12M, ahead of the S&P 500's +10.7% at 12M. I am not sure of the exact drivers, but defensive groups appear to have regained favor late in 2018 as markets sold off.
episodes.different: Today's VIX is 28 against 20 then, and the dollar is up 4.6% against down 2.3%. The industry P/E is at the 97th percentile against the 88th, so there is less valuation cushion; that cuts against a repeat.
episodes.lesson: Early dip, then defensive rebound

episodes.then: February 2021 had the vaccine rollout, a reflation trade, and rising Treasury yields and oil. Growth and defensive stocks were wobbling, and beverages lagged cyclicals.
episodes.after: The industry rose 9.7% in 1M and 13.2% in 3M, then 14.8% at 6M and 22.1% at 12M, ahead of the S&P 500's +16.6% at 12M. The worst drop was only 3.4%. The rebound likely came from the reopening and from a depressed starting valuation, but that is my inference.
episodes.different: The industry P/E was at the 72nd percentile then and is at the 97th now, so there is far less valuation support. Credit was also strengthening then (+8.5pp), while today it is flat (-0.1pp). Both cut against a repeat.
episodes.lesson: Washed-out starts rebound hardest when cheap

episodes.then: October 2016 came just before the US election, with Treasury yields starting to rise and the dollar strong. Staples were being sold as bond proxies.
episodes.after: The industry fell 6.5% in 1M and 3.9% in 3M, with a worst drop of 8.1%, then recovered to +2.8% at 6M and +6.4% at 12M. The S&P 500 gained 23.4% at 12M, so the industry lagged badly. The election-driven rotation into cyclicals, financials and tax-cut beneficiaries likely drove that.
episodes.different: Today's VIX is 28 against 17, and the S&P 500 is falling rather than steady, so the market backdrop is more stressed. The industry's valuation is also far higher now (97th pct against 52nd). The risk of a further drop looks greater today.
episodes.lesson: Bond-proxy selling can persist

episodes.then: November 2021 saw inflation worries, a hawkish Fed turn toward tapering, and the Omicron variant emerging. The VIX was high at 27, and the S&P 500 was near highs.
episodes.after: The industry rose 10.1% in 1M, 10.3% in 3M, 9.5% at 6M and 13.8% at 12M, with a worst drop of 10.1%. The S&P 500 fell 9.5% at 6M and 9.2% at 12M as rates rose and growth stocks sold off. Beverages held up as defensives while the market fell.
episodes.different: The S&P 500 was just 3% off its high then and is 5.9% off now, with the industry's 12-month drawdown larger today (-15.8% against -7.4%). Valuation is also much higher (97th percentile against 48th). Both make the defensive bid less certain.
episodes.lesson: Defensive bid when equities fell

episodes.then: February 2023 had sticky inflation, renewed Fed hike expectations and bond yields rising again. Beverages were consolidating after a defensive 2022.
episodes.after: The industry gained 3.8% in 1M, 2.8% in 3M, 4.4% at 6M and 5% at 12M, with a worst drop of 6.5%. The S&P 500 gained 30.2% at 12M on the AI rally, so the industry lagged sharply. Steady but unspectacular.
episodes.different: Then the market was rising on the AI theme. Today that trade is breaking, with tech having its worst day since 2020, so the relative picture could flip. The industry's valuation is also higher now.
episodes.lesson: Positive but lagging in a risk-on market

rules.body: SHCP/SAT — Mexico Ministry of Finance and Public Credit / Tax Administration Ser

rules.name: New IEPS per-liter excise on beverages with non-caloric sweeteners

rules.bottom_line: Taxing zero-sugar removes Mexico's untaxed diet alternative, structurally pressuring KOF and FMX Mexican volumes; diversified bottlers and concentrate owners can absorb it, so favor geographic diversification over Mexico

hist.read: The five episodes split: 3 of 5 were up at 1M, 3M and 6M, and 4 of 5 at 12M, while the base rates lean positive in absolute terms (75% up at 3M and 6M, median +3.8% at 6M and +4.4% at 12M). The industry beat the S&P 500 only 15 to 40% of the time, which supports the team's modest relative underweight but not an outright bearish call. The worst outcomes, and, came with rich valuations or rate fears, and today has some of both, though with a smaller valuation excess and better relative strength than. Today most resembles on VIX, drawdown and rates, but deserves real weight, so a tactical neutral stance fits better than a strongly negative one.

episodes.then: In February 2022 Russia invaded Ukraine, oil spiked, and the Fed was preparing its first hike as inflation ran hot. Equities were in a growth-led correction, and staples were pressured by input-cost inflation despite their defensive reputation.
episodes.after: The industry fell 2.4% in 1M, 6.6% in 3M, 11.9% in 6M and 14.5% in 12M, with a worst drop of 16.4% inside six months. The S&P 500 bounced 6% in 1M but was down 8.1% at 12M as the Fed tightened aggressively, so the rich multiple and cost squeeze hurt household products.
episodes.different: Today the industry is slightly above its 200-day average and has beaten the S&P 500 by 8.2pp over 6 months, while in 2022 it lagged. The P/E percentile is also lower (68th vs 88th), which cuts toward less downside than then.
episodes.lesson: Rich multiple plus rate fears hurt staples

episodes.then: In March 2025 tariff fears and growth worries drove a sharp equity pullback, with the dollar firm and yields volatile. Defensive sectors like staples were favoured, and the industry was near its highs with a rich valuation.
episodes.after: The industry rose 3.4% in 1M, 6.3% in 3M, 7% in 6M and 8.9% in 12M, though it suffered a worst drop of 9.3% along the way. The S&P 500 gained 19.8% over 6M and 18.5% over 12M as the equity rebound outpaced the defensive industry.
episodes.different: Today the VIX is higher (28 vs 22), the Fed leans toward hikes, and the industry sits 12.3% below its high, not 2.7%. That cuts both ways: a deeper drawdown leaves more room to recover, but the policy backdrop is less friendly.
episodes.lesson: Defensives gained but lagged the rebound

episodes.then: In October 2018 equities sold off on rising rates, trade-war fears and a strong dollar, ahead of the December slide. The industry was already well off its high and valuations were low (28th percentile).
episodes.after: The industry rose 4.1% in 1M, 4.3% in 3M, 15.1% in 6M and 21% in 12M, with a worst drop of 9.6%. The S&P 500 gained 9.3% over 6M and 15.4% over 12M, and the industry's cheap valuation helped it outperform once the Fed turned more cautious.
episodes.different: Valuation is the key gap: today's P/E percentile is 68th against 28th then, so there is less cushion. The Fed leans toward hikes rather than a pivot, which cuts against a repeat.
episodes.lesson: Cheap defensives rallied on a Fed pivot

episodes.then: In May 2023 the debt-ceiling standoff and the regional-bank aftermath hung over markets, while an AI-led rally lifted a narrow group of tech stocks. Staples lagged as investors preferred growth, and the industry was well off its high.
episodes.after: The industry rose 3.5% in 1M and 0.6% in 3M, fell 5% over 6M, then recovered to +1.1% over 12M, with a worst drop of 13.5%. The S&P 500 rose 28% over 12M, so the industry badly trailed a risk-on market.
episodes.different: Today the market is under stress, with the VIX at 28 against 18 and the S&P 500 down 2.6% over 6M against +3.4% then. The industry is leading the S&P by 8.2pp rather than trailing, which cuts toward continued relative strength but also toward crowding risk.
episodes.lesson: Defensives lag when risk-on returns

episodes.then: In October 2016 markets were heading into the US election with bond yields beginning to rise. Staples were weak as investors rotated out of bond-proxy sectors.
episodes.after: The industry fell 6.1% in 1M and 3.2% in 3M, then recovered to +5.1% over 6M and +5.5% over 12M, with a worst drop of 7.3%. The S&P 500 rallied 23.4% over 12M, so the industry lagged heavily.
episodes.different: Today the VIX is much higher (28 vs 17) and the S&P 500 is falling rather than rising. The industry has outperformed rather than lagged, so the rotation risk is the reverse of then.

Near term the evidence is mixed: 1-month results ran from -4.2% to +14.3%, and 3-month from -9.5% to +16.6%. A 10-22% drawdown inside 6 months was common, so sizing matters more than direction. Given today's 91st-percentile valuation, higher VIX and flat momentum, I would give the positive base rates only modest weight. is…

episodes.then: In March 2025 tariff fears were driving an S&P 500 correction, and investors were rotating into defensives just before the April tariff announcements. Discount-store leaders such as WMT and COST were trading at very rich multiples as safe havens.
episodes.after: The industry rose 14.3% in the first month and 11.5% over 3 months, then 8.1% at 6 months and 21.5% at 12 months. The S&P 500 slipped 0.9% in month one but gained 19.8% over 6 months and 18.5% over 12 months, as the tariff scare faded and stocks recovered. The industry still suffered a worst drop of 15.8% within 6 months.
episodes.different: Then the industry had strong momentum (3 months +8.8%, +3.7% vs its 200-day average), while today it is flat and slightly below its 200-day average. Today VIX is higher and oil has risen, so the cushion is thinner and this cuts against a repeat.
episodes.lesson: Rich valuations survived a scare, but with a deep drawdown first

episodes.then: In July 2022 inflation was high, the Fed was hiking aggressively and stocks were in a bear-market rally. Big retailers were hit by margin pressure and inventory problems, and I recall profit warnings from Walmart and Target around then.
episodes.after: The industry fell 4.2% in month one, 9.5% over 3 months and 10.7% over 6 months, and was still down 3.4% at 12 months. The S&P 500 was down 1.9% at 6 months but rose 12.6% by 12 months. The worst drop within 6 months was 21.5%, the deepest of the five.
episodes.different: Then yields were rising sharply (IEF -5.9% vs -0.8% today), and the sector was less expensive (79th percentile vs 91st). Today's higher valuation raises the risk of a similar derating even with milder rate pressure.
episodes.lesson: Margin and inventory shocks hit a stretched group hard

episodes.then: October 2018 brought a sharp equity selloff on Fed tightening worries, trade-war tension and a strong dollar. The industry had run up strongly (12 months +27.3%) and was leading the market.
episodes.after: The industry gained 0.9% in month one, fell 5.6% at 3 months, then recovered to +7.6% at 6 months and +23% at 12 months. The S&P 500 gained 1.9%, 1.1%, 9.3% and 15.4% over the same horizons. The worst drop within 6 months was 19.6%, consistent with the late-2018 volatility.
episodes.different: Then the industry sat well above its 200-day average (+5.7%) at a mid-range valuation (59th percentile). Today it is below its average and at 91st percentile, so there is less trend support and more valuation risk.
episodes.lesson: Choppy for a quarter, then the trend resumed

episodes.then: August 2015 saw the China devaluation and a global selloff, with VIX at 28 as it is today. Oil was falling and the industry was roughly in line with the market.
episodes.after: The industry fell 1% in month one, then gained 10.8% at 3 months, 5.5% at 6 months and 10.7% at 12 months. The S&P 500 gained 6.1%, 1.8% and 12.7% over 3, 6 and 12 months. The worst drop within 6 months was 13.3%.
episodes.different: Then the sector was cheap (36th percentile) and oil and credit signals were different (oil -12.2%, high-yield spreads widening). Today it is expensive and oil is rising, so the starting point is less forgiving.
episodes.lesson: A volatility spike from a cheap base was a buying chance

episodes.then: September 2023 was the higher-for-longer rates scare, with long yields climbing, oil rising and the S&P 500 weakening. The industry was still near its highs and growing steadily.
episodes.after: The industry fell 1.6% in month one, then rose 16.6% over 3 months, 22.7% over 6 months and 36.6% over 12 months. The S&P 500 gained 11.6%, 22.2% and 34.8% over the same horizons as rate fears eased. The worst drop within 6 months was only 10.3%.
episodes.different: Then VIX was a calm 18 and the industry sat above its 200-day average (+5.1%). Today's VIX of 28 and weaker trend point to a rougher path.
episodes.lesson: Rate scares faded into a broad rally

episodes.then: August 2015 was the China devaluation and flash-crash selloff, with the VIX spiking and the S&P 500 sliding toward correction territory. Oil was weak, high-yield spreads were widening, and tobacco was acting as a defensive haven.
episodes.after: Tobacco rose +2.2% in 1M, +8.8% in 3M and +13.6% in 6M, ending +21.2% at 12M. That beat the S&P 500's +1.8% at 6M and +12.7% at 12M, so the defensive bid held through the recovery, though the worst drawdown was -7.3% over six months.
episodes.different: Then tobacco's P/E percentile was a middling 58th, whereas today it is 89th, so there is less valuation cushion. Oil is also up 14.8% today versus down 12.2% then, which cuts against a repeat.
episodes.lesson: Defensive bid can persist when valuation is not stretched

episodes.after: Tobacco fell -5.4% in 1M as the post-election reflation rally favored cyclicals, then recovered to +4.8% at 3M and +12.8% at 6M, but only +3.9% at 12M. The S&P 500 gained +13.4% at 6M and +23.4% at 12M, so tobacco badly lagged. The worst six-month drop was -7.9%.
episodes.different: Then the VIX was calm at 17 and credit spreads were tightening, while today the VIX is 28 and the market is under stress. That makes the defensive case stronger now, though tobacco's rich valuation matches then.
episodes.lesson: Rich valuation lagged a risk-on rebound

episodes.then: May 2012 was the peak of the euro-zone crisis scare, with Greek election worries, a falling oil price and a flight to Treasuries. Tobacco was holding up as a defensive and pulling back modestly from highs.
episodes.after: Tobacco gained +5.7% in 1M, +7.6% in 3M and +5.6% in 6M, finishing +8.6% at 12M. That was a positive but far smaller return than the S&P 500's +27.2% at 12M, and the worst six-month drop was -11.7%.
episodes.different: Then Treasuries had rallied (+5.6% at 6M) and oil was falling, whereas today yields are up and oil is rising. Today's backdrop is more inflationary and tobacco's P/E percentile is higher (89th versus 67th).
episodes.lesson: Positive but lagging when the market recovers

episodes.then: September 2014 saw a strong dollar, falling oil at the start of its collapse, and a calm market near its highs. Tobacco was drifting sideways and slightly below its 12-month high.
episodes.after: Tobacco was up +2.2% in 1M but only +0.2% in 3M and -3.2% in 6M, recovering to +9.5% at 12M. The S&P 500 gained +5.5% at 6M but slipped -0.8% at 12M, so tobacco ultimately beat it only at the 12-month mark. The worst six-month drop was -10.3%.
episodes.different: The VIX was 16 and the market was near its highs, with no stress. Today's higher VIX of 28 and a market already 5.9% off its high mean a different regime, with more of the defensive rotation already priced in.
episodes.lesson: Calm-market starts gave weak mid-term returns

episodes.then: January 2022 was the start of the Fed tightening cycle, with surging oil, a rising dollar and a growth-stock selloff. Tobacco was near its highs on a value rotation, with a low P/E percentile.
episodes.after: Tobacco rose +1% in 1M but fell -2.6% in 3M and -11.2% in 6M, ending -8.7% at 12M. The S&P 500 also fell (-8.6% at 6M, -7.2% at 12M), and the worst six-month drop was -21.2%, making it the one clearly bad outcome.
episodes.different: Then tobacco was cheap (31st percentile) and had just rallied 11.8% in 3M, whereas today it is expensive (89th) with flat momentum. Today's yields rising is a milder shock than the 2022 hiking cycle, but the valuation cushion is smaller.
episodes.lesson: Rate shock hurt even defensives

reads.perf: The cap-weighted group is +48% versus SPY over one year, with 76% breadth and +13.3% over three months. The Iran-war oil and refining spike drove the move rather than any re-rating. The index is 15.1% above its 200-day average but 4.8% below its 52-week high.
reads.risk: A beta of -0.52 and Jensen's alpha of 50% reflect an oil-war factor that is uncorrelated with equities, not low risk. Volatility of 23.6% and OVX at 61.7 mean a single diplomatic headline can move the group 6-8%.
reads.fund: TTM net income rose 84.9% on revenue growth of 32.1%, lifting operating margin to 15.4% and ROIC to 15.7%. That is operating leverage on a $33/bbl European refining margin and Brent averaging $97 in Q3. Upstream earnings already slipped quarter on quarter, so refining and trading carry the peak.
reads.health: D/E is 0.42, net debt/EBITDA fell to 0.50 in Q2, and FCF covers dividends 2.9x. BP cut net debt to $13.9B and TTE's gearing is 9.1%. The 0.8x interest-cover aggregate looks like a data artefact against those figures. The genuinely stretched names (E, SLNG, SKYQ) are only 4% of the industry.
reads.val: A forward P/E of 10.0, EV/EBITDA of 5.5 and a 9.06% FCF yield imply free cash flow decaying 6.9% a year, so the market declines to capitalise the windfall. Dispersion sits in the mega-caps: XOM trades at 14.5x forward, while the group outside the top three trades at 7.5x.
reads.earn: Beat rate is 67% with a median EPS surprise of 7.4%, and NTM revisions are +9.6% over 30 days and +21.4% over 90 days. Analysts are still chasing realised prices. Consensus nonetheless has next-fiscal-year EPS down 14.2%, so the Q4 season starting 2027-01-29 tests whether that decline starts on…
