hist.read: The five episodes and the base rates lean cautious: the 20 closest months were up only 45% of the time at 6M with a median of -3.2%, and beat the S&P 500 in only 20% of cases, with 12M up 35% and a median of -3.6%. Four of five episodes saw the industry lose ground at 6M, and only was a clear win, driven by an oil shock still to come. Over 1M the odds are close to even (up 2 of 5), and over 3M the odds are similar. The differences are large, as oil is rising rather than falling and the P/E is mid-range, so I would give these analogs moderate weight. Today most resembles: a peaking oil price, an industry already 11.7% off its high and a market under pressure. That supports the team's neutral…

episodes.then: October 2018 saw a sharp global equity sell-off as the Fed kept hiking and trade-war fears grew. Oil had peaked in early October near $85 Brent and was about to fall hard, which hit energy shares.
episodes.after: The industry fell 4.3% in 1M, 4% in 3M, 4.8% in 6M and 13% in 12M, with a worst 6-month drawdown of -18.5%. The S&P 500 rose 1.9% in 1M, 9.3% in 6M and 15.4% in 12M, so energy lagged badly. Oil's late-2018 collapse and the market's recovery after the Fed's pivot fit that pattern, though I'm not certain of the exact path.
episodes.different: Today oil is up 14.8% over 6 months, whereas in 2018 it was flat at -0.1%, and the P/E sits at the 50th percentile versus the 76th. Today's earnings are better supported, but the geopolitical premium could still unwind, so this cuts both ways.
episodes.lesson: A peaking oil price drags the industry even in a market recovery

episodes.then: January 2010 brought a sharp equity pullback on Chinese tightening worries, the Volcker Rule and early European sovereign-debt concerns. Oil was range-bound around $70-80 and energy shares lagged the post-crisis recovery.
episodes.after: The industry rose 0.8% in 1M and 4.8% in 3M, then fell 7.5% by 6M before ending 12M up 14.7%, with a worst 6-month drop of -23.4%. The S&P 500 gained 11.1% in 3M and 21.3% in 12M. The mid-2010 slump was consistent with the Eurozone scare and the Gulf of Mexico spill, which I recall but cannot verify against this data.
episodes.different: In 2010 the economy was exiting a recession with credit spreads tightening (+5.4pp). Today the S&P 500 is down 2.6% over 6 months and there is a war-driven oil spike, so the backdrop is less of a recovery. That cuts against a repeat of the 12M rebound.
episodes.lesson: Dips can be violent but recover within a year

episodes.then: March 2025 had a tariff-driven equity correction and a growing growth scare, with oil drifting lower on OPEC+ supply and demand worries. The industry was holding up relatively well after a strong 3M.
episodes.after: The industry fell 6.9% in 1M, 11.8% in 3M and 4.9% in 6M, then ended 12M up 2.2%, with a worst 6-month drop of -12.7%. The S&P 500 rebounded 10.7% in 3M and 19.8% in 6M. The tariff shock and falling oil weighed on the industry while the broad market recovered, as I recall.
episodes.different: Back then the industry was at the 85th P/E percentile and 3M momentum was +7.6%. Today it is at the 50th percentile with 3M at -8%, so some de-rating has already happened, which cuts in favour of today.
episodes.lesson: The industry lagged a market rebound

episodes.then: November 2021 saw the Omicron variant emerge, inflation run hot and the Fed turn hawkish. Oil was recovering from the pandemic, and energy companies were about to benefit from tight supply.
episodes.after: The industry gained 3.3% in 1M, 28.2% in 3M, 40.4% in 6M and 32.3% in 12M, with a worst 6-month drop of only -8.6%. The S&P 500 fell 3.5% in 3M and 9.5% in 6M. Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the resulting oil spike drove the outperformance.
episodes.different: In 2021 the oil price shock was still ahead and earnings were rising from a low base. Today the war premium is already in the price (Brent $98.6) and the Q4 and Q1 prints may mark the peak, which cuts against a repeat.
episodes.lesson: A supply shock ahead rewards energy, a shock already priced does not

episodes.then: September 2014 saw a strong dollar and Brent starting to slide from about $100 as US shale output grew and global demand softened. OPEC then declined to cut in November, which I recall as the decisive event.
episodes.after: The industry fell 6% in 1M, 15.9% in 3M, 23.6% in 6M and 39.6% in 12M, with a worst 6-month drop of -26.4%. The S&P 500 rose 6% in 3M and 5.5% in 6M. The oil collapse hit earnings and the shares fell much further than they had by that point.
episodes.different: In 2014 oil was falling (-6% over 6M) and supply was growing. Today it is up 14.8% on war risk, so the downside needs a peace deal or supply return rather than a glut. That cuts in favour of today, but a US-Iran deal could trigger a similar fall.
episodes.lesson: A falling oil price turns a dip into a bear market

debates.resolves: Whether the group recovers alongside oil over the next two weeks, and whether Brent holds above $95 through the 12 Nov CPI release.

debates.q: Does the valuation already discount normalisation?
debates.bull: Forward P/E is 9.4 after the drop, the FCF yield is about 9.6%, and consensus already expects -14.2% FY EPS. Excluding the top three names, forward P/E is 7.5.

reads.fund: Revenue growth of 20.5% outpaces earnings growth of 15.8% because commodity pass-through (ENB commodity sales +137% y/y) inflates the top line. Operating margin is 18.8% and ROIC 9.8%, but FCF margin is only 6.3% because growth capex runs at 14% of sales.

hist.read: The five episodes are split: and saw strong rebounds, was flat to modestly positive, and and were severe losses driven by oil collapses and credit or pandemic shocks. The base rates are mildly supportive but not strong: the median is +1% at 1M, +5.3% at 3M, +7.7% at 6M and +12.9% at 12M, with 65-70% of cases up. Midstream beat the S&P 500 only 30-50% of the time, and 6M and 12M up-rates sit below the all-month rates. Today most resembles, with the industry down 18.1% from its high, oil rising and the P/E mid-range, but the VIX at 28 and spreads at 102bp warn of the tail, so the team's pause on new adds looks reasonable. With only five episodes and large differences, I would give these…

episodes.then: August 2015 brought the China devaluation shock and a VIX spike, with oil collapsing and energy credit under strain. Midstream was beginning to de-rate as commodity exposure and leverage came into question.
episodes.after: The industry fell 15.6% in 1M, 20% in 3M, 38.4% in 6M and 22.4% in 12M, with a worst drawdown of -49.4% in the next 6 months. The S&P 500 was +1.8% over 6M and +12.7% over 12M, so the damage was sector-specific, driven by the oil bust, high-yield stress and distribution cuts. I am not certain of every company-level detail.
episodes.different: Oil is up 14.8% over 6M today, not down 12.2%, and the P/E is at the 45th percentile versus the 79th, so the commodity-deflation shock is absent. That cuts toward a milder outcome, though credit is again the stress point.
episodes.lesson: Credit stress plus commodity bust is deadly

episodes.then: March 2018 saw a volatility return, tariff fears and the Fed tightening. Midstream was hit by the FERC MLP pipeline tax ruling and rising rates.
episodes.after: The industry rose 6.5% in 1M, 12.2% in 3M, 13.9% in 6M and 30.1% in 12M, with a worst drop of only -6.7%. The S&P 500 gained 11.5% over 6M and 10.7% over 12M. Oil strength and a sector washout that had already happened plausibly supported the rebound, though I am unsure of the exact drivers.
episodes.different: The VIX is 28 today versus 20, and credit spreads are widening, whereas then high yield was holding up. Tighter credit makes a rebound less reliable.
episodes.lesson: Washed-out sector with oil support can rebound

episodes.then: November 2021 had Omicron emerging, the Fed turning hawkish and inflation climbing, with oil and gas prices strong. Midstream was cheap and lagging the broader market.
episodes.after: The industry gained 0.2% in 1M, 17.7% in 3M, 26.1% in 6M and 14.5% in 12M, with a worst drop of -9.7%. The S&P 500 fell 3.5% over 3M, 9.5% over 6M and 9.2% over 12M. Energy cash flows and the 2022 commodity surge, plus a rotation away from growth, favored midstream.
episodes.different: The P/E was at the 15th percentile then versus the 45th now, so there is less valuation cushion today. That cuts against a repeat.
episodes.lesson: Cheap cash-flow value can outrun a weak market

episodes.then: February 2023 saw rate hikes resumed on sticky inflation, ahead of the March banking stress. Midstream was cheap but lagging after a strong 2022.
episodes.after: The industry fell 2% in 1M and 4.8% in 3M, then gained 1.4% in 6M and 3.8% in 12M, with a worst drop of -8.3%. The S&P 500 gained 14.2% over 6M and 30.2% over 12M, so midstream lagged a tech-led rally.
episodes.different: The VIX is 28 versus 21, and the industry's own 3M slide is far steeper (-13.6% versus -5.1%). That suggests more stress, but also more room to mean-revert.
episodes.lesson: Defensive yield lags in a risk-on rally

episodes.then: February 2020 was the start of the COVID panic, with oil about to collapse. The VIX was 40 and markets were falling fast.
episodes.after: The industry fell 49.8% in 1M, 34.2% in 3M, 38.8% in 6M and 31.4% in 12M, with a worst drop of -58.3%. The S&P 500 fell 11.2% in 1M but gained 3.3% in 3M, 18.8% in 6M and 34% in 12M on stimulus. The oil collapse and demand shock hit midstream much harder than the broad market.
episodes.different: Today has no pandemic shock, and oil is rising rather than about to crash. That cuts toward a much milder path, though a sudden oil-price reversal would be the tail risk.
episodes.lesson: Exogenous demand shock overwhelms valuation

hist.read: The five episodes lean negative. Only and were up at 12M, and the base rates show the industry up just 30% of the time at 6M and 12M, with a median of -4.4% at 6M and -7.4% at 12M. At 1M the evidence is roughly neutral (55% up, median +1%), at 3M and 6M it leans down and lags the S&P 500, and 12M is the weakest. The sample is small and today differs because oil is rising on a war premium, so I'd give it moderate weight; it supports the neutral-to-underweight stance but not an aggressive short. looks the most like today, with an industry lagging the market by about 8-9pp, a deep drawdown and oil at risk of unwinding, though cheap valuations leave-style or-style rebounds possible.

episodes.then: October 2018 saw a sharp global equity sell-off on Fed tightening worries and trade-war fears. Oil peaked in early October and then began a steep drop, which hit E&Ps hard.
episodes.after: Over the next 12 months the industry fell 19.3% while the S&P 500 gained 15.4%. Oil's late-2018 slide drove the weakness: the industry was down 3% at 1M, 4.4% at 3M and 2.8% at 6M, with a worst 6-month drawdown of 23.6%.
episodes.different: Then, oil was rolling over from a peak and the industry's P/E sat near the middle of its history (54th pct). Today oil is up 14.8% over 6 months on a war premium and valuations are cheap (18th pct), so the downside is more event-driven, though a deal could still pull oil down.
episodes.lesson: Oil rolling over punishes E&Ps even when the market recovers

episodes.then: February 2025 brought tariff uncertainty, a strong dollar and a soft oil backdrop, and E&Ps lagged the market. I'm not certain of every driver beyond that.
episodes.after: The industry was roughly flat at 1M (-0.4%) and 3M (-0.1%), then fell 12.6% by 6M and 5.3% by 12M. The S&P 500 rose 15.8% over 12M, so energy lagged badly, with a worst 6-month drawdown of 23.3%.
episodes.different: Then, oil was flat and the VIX was 20, so there was no war premium to lose. Today oil has rallied and VIX is 28, which means more upside if tensions persist and more downside if a deal removes the premium.
episodes.lesson: Energy can lag a rising market for a year

episodes.then: May 2010 had the Greek debt crisis, the flash crash and the Gulf of Mexico Deepwater Horizon spill, with the VIX above 30 and a stronger dollar. Oil was weak and risk assets sold off.
episodes.after: This was the one strong rebound: the industry rose 4.1% at 1M, 6.5% at 3M, 32.5% at 6M and 43.1% at 12M, versus 24.5% for the S&P 500. The panic faded and the economy and oil recovered, though the worst 6-month drop was still 11.8%.
episodes.different: Then, oil had been falling (-13.1% over 6 months) and the sell-off was a broad panic that reversed. Today oil is rising on a geopolitical premium, so a rebound depends on the war premium persisting rather than on a macro recovery.
episodes.lesson: Panic lows with cheap valuations can reverse sharply

episodes.then: January 2023 followed the 2022 energy boom. Oil and gas prices were falling back, rates were high and the market was recovering from the 2022 bear market. The industry's valuation was at a very low percentile (4th).
episodes.after: The industry slid 7.2% at 1M, 16.6% at 3M and 8.3% at 6M, and was down 15.6% at 12M, while the S&P 500 gained 22.2%. Falling commodity prices outweighed cheap valuations, and the worst 6-month drop was 21.3%.
episodes.different: Then, oil and the dollar were drifting down and the VIX was only 19. Today an oil spike and supply risk are in play, and payouts are still rising (EOG +8%, COP +11%).
episodes.lesson: Cheap valuation did not stop a commodity-led slide

episodes.then: January 2024 had a calm market (VIX 14) near highs, with oil range-bound and E&Ps lagging badly after a weak 2023 (-15% over 12M). Valuations were low (11th pct).
episodes.after: The industry rose 6% at 1M, 14.4% at 3M and 7.5% at 6M, and was up 10.3% at 12M, while the S&P 500 gained 25.4%. Cheap valuations supported a rebound, though it still lagged the market, with a worst 6-month drop of 11.2%.
episodes.different: Then, the market was calm and near its highs. Today the S&P 500 is 5.9% off its high with a VIX of 28, so stress is higher and the outcome depends more on oil.
episodes.lesson: Cheap, hated energy can rebound but still lag

reads.risk: Beta to the S&P is -0.33 and the Sharpe ratio is 2.27, but the real factor is oil (+2.9% per +10%), and 20-day volatility has jumped to 44% from 33% as OVX reached 61.69. The 1Y max drawdown of -13.8% understates the history of five 20%+ drawdowns, including -82% and -78%.
reads.fund: TTM revenue rose 24.7% and earnings 1,108%. Net margin is 6.8%, ROIC 32.4% and FCF conversion 122%, all driven by windfall cracks with high operating leverage. Q3 EPS of $26.93 at MPC and $23.90 at VLO are peak prints, and PSX sizes the excess at about $2B over normal.

hist.read: The five episodes split: and were large rallies from low valuations (15th and 23rd percentile), while and saw drawdowns of -31.2% and -23.5% and was a bounce that faded. The base rates are modestly positive: 3M up 70% of the time with a median +7.8%, 6M up 65% with a median +8.6%, 12M median +7.2%, but a wide middle half and a beat of the S&P 500 only 40-55% of the time. Today's valuation is mid-range (45th percentile) and the group is extended (+33.3% over 12M, +23pp vs the S&P 500), so and deserve less weight than, the closest analogue and the one today most resembles. I would expect a possible 1-3M bounce with a drawdown of 20% or more still possible, and a flat to modest 12M, so size…

episodes.then: In July 2022 inflation was running hot, the Fed was hiking aggressively, and the dollar was strong. Oil had come off its post-Ukraine-invasion highs, and refiners were still earning record margins but had pulled back from their June peak.
episodes.after: The industry gained 9% over 1M, 9.1% over 3M and 10% over 6M, as margins stayed strong, but it was only +0.6% at 12M. The S&P 500 fell 2.3% at 1M and 7.4% at 3M, then recovered to +12.6% at 12M. The worst drawdown in the next 6 months was still -19.7%, so refiners rebounded on margins but the path was rough.
episodes.different: Today's S&P 500 is closer to its high (-5.9% vs -13.1%) and VIX is higher (28 vs 21). Refiners' 12-month gain is larger (+33.3% vs +17.8%), and the market is not in a rate-hike shock. This cuts mixed: less macro stress but more already priced in.
episodes.lesson: Refiners can bounce after a pullback, but gains fade by 12M

episodes.then: In August 2015 China devaluation fears set off a sharp global selloff with a VIX spike, and oil was collapsing. Refiners had enjoyed strong margins from cheap crude but were pulling back.
episodes.after: The industry fell 3.2% at 1M, rebounded 12.3% at 3M, then gave back to -11.4% at 6M and -5% at 12M. The S&P 500 was -2.6% at 1M, +6.1% at 3M, +1.8% at 6M and +12.7% at 12M. The worst drawdown in the next 6 months was -31.2%, as margins peaked and the cycle turned.
episodes.different: Oil then was falling (-12.2% over 6M), while today oil is up +14.8%. Today's industry also has strong relative momentum (+23pp vs +2pp). This cuts both ways: higher oil signals a supply shock that may fade, and the momentum leaves more to unwind.
episodes.lesson: A bounce in a falling peak-margin cycle can still be sold

episodes.then: In October 2018 a market selloff was driven by Fed tightening and trade-war worries, and oil topped out and then fell sharply. A strong dollar weighed on the market and refiners were already lagging.
episodes.after: The industry fell 8.6% at 1M, 9.2% at 3M and 12.8% at 6M, and was -2.8% at 12M. The S&P 500 was +1.9% at 1M, +1.1% at 3M, +9.3% at 6M and +15.4% at 12M. The worst drawdown in the next 6 months was -23.5%, so refiners kept lagging a market that recovered.
episodes.different: Refiners then were lagging (-9.5pp vs the S&P 500 over 6M) with a higher P/E percentile (63rd). Today they lead (+23pp) at a lower multiple (45th pct). Today's setup is more resilient on valuation, but the group is far more extended on relative strength.
episodes.lesson: Falling momentum in the group can persist even when the market recovers

episodes.then: In January 2010 markets corrected on Volcker-rule and China-tightening worries during the early recovery from the financial crisis. Refiners were cheap, with depressed earnings and a low P/E percentile.
episodes.after: The industry gained 2.9% at 1M, 34.3% at 3M, 22.6% at 6M and 70.6% at 12M, beating the S&P 500 (+4.5%, +11.1%, +3.6%, +21.3%). The worst drawdown in the next 6 months was -15.9%, and the rally came as earnings recovered from trough.
episodes.different: The industry was at the 15th P/E percentile then, against 45th now. The macro backdrop was a trough-earnings recovery, while today's setup is later-cycle and oil is up. That cuts against repeating the large upside.
episodes.lesson: Big gains came from trough valuations, not momentum

episodes.then: In May 2012 euro-zone crisis fears and a Greek election scare drove a risk-off move, with oil falling. Refiners were benefiting from wide crude differentials and strong margins.
episodes.after: The industry rose 12.2% at 1M, 23.4% at 3M, 38.4% at 6M and 84.5% at 12M, against the S&P 500's +4.1%, +8.2%, +9.3% and +27.2%. The worst drawdown in the next 6 months was only -8.1%, as margin windfalls lifted earnings.
episodes.different: Then oil fell (-15.9%) and the industry sat at the 23rd P/E percentile, with a supportive margin tailwind. Today oil is rising and the multiple is at the 45th percentile, so the setup is less favourable.
episodes.lesson: Strong margin tailwinds at low multiples drive outsized gains

hist.read: The five episodes are split: and rebounded strongly, was flat to modestly lower, fell hard, and recovered only after a rough 3M. The base rates are mildly negative: 6M up only 35% of the time with a median of -2%, and 12M median -3%, with the group beating the S&P 500 only 25-30% of the time at 6-12M. That fits the team's neutral view, roughly -3% at 12M. I would weight the evidence modestly given the wide spread and 5 samples. Today most resembles, a rate and credit-driven selloff with elevated VIX and a larger lag than the S&P 500, though is the key downside risk if the AI selloff widens credit stress.

episodes.then: October 2018 saw a sharp global equity selloff driven by Fed tightening worries, rising Treasury yields and US-China trade tension. Banks fell with the market and a flattening yield curve, even though credit quality was solid.
episodes.after: The industry was roughly flat to slightly lower afterward: 1M +0.3%, 3M -3.5%, 6M -0.9% and 12M -3.4%, with a worst drop of -17% inside six months. The S&P 500 meanwhile gained +15.4% over 12M, so banks lagged. The late-2018 rout, then the Fed's pivot toward patience in early 2019, probably explain the swings, though I am not certain of the exact attribution.
episodes.different: Today's VIX is 28 against 21 then, the industry is more stretched below its 200-day average (-17.4% vs -10.8%), and valuation is mid-range rather than cheap. That cuts both ways: more panic, but less valuation cushion.
episodes.lesson: Bank weakness can persist even as the S&P recovers

episodes.then: August 2015 was the China devaluation shock and flash-crash volatility, with oil falling and the market worried about global growth ahead of the Fed's first hike. Banks were weak on low rates, energy credit worries and emerging-market exposure.
episodes.after: The industry kept falling: 1M -6.2%, 3M -2.1%, 6M -18.9% and 12M -13.1%, with a worst drop of -27.8% in six months. The S&P 500 was still +12.7% at 12M. The group's drawdown was deeper than the index's, consistent with the early-2016 growth and credit scare, though I'm not sure of every driver.
episodes.different: Oil is up +14.8% over 6M today, against -12.2% then, so there is no energy-credit deflation shock now. Today's industry underperformance (-17.6pp) is much larger than then (+0.4pp), which cuts toward more mean-reversion potential.
episodes.lesson: Growth scares can cause a second leg lower

episodes.then: July 2022 was a bear-market low point for risk assets, with aggressive Fed hikes, high inflation, a strong dollar and oil elevated after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Banks were cheap and depressed on recession fears.
episodes.after: The group recovered at 6M (+7.9%) and 12M (+6.1%), though 1M was -1.6% and 3M -3.5%, and the worst drop in six months was -19.1%. That was likely due to rate-driven earnings strength offset by the early 2023 regional bank failures; I should not lean on that attribution too much. The S&P 500 was +12.6% at 12M.
episodes.different: Valuation then sat at the 4th percentile versus the 40th today, so there was far more valuation support. Today the Treasury move is mild (-0.8% vs -5.9%), so rates are less of a driver, which cuts toward less rate relief.
episodes.lesson: Deeply cheap starts can still suffer a drawdown first

episodes.then: May 2012 was the peak of the euro-area crisis scare, with Greek election fears, falling Treasury yields and a growing risk-off tone. Banks were depressed after a 12M decline of -33.7%, with European exposure and regulation a worry.
episodes.after: The industry rebounded strongly: 1M +6.3%, 3M +9.5%, 6M +20.8% and 12M +41.5%, with the worst drop in six months only -9%. The S&P 500 gained +27.2% at 12M. Central bank backstops then lifted financials and sentiment, which fits the strong recovery.
episodes.different: Then the group was recovering from a larger -33.7% 12M slide, bond yields were falling (+5.6%) and the policy backstop was clear. Today yields are up slightly and the policy backdrop is less supportive, which cuts against a similar rebound.
episodes.lesson: Policy backstops can fuel sharp rebounds

episodes.then: May 2023 was after the SVB, Signature and First Republic failures, with debt-ceiling drama and deposit-flight worries in regional banks. The broader market was near highs (only -1.5% below), led by large-cap tech.
episodes.after: The industry rose: 1M +6%, 3M +6.6%, 6M +7.5% and 12M +25%, with a worst drop of -13.4%. The S&P 500 gained +28% at 12M, so banks participated but did not outperform. Fears faded as deposit flight stabilized, and the rate cuts expected in 2024 plus the rally lifted banks, though I am hazy on exact details.
episodes.different: Then the S&P was near its high and VIX was 18, with a clear banking-specific shock. Today VIX is 28 and the market is weaker, with an AI selloff and wider credit spreads, which cuts toward more downside risk.
episodes.lesson: Shocks that fade can be followed by a rebound

episodes.then: In March 2025 US equities were in a tariff-driven correction, with growth worries and a rising dollar. Credit-services stocks, led by the card networks, were holding up well relative to the market.
episodes.after: The industry rose 4.6% in 1 month, 4% in 3 months and 8.6% in 6 months, but the 12-month return was -0.7%. The S&P 500 recovered strongly after the spring selloff (+19.8% over 6 months, +18.5% over 12), so the industry lagged badly over the year. The worst drop in the first 6 months was -9.7%.
episodes.different: Back then the industry sat at its 12-month high and valuations were at the 78th percentile, with high-yield spreads steady. Today it is 7.5% below its high, with a VIX of 28 and wider IG spreads, so there is more stress but also a lower valuation starting point.
episodes.lesson: Early defensive outperformance, then lagging the rebound

episodes.then: In August 2015 China's devaluation triggered a global selloff and a VIX spike, with oil falling and credit spreads widening. Financials were weak ahead of the Fed's first hike debate.
episodes.after: The industry fell 4.4% in 1 month and gained 3% in 3 months. It then slid to -9.6% over 6 months and -5.4% over 12, while the S&P 500 returned +1.8% over 6 months and +12.7% over 12. The worst drop in the 6 months was -22.5%, the second-deepest of the five.
episodes.different: In 2015 the industry was below its 200-day average and cheap, at the 38th percentile for valuation, and oil was falling. Today it is above its 200-day average, oil is rising and valuation is higher, so the downside from de-rating is larger.
episodes.lesson: Stress plus a deep drawdown, with lagging recovery

episodes.then: In October 2018 equities sold off sharply as the Fed kept hiking and rate fears and trade tensions mounted, with the dollar strong. Financials were soft, and the market's slide deepened into December.
episodes.after: The industry gained 1.8% in 1 month, lost 1% over 3 months, then rose 10.1% over 6 months and 16.2% over 12. The S&P 500 was +1.9%, +1.1%, +9.3% and +15.4% over the same windows. The worst drop within 6 months was -18.4%, reflecting the December 2018 low before the Fed pivot.
episodes.different: In 2018 the industry was lagging the S&P 500 and was below its 200-day average, and the Fed was about to pivot. Today the industry is leading and the Fed still leans toward hiking, so there is no easing catalyst yet.
episodes.lesson: Hawkish Fed scare resolves only after a deep dip

episodes.then: In January 2010 markets were pulling back from the post-crisis rally on sovereign debt worries and bank regulation proposals. Credit-services stocks were still recovering from the crisis lows.
episodes.after: The industry fell 0.9% in 1 month, then rose 28% over 3 months, 9.4% over 6 months and 4.9% over 12. The S&P 500 gained 4.5%, 11.1%, 3.6% and 21.3% over the same windows. The worst drop within 6 months was -24.3%, the deepest of the five.
episodes.different: In 2010 the industry was 19% below its high and rebounding from a credit-cycle trough with a recovery ahead. Today it is near highs, with lender credit cushions thinning, so a cyclical rebound is not on offer.
episodes.lesson: Recovery-phase rebound; not a late-cycle analogue

episodes.then: In July 2012 the euro crisis peaked until Draghi's 'whatever it takes' pledge, and the US recovery was modest. Credit-services stocks had outperformed strongly, with valuations stretched.
episodes.after: The industry slipped 0.4% in 1 month and fell 4.3% over 3 months, then gained 1.9% over 6 months and 22.7% over 12. The S&P 500 returned +2.8%, +3.2%, +11.2% and +26.9%. The worst drop within 6 months was -10.4%.
episodes.different: In 2012 the VIX was only 19, oil was falling and Treasuries were rallying. Today the VIX is 28, oil and the dollar are rising and yields are up, a tighter backdrop, though valuations are less stretched at the 65th percentile.
episodes.lesson: Leaders stall short-term, then grind higher

hist.read: The five episodes and the base rates tilt positive for the group beyond the 1M horizon. About 60% of the 20 closest months were up at 1M, 75% at 3M (median +6%), 65% at 6M (median +9%) and 80% at 12M (median +11.8%). At 1M the picture is mixed: and fell and, and rose, and the group beat the S&P 500 only 45% of the time then, and only 20% at 12M. Those base rates favour absolute gains, not outperformance, so they fit the team's neutral index view with selective stock picks and they sit above the +1% price case. The five analogs are a small sample and each had a different cause, so I'd give them modest weight. Today most resembles, with a VIX of 28, a market selloff, and a bank drawdown of…

episodes.then: In August 2015 China's yuan devaluation set off a global equity selloff and a VIX spike, with oil in a slump and the Fed debating its first hike. Regional banks fell with the market on worries about global growth and low rates.
episodes.after: The industry returned -3.3% over 1M, -3.4% over 3M and -2.4% over 6M, with a worst drop of -14.9% inside six months, as the market chopped through early 2016. It then recovered to +15.7% at 12M, versus +12.7% for the S&P 500. I am not certain of every driver, but the rebound is consistent with the Fed's first hike and the late-2016 rise in yields.
episodes.different: Today oil is up 14.8% over 6M and the dollar is up 4.6%, whereas oil was falling then, and the industry is 19.1% below its high, which is deeper than the 13% then. That cuts both ways: a deeper drawdown leaves more room to recover but suggests more stress.
episodes.lesson: Panic-driven drawdowns can bottom late, then recover within a year

episodes.then: In October 2018 equities sold off sharply as the Fed kept hiking and Treasury yields rose, with trade-war worries on top. Banks were weak as the yield curve flattened and growth fears grew.
episodes.after: The industry rose +3.8% in 1M, +6.7% in 3M and +5.2% in 6M, even though the worst drop in the next six months was -12.4%. At 12M it was +5.4%, versus +15.4% for the S&P 500. The Fed's pause in early 2019 helped, but I don't have the full detail of the path.
episodes.different: Today the P/E percentile is 25th versus 65th then, so valuation is cheaper now, which cuts in favour. Oil and the dollar are rising, which points to an inflation-type shock, not the tightening scare of 2018.
episodes.lesson: Banks can bounce but still lag the index

episodes.then: In May 2023 the regional bank crisis (SVB, Signature, then First Republic) had hit the industry hard, with deposit flight and commercial real estate worries. The broad market was calm by comparison, with the S&P 500 only 1.5% off its high.
episodes.after: The industry rose +6.2% in 1M, +5.3% in 3M and +5.5% in 6M, but suffered a -18.6% worst drop within six months as yields surged in autumn 2023. At 12M it was +13.9%, versus +28% for the S&P 500, so the group recovered but lagged badly.
episodes.different: Today the market itself is stressed, with VIX at 28 and the S&P 500 5.9% off its high, while then the pain was confined to banks. The cause today looks macro rather than a sector-specific funding crisis, which cuts both ways.
episodes.lesson: Recovery came with a gut-check on the way

episodes.then: In May 2010 the Greek debt crisis and the flash crash pushed the VIX to 32 and led to a risk-off market. Banks were also dealing with the Dodd-Frank financial reform debate and the aftermath of the credit crisis.
episodes.after: The industry fell -3.5% in 1M, then gained +2.9% in 3M and +9.9% in 6M, with a worst drop of -9.8%. At 12M it was +12.1%, versus +24.5% for the S&P 500. The recovery came as the market rallied after the summer 2010 lows, with the Fed's QE2 as the likely driver, though I'm not sure of the exact path.
episodes.different: In 2010 banks were still recovering from the credit crisis, with credit losses ahead of them to work through. Today's banks are better capitalised, but the cycle is older, which cuts mildly against.
episodes.lesson: Early dips were followed by a good 6M rebound

episodes.then: In March 2025 tariff fears and growth worries were hitting equities, with the S&P 500 8.5% off its high and the dollar strong. Banks were holding up better than the market after the late-2024 rally.
episodes.after: The industry surged +11.3% in 1M, +24.4% in 3M and +26.5% in 6M, with a mild worst drop of -5.7%. At 12M it was +31.4%, versus +18.5% for the S&P 500. The rally followed the tariff pause and deregulation hopes, though the cause of every move is something I'm not certain about.
episodes.different: Then the industry was only 5.8% off its high and outperforming by 2.2pp, while today it is 19.1% off its high and trails by 11.6pp. That cuts both ways: more damage leaves more to recover, but it is weaker momentum.
episodes.lesson: Resilient sector, strong rebound from a tariff scare

Because the sample is five episodes, I would give them moderate weight. The likely path is a choppy 1-3 months with the…

episodes.then: February 2022 was the month Russia invaded Ukraine. Oil spiked, the Fed was about to start hiking, and growth stocks were selling off while value and insurers held up.
episodes.after: The industry jumped 10.1% in the first month, then faded: 3M -1.6%, 6M -12.7%, 12M -9.6%. The worst drop inside six months was -26.1%. The S&P 500 also fell (6M -7.1%, 12M -8.1%), so the industry fell harder than the market as rate hikes and the bear market played out. I am not certain of the exact drivers for the industry's relative drop.
episodes.different: Today the P/E percentile is 80th rather than 95th and oil is up less (+14.8% vs +40.5%). The industry's 6-month lead is bigger (+23.5pp vs +10.4pp), which cuts against today because there is more outperformance to give back.
episodes.lesson: Crowded defensive leaders can reverse hard

episodes.then: September 2023 saw 10-year yields surging toward 5% on 'higher for longer' Fed talk. Oil had rallied and the S&P 500 was in a pullback ahead of the late-October low.
episodes.after: The industry slipped 3.8% in the first month, then recovered: 3M +1.9%, 6M +17.7%, 12M +7.9%. The worst drop in six months was only -5.5%. The S&P 500 did better (3M +11.6%, 12M +34.8%) once yields fell and the rally broadened, so the industry gained but lagged.
episodes.different: Today's VIX is 28 vs 18, which signals more stress. The industry's trailing gains are also larger (12M +38.2% vs +24.6%). Both make today riskier, though higher VIX can also mark a better entry point.
episodes.lesson: Dips resolved up, but the market ran faster

episodes.then: May 2013 was just before the Fed taper tantrum. The S&P 500 was near highs and insurers had run up strongly.
episodes.after: The industry gave back 1.4% in 1M and 3.2% in 3M, then ended 6M +1.8% and 12M +9.2%. The worst drop in six months was -6.4%. The S&P 500 rose (6M +11.9%, 12M +20.4%), so the industry lagged in a strong market after the rate scare.
episodes.different: The market was strong then (S&P 6M +16.3%, VIX 16) and is weak now (S&P 6M -2.6%, VIX 28). With a weak tape, there is less broad strength to carry the industry along, which cuts against it.
episodes.lesson: After a strong run, expect lagging returns

episodes.then: January 2010 was the middle of the post-crisis recovery. A sovereign-debt and regulatory scare was knocking the S&P 500 down from its highs, and insurers were still rebounding from the 2008-09 lows.
episodes.after: The industry rose 6.0% in the first month, then gave up gains: 3M +5.0%, 6M +3.2%, 12M +5.8%. It suffered a worst drop of -16.8% within six months, amid the spring 2010 flash-crash and Europe sell-off. The S&P 500 gained 21.3% over 12M, so the industry lagged.
episodes.different: The industry then was cheap (P/E 11th percentile) and is expensive now (80th). This was a recovery from depressed levels, so today has less valuation cushion, which cuts against.
episodes.lesson: Volatile path even when it ends positive

episodes.then: September 2014 saw a strong dollar, falling oil and the end of QE. The S&P 500 was near highs ahead of a brief October wobble.
episodes.after: The industry was flat to up (1M +0.6%, 3M +6.8%, 6M +1.4%), then fell to -6.7% at 12M. The S&P 500 did better at 6M (+5.5%) and also slipped over the year (12M -0.8%). The 12M decline was probably driven by the oil collapse and a stronger dollar, but I am not sure of the specific drivers.
episodes.different: The industry's lead was tiny then (+0.6pp vs +23.5pp now) and oil was falling rather than rising. Today's crowding is much larger, which cuts against.
episodes.lesson: Modest gains, then a 12M slide

hist.read: The five episodes give mixed signals. At 1 and 3 months the industry was up in 3 of 5 episodes, and the 20-month base rate has a 3-month median of +6.8% with 65% up, so a rebound is plausible, though a retest like or is just as possible. At 6 months only 1 of 5 episodes was up, the base-rate median is -0.3% and the industry beat the S&P 500 only 25% of the time, which argues against expecting quick outperformance. The 12-month outcomes range from +38.3% to -16.5%, and 6-month worst drawdowns of 17-31% mean more downside is possible even if the endpoint is fine. Today is closest to by the code's measure, with the VIX and broad stress of and, but the differences (rising oil, a market-wide…

episodes.then: October 2018 brought a sharp global equity selloff as the Fed kept hiking, the dollar rose and trade-war worries weighed on sentiment. Capital-markets stocks fell with the market, and the December 2018 low was still ahead.
episodes.after: The industry fell 5.2% in the first month and 7.9% over 3 months as the Q4 2018 selloff deepened. It was still down 2.1% at 6 months and 6.4% at 12 months, while the S&P 500 gained 9.3% at 6 months and 15.4% at 12 months. The worst drop within 6 months was 24.7%, so the industry lagged a rebounding market after an already deep drawdown.
episodes.different: Today the VIX is 28 against 21 then, and oil is up 14.8% where it was flat, so the stress is sharper and comes from an AI-led Nasdaq correction rather than Fed tightening. The industry is also further below its 12-month high (-40.8% vs -31.7%), which cuts both ways: it is more washed out, but the…
episodes.lesson: Deep drawdowns can keep lagging a recovering market

episodes.then: In May 2023 the regional bank crisis (SVB, First Republic) had just hit financials, and IPO and M&A activity was depressed. The broad market was near its highs, led by an AI-driven megacap rally.
episodes.after: The industry rose 4.1% in the first month and 7.5% over 3 months, slipped 1.4% at 6 months, then recovered to +12.9% at 12 months. The S&P 500 gained 28% over 12 months. The worst drop within 6 months was still 23.7%, so the path was bumpy even though the 12-month result was positive.
episodes.different: In 2023 the S&P 500 was only 1.5% off its high and the VIX was 18, so the weakness was sector-specific. Today the whole market is under pressure (S&P 500 5.9% below its high, VIX 28), which is a weaker backdrop for a quick catch-up.
episodes.lesson: Sector-specific washouts rebound more easily than broad ones

episodes.then: November 2011 was the height of the eurozone sovereign debt crisis, with the US downgrade still fresh, a high VIX and heavy pressure on investment banks and brokers. Treasuries had rallied as investors fled to safety.
episodes.after: The industry fell 3.6% in the first month, then jumped 27.6% over 3 months as fears eased. It was at -0.7% at 6 months and +38.3% at 12 months, against +15.6% for the S&P 500. The worst drop within 6 months was 29.1%, so the path was volatile but the 12-month payoff was large.
episodes.different: In 2011 Treasuries had rallied 9% and high yield had lagged by 11.8pp, a flight-to-safety pattern. Today yields are slightly higher (IEF -0.8%) and credit is calm (-0.1pp), so the stress looks equity-led, and I would not assume a comparable rescue.
episodes.lesson: Capitulation can pay off hugely, but the ride is rough

episodes.then: September 2015 followed the August China devaluation shock and flash crash, with oil weak and the Fed hesitating over its first hike. The VIX was elevated and the market was in correction.
episodes.after: The industry bounced 9.4% in the first month and 7.2% over 3 months, then gave it back in the early-2016 selloff, ending 13% lower at 6 months and 15.5% lower at 12 months. The S&P 500 was up 9.2% at 6 months and 14.4% at 12 months. The worst drop within 6 months was 30.7%.
episodes.different: In 2015 oil was falling (-12.8%) and the dollar was weaker (-3.1%); today oil is up 14.8% and the dollar up 4.6%, a tighter, more inflationary tilt. The industry's relative slump was also much smaller then (-6.1pp vs -34.6pp), so today starts from a bigger discount.
episodes.lesson: Early bounces can fade into a retest

episodes.then: April 2022 was a bear-market stretch with aggressive Fed tightening, a war-driven oil spike, a strong dollar and falling bond prices. The VIX was 33 and the IPO window had largely shut.
episodes.after: The industry rose 2.8% in the first month, was down 1.3% at 3 months, up 0.1% at 6 months and down 16.5% at 12 months. The S&P 500 was down 4.8% at 6 months and up only 1.4% at 12 months. The worst drop within 6 months was 17.3%, so it was a long grind with no lasting recovery.
episodes.different: In 2022 bonds were collapsing (IEF -9.8%) as the Fed hiked, whereas today bond moves are small. The driver now is an equity rout, not a rate shock, which means less valuation squeeze but also no obvious catalyst.
episodes.lesson: Bear markets grind on after relief bounces

hist.read: The five episodes lean positive for the industry in absolute terms: four of five were up at 1M, 3M, 6M and 12M, and the 20-month base rates show 90% up at 6M with a median of +6.2%. They also show it beating the S&P 500 only 40% at 6M and 20% at 12M, so the edge is mostly absolute, not relative. The analogs that match best on market stress were helped by the defensive bid, while and show the group trailing once stocks recovered, and today's 12.7x multiple and large 6M lead over the S&P 500 favour the latter. I give the base rates modest weight, since the industry's lead is unusual and the episodes disagree on size, and the setup most resembles, a haven rally after a market selloff, which…

episodes.then: In March 2025 US stocks were in a tariff-driven correction, with growth worries and a rising dollar, while P&C insurers acted as a defensive haven after a strong run. Oil had been firm and long yields were elevated.
episodes.after: The industry slipped 1.4% in the first month and was up only 1.5% at 3M and 0.4% at 6M. It ended 12M at -1.3% while the S&P 500 rallied 10.7% over 3M and 19.8% over 6M, so the haven trade faded as risk appetite returned. The worst drop in the next 6 months was -8%.
episodes.different: Today's VIX is higher (28 vs 22) and the industry's 6-month lead over the S&P 500 is larger (+9.3pp vs +2.5pp), so more of the haven premium is already in the price, which cuts toward weaker relative returns.
episodes.lesson: Haven premium faded as stocks rebounded

episodes.then: In August 2015 the China devaluation and a global growth scare produced a sharp equity selloff and a VIX spike, with oil falling and credit spreads widening. P&C stocks were already off their highs and had lagged the market.
episodes.after: The industry gained 5% in the first month, even as the S&P 500 fell 2.6%, and was up 13.7% at 3M and 10.7% at 6M. It reached +17.6% at 12M against +12.7% for the S&P 500, helped by the defensive bid during the volatility and a valuation reset. The worst drop in the next 6 months was -10.8%.
episodes.different: Then the industry was trailing the market and sat below its 200-day average, whereas today it has outperformed by 9.3pp and sits at its 200-day average, which cuts against a repeat. Oil is rising now, not collapsing.
episodes.lesson: Cheap defensives rallied through a selloff

episodes.then: In February 2022 Russia invaded Ukraine, oil surged, inflation was high and the Fed was about to start hiking. Insurers were seen as beneficiaries of rising rates and firm pricing, and had been outperforming.
episodes.after: The industry gained 8.4% in the first month and 5.6% at 3M, then fell 3% at 6M and recovered to +3.2% at 12M. The S&P 500 fell 7.1% at 6M and 8.1% at 12M, so insurers beat the bear market clearly, though the drawdown along the way was -15.4%. Relative strength came from the defensive and pricing-power story.
episodes.different: In 2022 the industry had strong 12M momentum (+9.1%) and a higher valuation percentile (52nd), whereas today it is down 2.4% over 12 months at a lower percentile (31st). That gives a cheaper starting point but less earnings momentum.
episodes.lesson: Defensive relative gains, with a deep dip

episodes.then: In October 2018 stocks sold off on rate fears and trade-war worries, with the dollar strong and volatility rising into year-end. P&C insurers were lagging, hit by catastrophe losses.
episodes.after: The industry gained 1.4% in the first month, fell 1.5% at 3M, then was up 6.8% at 6M and 5% at 12M. The S&P 500 gained 9.3% at 6M and 15.4% at 12M, so the industry trailed the rebound. The worst drop in the next 6 months was -15%, which came as the late-2018 selloff deepened.
episodes.different: In 2018 the industry was a laggard (-6.8pp vs the S&P 500 over 6M), while today it leads by 9.3pp. That removes the catch-up potential seen then.
episodes.lesson: Laggard recovered but trailed rebound

episodes.then: In October 2016 markets were calm ahead of the US election, VIX was low at 17 and bond yields were starting to climb. Insurers were flat to soft on the year.
episodes.after: The industry gained 3.9% in the first month and 7.9% at 3M, 13.7% at 6M and 22.9% at 12M. This closely tracked the S&P 500 (+23.4% at 12M), which rallied on the post-election reflation trade. The worst drop in the next 6 months was only -3.7%.
episodes.different: Then VIX was 17 and credit was strengthening (+4.5pp). Today VIX is 28 and stocks are in a drawdown, so the benign risk-on setting that lifted everything does not apply.
episodes.lesson: Calm backdrop lifted everything

hist.read: Near-term the episodes lean cautious: only 1 of 5 was up at 1M and 2 of 5 at 3M, with a 20-month base rate of 50% up at 1M and 60% at 3M, both below the all-month rates. At 6M and 12M the base rates recover (70% and 75% up, medians +6% and +10.6%), though the group beat the S&P 500 only 45% of the time and lagged in, and. The five episodes differ from today in volatility, valuation and relative strength, so they deserve moderate weight, and they support trimming into strength rather than a bearish call. Today most resembles on valuation and trend, but and on risk and the relative-strength overhang.

episodes.then: February 2019 followed the Q4 2018 selloff and the Fed's dovish pivot, so stocks were rebounding and rate-hike fears had faded. Insurance brokers were steady defensive compounders near their highs.
episodes.after: The industry was roughly flat after 1 month (-0.1%), then rose +4.6% over 3M, +7.8% over 6M and +13% over 12M, slightly ahead of the S&P 500's +8.3% at 12M. The worst drawdown within 6 months was -6.9%, so the gains came with only a modest dip.
episodes.different: Today VIX is 28 against 15 then, oil is up 14.8% rather than down 18.8%, and the industry has pulled back 5.7% from its high instead of sitting at it. Today's stress is greater and the Fed backdrop is less supportive, which cuts against a repeat of this benign outcome.
episodes.lesson: Calm defensive uptrend after a Fed pivot

episodes.then: November 2022 came during the aggressive Fed hiking cycle, with the S&P 500 still well below its high and the dollar strong. Brokers had held up far better than the market and were richly valued.
episodes.after: The industry fell 4.3% in 1M and 4.4% in 3M, was down 0.3% at 6M, and then recovered to +9.7% at 12M. The worst drop in the first 6 months was -11.7%, while the S&P 500 rose +14.4% over 12M, so brokers lagged in the rebound.
episodes.different: The S&P 500 is only 5.9% below its high today, against 13.7% then, and the industry's valuation percentile is lower (59th vs 81st), leaving less valuation risk but also a less washed-out market. The rate backdrop is less hostile today, which cuts mildly in favour.
episodes.lesson: Relative winners lag when the market rebounds

episodes.then: September 2021 saw a wobble from supply-chain worries, rising oil and the Fed starting to signal tapering. Brokers were strong on firm pricing and high valuations.
episodes.after: The industry jumped +10.4% in 1M and +9.5% in 3M, and was +7.8% at 6M. It then slipped to -9.8% at 12M, with the S&P 500 at -15.5% over the same window, as 2022 rate hikes hit. The worst drop within 6 months was -15.3%.
episodes.different: Today the industry's 12M momentum is much weaker (+7.7% vs +24.6%) and its valuation percentile is lower (59th vs 87th). The S&P 500 is also weaker today (-2.6% over 6M vs +9%), which cuts toward more caution.
episodes.lesson: Early strength, then a rate-driven fade

episodes.then: March 2025 had a tariff-driven growth scare, with the S&P 500 in correction territory and VIX elevated. Brokers were at peak relative valuation but starting to see organic growth cool and the pricing cycle soften.
episodes.after: The industry fell 6.5% in 1M, 7.4% in 3M, 10.6% at 6M and 20.4% at 12M. The S&P 500 gained +18.5% over 12M, so brokers lagged badly as the market recovered and growth concerns hit the group. The worst 6-month drop was -12.6%.
episodes.different: The industry's valuation percentile was 100th then versus 59th today, so there is less de-rating risk. Today the group has outperformed the S&P 500 by 23.7pp over 6M versus 2.3pp then, which makes the relative-strength unwind risk larger.
episodes.lesson: Peak valuations and a slowing cycle punished brokers

episodes.then: September 2023 saw rates rising, long yields spiking and oil climbing, with the S&P 500 about 6% off its high. Brokers were outperforming and trading at elevated multiples.
episodes.after: The industry slipped 0.9% in 1M and 1.8% in 3M, then rose +7.7% at 6M and +11.4% at 12M. The S&P 500 gained +34.8% over 12M, so brokers lagged the market by a wide margin. The worst 6-month drop was -9.2%.
episodes.different: Today the S&P 500 is weaker (-2.6% over 6M vs +5.2%) and VIX is 28 versus 18, so the equity backdrop is shakier. Brokers are far more extended against the market today, which cuts toward giving back relative gains.
episodes.lesson: Positive absolute return, lagging the market

hist.read: Across the five episodes the industry was up at 1 month in four of five, and the 3-month results were mixed: and rose while and fell. The 6-month and 12-month results were positive in four of five, with the clear failure. The base rates agree: median +3% at 1 month, +6.5% at 3, +7.1% at 6 and +7.7% at 12, with the group beating the S&P 500 only 35-50% of the time. That is a modestly positive drift, not an edge, and today's VIX of 28 and the AI selloff differ from the calmer, and, so the history deserves limited weight. The case that most resembles today is on stress, and on the type of selloff and the rebound that followed. Together they support holding neutral weight, expecting a volatile…

episodes.then: In March 2025 the S&P 500 was in a tariff-driven correction, and yields and the dollar were elevated. Exchanges and data firms held up better than the broad market as volatility lifted trading volumes.
episodes.after: The industry fell 2.4% in the first month, then rebounded 11.3% over 3 months and was up 4.8% at 6 months. It ended 12 months up only 3.7%, against 18.5% for the S&P 500, which recovered strongly as tariff fears eased. The worst drop within 6 months was 10.2%.
episodes.different: Today's P/E percentile is 62 versus 93 then, so valuation is less stretched, which helps. But VIX is 28 against 22, and the selloff is an AI-driven one rather than a tariff scare, which cuts against it.
episodes.lesson: Defensive volume winners lag in the rebound

episodes.then: In June 2015 markets were drifting near highs while Greece's debt crisis and worries about China built, ahead of the August 2015 growth scare. The dollar was strong and oil was weak, and exchanges had outperformed after a strong prior year.
episodes.after: The industry gained 3.5% in the first month, then lost 6.3% over 3 months as the August volatility hit. It recovered to +1.2% at 6 months and +0.2% at 12 months, versus +2.6% for the S&P 500. The worst drop was 11%.
episodes.different: Today VIX is 28 against 18, and oil is up 14.8% rather than falling, so stress is higher. The S&P 500 is already down 2.6% over 6 months, whereas it was up 1.1% then.
episodes.lesson: Late-cycle leadership stalls, flat year

episodes.then: In October 2018 equities sold off sharply on Fed tightening worries, trade war fears and rising yields. The industry had been a strong performer, and it was then hit by the broad risk-off move into the December low.
episodes.after: The industry rose 4% in the first month and 2.2% at 3 months, despite the December 2018 slump, and was up 11.9% at 6 months. It was up 22.9% at 12 months versus 15.4% for the S&P 500 after the Fed pivoted. The worst drop was 13.1%.
episodes.different: The 2018 rebound rested on a Fed pivot toward easing. Today yields are rising, with IEF down 0.8% over 6 months, so that support is less certain. On the other hand, the industry now leads the S&P 500 by 5.9pp, whereas in 2018 it trailed by 0.5pp.
episodes.lesson: Selloffs can resolve upward if policy eases

episodes.then: In February 2022 Russia invaded Ukraine, oil spiked, and the Fed was about to begin hiking while growth stocks de-rated. VIX was 30, close to today's level.
episodes.after: The industry rose 4.4% in the first month, then fell 7.9% over 3 months and 10.1% over 6 months. It was down 16.7% at 12 months versus 8.1% for the S&P 500. The worst drop was 24.3%, the deepest of the five, as rate hikes drove a bear market.
episodes.different: Oil rose 40.5% then versus 14.8% now, and the Fed was only starting to tighten. Today's setup has a milder rate shock, and the industry is above its 200-day average (+5%) while it was below then (-3.6%).
episodes.lesson: Rate-shock bear markets hit the group hard

episodes.then: In October 2016 markets were calm ahead of the US election, with yields beginning to rise and the dollar firm. Exchanges had lagged over the prior few months and were cheap relative to their history.
episodes.after: The industry gained 3% in the first month and 7.6% at 3 months, then 12.2% at 6 months and 27.2% at 12 months, versus 23.4% for the S&P 500. The post-election reflation rally and higher yields lifted financials. The worst drop was only 5.8%.
episodes.different: VIX was 17 against 28 now, and the P/E percentile was 36 against 62. Today starts from higher stress and a richer valuation, so a repeat is less likely.
episodes.lesson: Calm backdrop and cheap start gave a strong run

episodes.then: In August 2015 China's yuan devaluation set off a global equity selloff and a VIX spike above 40 intraday, with oil near multi-year lows. Pharma had topped in mid-2015 after a strong run and was hit by drug-pricing rhetoric heading into the 2016 election.
episodes.after: The industry kept slipping: 1M -4.9%, 3M -1.1%, 6M -7.7%, and the worst drop in the next 6 months was -13.6%. The 12M return was 0%, while the S&P 500 recovered to +6.1% at 3M and +12.7% at 12M. The pricing-politics overhang and the sector's rich valuation kept it behind the market.
episodes.different: Today the industry is more depressed (12M -16.4% vs -2.4%), valuation is higher (85th vs 70th pct), and oil and the dollar are rising rather than falling and flat. The deeper drawdown cuts toward more room to rebound, but the richer multiple cuts the other way.
episodes.lesson: Panic lows can still be followed by a lagging, politically capped sector

episodes.then: In February 2025 the market was near highs but worried about tariffs and the new administration's policies. Pharma had lagged badly after GLP-1 disappointments and drug-pricing and HHS policy fears, while its valuation percentile stayed high.
episodes.after: The industry fell further: 1M -1.4%, 3M -4.7%, 6M -4.5%, with a worst drop of -14.4% in the next 6 months. It then recovered strongly to +30.2% at 12M, beating the S&P 500's +15.8%. I am not sure of the exact drivers, but the rebound came after the policy fears eased and the industry started from a depressed level.
episodes.different: Today the VIX is 28 vs 20 and the industry is below its 200-day average (-6% vs +0.4%), and the S&P 500 has been falling rather than rising. A Fed that is hiking, not easing, argues against assuming the same rebound.
episodes.lesson: Same rich multiple and lagging stance; a weak first half-year, then a big rebound

episodes.then: In October 2016 the election was weeks away. Pharma was being hit by Clinton's drug-pricing rhetoric, and bond yields were starting to rise.
episodes.after: The industry was nearly flat at first (1M -0.6%, 3M +0.4%), then rose to +5.7% at 6M and +12.2% at 12M. The S&P 500 was far stronger, at +13.4% at 6M and +23.4% at 12M, so pharma lagged the post-election reflation rally. The worst drop in the next 6 months was only -7.5%.
episodes.different: Today the VIX is 28 vs 17, valuation is much higher (85th vs 45th pct), and the S&P 500 is falling rather than rising. A political overhang that cleared in 2016 appears to be arriving now with a Democratic Congress.
episodes.lesson: Cheap, hated pharma drifted up while the market ran ahead

episodes.then: In June 2018 trade-war tensions with China were escalating, the Fed was hiking and oil had rallied about 25%. Pharma was lagging growth stocks despite the tax cut.
episodes.after: The industry rebounded: 1M +7.6%, 3M +12.7%, 6M +5.9%, 12M +6%. It acted as a defensive as the S&P 500 fell -6.9% at 6M, but the worst drop in the next 6 months was still -12.6%. The 12M S&P 500 return was +11.4%.
episodes.different: The valuation was cheap then (35th pct) and is expensive now (85th pct). The VIX was calm at 16 vs 28 today, so less fear was priced in then. Today's richer multiple makes the defensive bid less secure.
episodes.lesson: Defensive rotation worked when the multiple was cheap

episodes.then: In October 2023 the 10-year Treasury yield hit 5% and equities sold off. Pharma was weak and expensive as the sector was hit by the Covid-product fade, while the obesity theme was starting to build.
episodes.after: The industry rebounded: 1M +2.5%, 3M +11.7%, 6M +9.2%, then slowed to +2.7% at 12M. The S&P 500 was far stronger: +17.5% at 3M, +21.6% at 6M and +37.8% at 12M. The worst drop in the next 6 months was -10.6%.
episodes.different: Yields had fallen sharply then (IEF -8.8%) and the Fed had just finished hiking. Today yields are only slightly higher and the Fed is hiking, which is a worse setup for the multiple.
episodes.lesson: Pharma bounced but lagged a roaring market

moves.label: US core PPI MoM
moves.move: September core PPI rose +0.7% m/m, versus 0.2% prior and 0.3% consensus.
moves.driver: It shows inflation spilling past energy into goods and services, and it feeds a September core PCE estimate of 0.32%.
moves.so_what: It raises the odds that core PCE reaccelerates, which keeps real yields high and caps further multiple expansion for long-duration LLY and ABBV.

moves.label: US GDP
moves.move: Q2 GDP grew 2.2%, versus 2.5% prior and 1.5% consensus.
moves.driver: The analysts found no news coverage of the release.
moves.so_what: Resilient, late-cycle growth barely affects inelastic prescription demand; it matters mainly through the rates path.

moves.label: High-grade corporate 10-year yield (HQM, monthly)
moves.move: The high-grade 10Y corporate yield (HQM) rose to 5.86% for September from 5.58%, a +28bp move.
moves.driver: Rising Treasury yields ahead of the early-October 10Y peak, plus heavy investment-grade supply from hyperscalers funding AI capex.
moves.so_what: Funding costs for debt-financed business development (GILD's $11.2B IPR&D, MRK's Terns deal) rise. At 9.9x interest cover this is not a constraint, but it raises the hurdle rate for M&A.

moves.label: 30Y Treasury yield
moves.move: The 30Y Treasury yield fell to 5.30% from 5.59% a month ago, a -29bp move, after peaking at 5.73%.
moves.driver: A semiconductor rout drove a flight to bonds, and safe-haven demand during French bond turmoil on Oct 22 added to it.
moves.so_what: Easing long-duration yields relieve some pressure on 95th-percentile pharma multiples, but the level remains near two-decade highs.

watch_next.why: A hot print cements a December hike and pressures pharma multiples.

verdict.headline: US federal price regulation is the dominant headwind, compressing Medicare and Medicaid net prices on mature blockbusters, while incretin volume levers and fresh exclusivity clocks make the net effect a split verdict that favors LLY and young-franchise growers over legacy and vaccine-heavy names.
verdict.summary: The offset is volume. Biosimilar, Hatch-Waxman and EU SPC clocks set hard cliffs for mature franchises such as JNJ's STELARA and AMGN's Prolia/XGEVA, and those cliffs drive acquired IPR&D spend and M&A that FTC/HSR review can slow or condition.

episodes.then: November 2021 had the Omicron variant scare and a hawkish turn at the Fed, which sped up its taper as inflation ran hot. Biotech had been weak since its early-2021 peak, and speculative, loss-making names were already sliding.
episodes.after: The industry was down 9% after 1M, 27.8% after 3M, 43.4% after 6M and 36.2% after 12M, with a worst drop of 46.3% inside six months. The S&P 500 also fell, by 9.5% at 6M and 9.2% at 12M. The likely driver was rising rates, which hit long-duration, unprofitable biotech hardest, though I'm not certain of every step of the sequence.
episodes.different: Today the industry sits only 9.7% below its 12-month high against 18.8% then, and its 6-month relative strength is +2.7pp rather than -3.5pp. That cuts mildly in favour of today, though the Treasury and oil backdrop is less benign.
episodes.lesson: Weak biotech tape plus tightening rates can compound into a long drawdown

episodes.then: March 2025 saw tariff fears and a growth scare hit equities ahead of the April tariff announcements. Biotech was also dealing with uncertainty over FDA and HHS leadership and policy.
episodes.after: The industry rose 3.1% after 1M, 4.6% after 3M, 10.7% after 6M and 29.6% after 12M, with a worst 6-month drop of only 9.2%. The S&P 500 gained 19.8% at 6M and 18.5% at 12M. The rebound likely reflected policy fears fading and a recovery in sentiment, but the industry still lagged the market over the first 6 months.
episodes.different: Then the industry P/E was at the 67th percentile and VIX at 22. Today the P/E is at the 42nd percentile with VIX at 28, so valuation is cheaper but the market is more stressed, and the new drug-pricing threat is a political risk with legislative reach.
episodes.lesson: Policy-scare lows can resolve into sharp rebounds

episodes.then: June 2018 had trade-war escalation, a firming dollar, rising oil and a Fed that was hiking rates. Biotech was near its highs for the year, though the data show it 20.8% below its 12-month high.
episodes.after: The industry first rose 3.3% after 1M and 7.3% after 3M, then collapsed to -52.2% after 6M and -51.4% after 12M, with a worst drop of 65.4%. The S&P 500 was -6.9% at 6M but +11.4% at 12M. The late-2018 equity sell-off, with the Fed still hiking, is the likely trigger, but I can't confirm why biotech fell so much further than the market.
episodes.different: VIX was only 16 then versus 28 now, so today's market already prices stress and complacency is lower. That cuts in today's favour, but the deep 6-month fall shows early gains can reverse.
episodes.lesson: An early bounce can be a trap

episodes.then: October 2012 followed the Fed's QE3 launch, with the US election and the looming fiscal cliff ahead. Biotech was in the early stage of a multi-year bull run.
episodes.after: The industry gained 4.2% after 1M, 10.4% after 3M, 28.4% after 6M and 46.6% after 12M, beating the S&P 500 at every horizon (+0.6%, +7.8%, +15.5%, +27.1%). Easy money and a strengthening biotech cycle drove it, and the worst 6-month drop was only 9.3%.
episodes.different: Yields were falling then (IEF +3%) and oil was down 19.9%. Today yields are rising and oil is up 14.8%, which is a tougher macro backdrop that cuts against a repeat.
episodes.lesson: Easy money lifts biotech

episodes.then: August 2015 saw China's yuan devaluation and a global equity flash-crash, with VIX near 28, the same as today. Biotech was coming off a peak in July 2015 on a very high valuation, with drug-pricing criticism building in the autumn.
episodes.after: The industry fell 21.9% after 1M, 14% after 3M, 38% after 6M and 37.7% after 12M, with a worst drop of 48.1%. The S&P 500 was roughly flat to up (+1.8% at 6M, +12.7% at 12M), so the industry lagged badly. A stretched valuation (92nd percentile) and pricing scrutiny were the likely drivers.
episodes.different: Today's P/E percentile is 42nd versus 92nd then, so there is less valuation to deflate. That cuts in today's favour, though drug-pricing risk is again live.
episodes.lesson: Pricing scrutiny hurts, but starting valuation decides how much

The 1M picture is mixed (3 of 5 up, median +2.4%), with showing a sharp early drop. Over 6M the odds improve (75% up, median +4.3%) but the industry usually lags the S&P 500 (30% beat), and 12M is roughly +13.4% at the median with a wide range (-3.9% to +20.2%), with and ending negative. These analogs deserve modest weight because today's 83rd percentile P/E, +20.3% stretch over the 200-day average and +33.2pp 6M lead are more extreme than in any episode. Today most resembles, with a stressed VIX, a strong dollar, an S&P 500 drawdown…

episodes.then: October 2018 brought a sharp equity selloff as the Fed kept hiking and 10-year yields reached about 3.2%, with a strong dollar and the S&P 500 about 7% off its high. Healthcare had been a market leader that year; I am not certain how diagnostics specifically traded within the month.
episodes.after: The industry gained 0.3% at 1M, fell 5.9% at 3M, then was up 4.5% at 6M and 2% at 12M, with a worst drop of -21.5% in the next 6 months. The S&P 500 gained 1.9% at 1M, 1.1% at 3M, 9.3% at 6M and 15.4% at 12M. The Q4 2018 selloff and the Fed's pivot in early 2019 fit a pattern of the market recovering while a previous leader lagged, though I am not sure of the sector-specific drivers.
episodes.different: Today's industry is far more stretched: +20.3% above its 200-day average versus +8.5%, a P/E at the 83rd percentile versus the 59th, and a VIX of 28 versus 21. That cuts toward a bumpier path, and oil is up 14.8% now versus roughly flat then.
episodes.lesson: Stretched leaders lag the rebound

episodes.then: February 2021 was the reflation trade, with Treasury yields rising, oil surging and the VIX near 28 after the January retail-trading squeeze. Diagnostics were still riding pandemic testing demand during the vaccine rollout and sat about 9% below their high.
episodes.after: The industry slipped 1.5% at 1M, then gained 5% at 3M and 21.1% at 6M, but was down 5% at 12M, with a worst drop of -8.4% in the next 6 months. The S&P 500 gained 4.4% at 1M, 10.6% at 3M, 18.1% at 6M and 16.6% at 12M. The 12M fade is consistent with COVID-testing demand rolling over, though I would not pin it on a single cause.
episodes.different: In 2021 the S&P 500 was up 9.8% over 6M and credit was strong (+8.5pp), while today the S&P 500 is down 2.6% and credit is flat, so market support is much weaker. Treasuries are also down only 0.8% over 6M now versus 4.4% then.
episodes.lesson: A strong 6M can precede a 12M fade

episodes.then: January 2014 saw a modest equity wobble from emerging-market stress and Fed tapering, while the US economy was recovering steadily. Life-science tools and diagnostics were strong, with the industry up about 38% over 12 months.
episodes.after: The industry gained 7.1% at 1M, fell 1.7% at 3M, then was up 4.7% at 6M and 15.6% at 12M, with a worst drop of -8.9% in the next 6 months. The S&P 500 gained 5.3% at 1M, 6% at 3M, 9% at 6M and 15.5% at 12M. After a quick bounce the industry lagged the market for several months before roughly matching it at 12M.
episodes.different: Valuation was cheap then (35th percentile) with a VIX of 18, against an 83rd percentile P/E and a VIX of 28 today. That cuts toward more downside risk now, since there is less valuation cushion and more market stress.
episodes.lesson: Early bounce, then lagging

episodes.then: June 2015 came ahead of the Greek debt crisis and the August China devaluation shock, with a strong dollar and weak oil. Healthcare was in a late-cycle leadership phase and the industry was near its high.
episodes.after: The industry gained 3% at 1M, then fell 13.5% at 3M, was down 2.6% at 6M and down 9% at 12M, with a worst drop of -16.7% in the next 6 months. The S&P 500 gained 2.4% at 1M, fell 8.1% at 3M, and was up 1.9% at 6M and 2.6% at 12M. The August 2015 selloff and drug-pricing pressure on healthcare likely contributed, though I am less sure of the diagnostics specifics.
episodes.different: The industry was near its high then (-0.4%) with a P/E at the 40th percentile. Today it is already 10.1% below its high but with a much richer valuation, so some de-rating has begun while the multiple is still elevated.
episodes.lesson: Late-cycle leaders fall hardest in selloffs

episodes.then: September 2016 was a calm, low-volatility market (VIX 13) ahead of the US election, with the S&P 500 near its high and oil recovering. Healthcare was wobbling on drug-pricing rhetoric.
episodes.after: The industry fell 9.1% at 1M and 8.6% at 3M, then recovered to +3.3% at 6M and +15.4% at 12M, with a worst drop of -10.7% in the next 6 months. The S&P 500 fell 1.7% at 1M, then gained 4% at 3M, 9.9% at 6M and 19% at 12M. The post-election rotation into cyclicals and financials likely left healthcare-linked groups behind early on.
episodes.different: Today's VIX is 28 against 13, and the S&P 500 is 5.9% off its high rather than at it. Stress is already more visible, which cuts toward a rockier path but possibly less of a sudden shock.
episodes.lesson: Rotation can hurt before the recovery

scenarios.name: Base case
scenarios.trigger: Hold on Oct 28 with a hawkish-leaning tone, then a 25bp December hike to 4.00-4.25% as inflation stays above 3%.
scenarios.outcome: 10Y trades 4.85-5.15% (estimate) and real yields stay 2.5-2.8% (estimate). High-multiple tech multiples drift lower while AI capex plans hold but get financed at higher spreads.

scenarios.name: Escalation
scenarios.trigger: Firm PPI and oil readings plus Warsh signaling more than one further hike (Ferguson-style 'two hikes' path).
scenarios.outcome: 10Y breaks to 5.25-5.50% (estimate) and IG spreads widen 20-50bp (estimate). Neocloud and AI-lab funding windows narrow, marginal AI capex is deferred, and long-duration equities derate sharply.

scenarios.name: De-escalation
scenarios.trigger: Weaker job growth and tighter AI financing do part of the Fed's work, so Warsh gets 'fewer rate hikes'.
scenarios.outcome: December hike priced out, 10Y retreats to 4.50-4.75% (estimate), and multiples on long-duration software and AI chips partially re-rate.

reads.perf: The group is +19.2% vs SPY over 1M and +12.4% over 3M but still -14.8% over 1Y. The bounce came from money rotating out of AI and tech into defensives (XLV +9.5% in October), not from earnings.
reads.risk: Beta of 0.37 and downside vol of 14.6% are defensive. The stock-specific shocks behind last year's -9.3% alpha and -28.7% max drawdown were mainly the BSX, SYK and ABT cyber incidents.
reads.fund: Revenue grew 8.1%, but earnings fell 5.4% as cyber outages, tariffs and input costs broke the conversion from sales to profit. Gross margin of 59.9% and an FCF margin of 13.7% (126% of net income) show the cash engine is intact.
reads.health: D/E of 0.56, interest cover of 7.0x and net debt/EBITDA of 1.97 are comfortable for the large caps. The stretched balance sheets (GKOS, ITGR, ATEC and others, about 7% of the industry) are the names exposed to widening credit spreads.
reads.val: A trailing P/E of 33.8 (30th percentile of 5Y) against a forward 19.1 assumes adjusted EPS recovers. The reverse DCF implies just 2.7% FCF growth, so the multiple is fair and undemanding. It offers no cushion against a 10Y retest of 5.2%.
reads.earn: The beat rate is 73% with a 7.5% median surprise, but revision breadth is -0.07 and only 33% of companies have rising estimates. BSX (-7.4%) and SYK (-2.3%) are being cut, while EW, GEHC and DXCM raised guidance.
reads.cycle: Cycle: expansion, pricing power moderate. Med-device demand remains healthy at the procedure level. The 50-company group grew TTM revenue +8.5%, and large caps posted organic growth of 6-14%: MDT +13.7% including about 670bp from an extra week, EW +12.5%, SYK +9%, ABT +7% and GEHC +6.2%.
reads.macro: MIXED: MIXED: procedure demand holds (TTM revenue +8.1%, EW TMTT +44.8%) but the Gulf energy shock (Brent $115.4, PPI +1.3% m/m) and a 4.84% 10Y with a December Fed hike priced cap margins and multiples
reads.world: Iran war and Gulf energy shock: Hormuz blockade, Houthi strikes on Saudi oil, start of US-Iran talks (adverse)
reads.trade: manageable: Demand is in expansion and the supply base runs through allied, duty-free nearshore hubs, but single-site concentration in Ireland, Malaysia and Mexico, Gulf energy escalation and China price erosion cap the system at manageable rather than healthy.

hist.read: The episodes agree on a near-term bounce: all five were up at 1M (median +2.6%, 85% positive in the base rate). Beyond that they split, with three of five negative at 3M, four of five negative at 6M and three of five negative at 12M, and all five suffered drawdowns of 6% to 25% in the next 6 months. Devices beat the S&P only about 30-35% of the time at every horizon, and the S&P rebounded strongly after, and. That argues against paying up for the safe-haven rally, and the sample is just five episodes with real differences (VIX 28, a 15pp lead, and no extreme valuation), so I would give it modest weight, which supports the team's roughly 0% 12-month expectation and the market-weight stance.…

episodes.then: In June 2015 markets were focused on the Greek debt crisis and an approaching first Fed hike, with the dollar strong and oil already well off its 2014 peak. Medical devices were in a strong run, helped by a wave of sector M&A, though I'm not certain of the specific deals that month.
episodes.after: The industry rose 7.7% over 1M, then slid 8.1% over 3M as the August 2015 China-devaluation selloff hit, with a worst drop of 17.1% in the next 6 months. It was -0.6% at 6M and -4.3% at 12M, while the S&P 500 was +2.6% at 12M. A quick bounce, then a drawdown, left devices lagging the index.
episodes.different: Today's VIX of 28 is well above the 18 then, and the industry's 12-month return of -10.5% compares with +19.6% then, so today is a washed-out sector rather than an extended one. That cuts mildly in favour of less downside than saw.
episodes.lesson: Early bounce, then a stress-driven fade

episodes.then: In March 2025 the S&P 500 was in a tariff-driven correction, with growth worries and a stronger dollar. Devices were holding up relatively well, though their valuation was already stretched.
episodes.after: The industry gained 0.5% over 1M, 5.7% over 3M and 6.4% over 6M, ending +2.7% at 12M, with a worst drop of only 5.9%. The S&P 500 rebounded much harder (+19.8% at 6M, +18.5% at 12M) as tariff fears faded, so devices kept their gains but lagged badly. Defensive positioning paid off in the drawdown but not in the recovery.
episodes.different: The industry P/E percentile was 98th then versus 47th today, so valuation is far less demanding now. Today's 6M relative strength of +15pp against +4pp then also suggests a bigger safe-haven bid that could unwind. The valuation gap cuts favourably, the crowding cuts the other way.
episodes.lesson: Defensive gains held, but lagged the rebound

episodes.then: January 2010 saw a sharp pullback in equities on Greek and sovereign-debt worries and Obama's bank-reform proposals, in the early recovery from the financial crisis. Devices were cheap on their own history (11th percentile) and had lagged the market rally.
episodes.after: The industry was +0.8% at 1M and -0.6% at 3M, then fell to -13.2% at 6M and -11.5% at 12M, with a worst drop of 17.4%. The S&P 500 was +21.3% at 12M. I'm not certain what drove the sector's weakness, though the healthcare-reform debate and the May 2010 flash-crash and Europe scare fall inside the window.
episodes.different: The S&P 500 was up 9.8% over 6M then, whereas today it is down 2.6%, so the market is weaker now. The valuation start was also very different, at the 11th percentile versus the 47th. That cuts against using's relative weakness.
episodes.lesson: Cheap sectors can still lag a recovering market

episodes.then: June 2018 had the start of US-China tariff escalation, rising oil, a strengthening dollar and a Fed in hiking mode. Devices were leading the market, with a high valuation percentile (81st).
episodes.after: The industry was +2.6% at 1M and +11.5% at 3M, then fell back to -1.8% at 6M, but finished +12.3% at 12M. The worst drop in the next 6 months was 19%, probably tied to the Q4 2018 selloff. The S&P 500 was -6.9% at 6M and +11.4% at 12M, so devices ended roughly level with it after a violent round trip.
episodes.different: VIX was 16 then and is 28 now, so stress is already priced in today. The industry's 12-month return was +13.1% then against -10.5% now, so there is less froth to unwind. Both cut in favour of a milder path.
episodes.lesson: Big drawdown, then recovery by 12M

episodes.then: May 2023 featured the debt-ceiling standoff, aftershocks of the regional-bank failures and an AI-led narrow rally. Devices were still lagging after a weak year, with post-pandemic procedure volumes recovering.
episodes.after: The industry rose 9.4% over 1M, then fell 0.9% at 3M and 7.4% at 6M, ending -1% at 12M, with a worst drop of 24.5%. The S&P 500 was +28% at 12M, driven by the AI rally and by rate-cut hopes. Devices lagged very badly even as the market soared.
episodes.different: Today the industry leads the S&P by 15pp over 6M, whereas it was lagging by 2.6pp then, and the S&P is under stress rather than at highs. Today's relative strength has more to lose if the market stabilizes. That cuts against the sector.
episodes.lesson: Rebounds faded while the market ran away
