Given today's much larger lead over the S&P 500 and the stretch above the 200-day average, is the closest analog: a defensive rally with rising yields and oil, followed by a 6M give-back and later recovery. That supports staying neutral with a cautious tilt rather than…

episodes.then: In June 2018 the Fed was hiking, the dollar was firming, oil was rallying and US-China tariff escalation was starting to unsettle markets. Healthcare equipment was a leadership group after a strong year.
episodes.after: The industry gained 4.8% in 1M and 10.9% in 3M, then gave it back, with a 6M return of -6.1% and a worst drop of -21.7%. That fits the Q4 2018 selloff on Fed tightening and growth fears. The 12M return was +12.2% versus +11.4% for the S&P 500, so the group recovered with the market in 2019.
episodes.different: Today VIX is 28 against 16 then, the industry's lead over the S&P 500 is +36.9pp versus +10.7pp, and it trades 18.8% above its 200-day average versus 7.9%. The stretch is far greater now, which cuts toward a harsher pullback.
episodes.lesson: Rally first, drawdown later, then recovery

episodes.then: In June 2017 markets were calm, with VIX near 11, a falling dollar, and synchronized global growth. The industry was at a 12-month high after a strong run.
episodes.after: The industry slipped 0.5% in 1M, then returned +1.9% in 3M and +6.3% in 6M, with only a 6.5% worst drop. It reached +21.5% in 12M, but trailed the S&P 500's +14.5% only in the shorter windows. The calm, rising market let the strength carry on.
episodes.different: Today has VIX at 28, a rising dollar, oil up 14.8% and the S&P 500 down 2.6% over 6M, compared with a calm, rising market then. The stress backdrop cuts against repeating this smooth path.
episodes.lesson: Calm markets let leaders keep running

episodes.then: In July 2011 the US debt-ceiling fight and the S&P downgrade, plus the euro-area crisis, drove a sharp risk-off move. Medical device stocks had outperformed on defensive demand.
episodes.after: The industry fell 11.6% in 1M and was down 4.2% over 3M, with a worst drop of -17.9%. It was still down 2.5% at 12M while the S&P 500 gained 9.5%. Defensives were hit in the panic and then lagged the recovery.
episodes.different: The industry's P/E percentile is 77th today versus 13th then, so valuation offers less cushion. That cuts toward a worse outcome now.
episodes.lesson: Defensive leaders can still be sold in panics

episodes.then: In April 2025 tariff shock and a sharp market selloff drove VIX up to the mid-20s. The industry held up relatively well, though it was richly valued.
episodes.after: The industry rose 2.1% in 1M but was down 1.4% at 3M and 6.6% at 6M, with a worst drop of -15.3%. At 12M it was down 2.5% while the S&P 500 returned +31.4%. The market rebounded strongly and the defensive group was left behind.
episodes.different: Today the S&P 500 is only 5.9% below its high, versus 9.3% then, and yields are rising, so the market has not yet had a washout. That could cut either way: less room for a V-shaped rebound, but also less damage already done.
episodes.lesson: Defensive winners lag when the market rebounds

episodes.then: In September 2021 inflation worries, the Fed's taper talk and an oil surge hit markets. Medtech was richly valued after a pandemic-recovery run.
episodes.after: The industry gained 2.1% in 1M and 2% in 3M, then fell 9.7% over 6M, with a worst drop of -18.9%. At 12M it was down 40.2% versus -15.5% for the S&P 500, which reflects the 2022 rate-driven derating. I don't know the exact industry-level drivers beyond that.
episodes.different: Today the industry is up 12.4% in 3M and sits 18.8% above its 200-day average, a much more stretched run than then. That cuts toward more downside risk if rates push higher.
episodes.lesson: Rich valuations plus rising yields hurt

hist.read: The five episodes and the base rates lean mildly positive, but they are dispersed. The industry rose in 3 of 5 episodes at 1 month and only 2 of 5 at 3 months, with 4 of 5 up at 6 and 12 months. The 20-month base rates show medians of +4% at 1 month and +5.4% at 3 months, and the industry beat the S&P 500 only 40-55% of the time. Two episodes saw 6-month drawdowns of roughly 18-20%, and and lagged the S&P 500 badly at every horizon, so further downside before any recovery is plausible. I would give these analogs moderate weight because oil, the dollar and yields are all rising today, unlike in most of these episodes, and valuation is not cheap. Today most resembles, which fits the team's…

episodes.then: April 2025 was the tariff shock: a violent equity selloff with VIX in the mid-20s and high-yield spreads widening. Managed care was already under pressure from rising Medicare Advantage cost trends and UnitedHealth's guidance cut that month.
episodes.after: The industry fell 9% in the first month and 12.6% over three months, while the S&P 500 rose 6.3% and then 14.3%. It recovered to +2% at 6 months and +11.3% at 12 months, against +24.7% and +31.4% for the S&P. The worst drop inside the first 6 months was 19.5%. I believe the early slide came from guidance withdrawals and cost-trend worries, but I am not certain of every detail.
episodes.different: Then, yields were falling (IEF +3.6%) and oil was down 13%. Today yields are rising, oil is up 14.8% and the dollar is up 4.6%, a more inflationary backdrop that cuts against a clean rebound. Today's 12-month industry return is about flat (+0.9%) versus -16.7% then, so less washout has already…
episodes.lesson: Closest match: the recovery came only after a further 10-20% air pocket

episodes.then: February 2023 had sticky inflation, a hawkish Fed and rising yields, a month before the Silicon Valley Bank stress. Managed care had sold off on a weak proposed Medicare Advantage rate notice and on questions about utilization.
episodes.after: The industry was down 4.9% at 1 month, 6.1% at 3 months, 4.5% at 6 months and 3% at 12 months. The S&P 500 gained 14.2% over 6 months and 30.2% over 12 months, so the sector lagged badly. The worst drop in the first 6 months was 14%. I can't pin down the drivers with confidence beyond cost-trend and policy worries.
episodes.different: VIX was 21 then versus 28 now, so today's market stress is higher. Today's 67th-percentile valuation sits above the 58th then, which leaves a little less cushion.
episodes.lesson: A defensive-looking sector can still lag a rising market

episodes.then: March 2018 was a choppy, risk-off month after the February volatility spike, with trade-war fears and a tech wobble. Insurers had pulled back after a strong run, and Cigna's Express Scripts deal showed continued consolidation.
episodes.after: The industry rose 8.9% in a month, 10.6% over 3 months and 24.4% over 6 months, then ended at +13.9% at 12 months. The S&P 500 gained 11.5% over 6 months and 10.7% over 12 months. The worst drop in the first 6 months was only 6%, so the dip was bought quickly.
episodes.different: The industry's slump was shallower then (3M -6.4%, 200-day gap -2.5%) and VIX was 20. Today's deeper damage (3M -12.8%, 200-day gap -13%) comes with a more fragile earnings story, which cuts both ways: more room to rebound, but more risk that the earnings problem is real.
episodes.lesson: Fast rebound when the earnings backdrop was intact

episodes.then: October 2016 was the pre-election month, with low volatility (VIX 17) and a modest equity pullback. Managed care was weak on ACA exchange losses and antitrust challenges to the Aetna-Humana and Anthem-Cigna mergers.
episodes.after: The industry rose 8.9% in a month and 11.5% in 3 months, finishing +19.7% at 6 months and +34.5% at 12 months. The S&P 500 rose 13.4% and 23.4% over those last two horizons. The worst drop in the first 6 months was just 4%. The election outcome and the reduced regulatory overhang were the main drivers.
episodes.different: There was a visible policy catalyst then, and the market was calm. Today, VIX is 28 and the catalysts are the January 2027 guidance updates, which could go either way.
episodes.lesson: A resolved policy overhang can unleash a big rally

episodes.then: May 2019 brought the escalation in US-China tariffs, a drop in yields, and the market starting to price Fed cuts. Managed care was hit by the Democratic Medicare for All debate.
episodes.after: The industry rose 1.3% at 1 month, fell 3.1% at 3 months, then gained 15.2% at 6 months and ended at +1.8% at 12 months. The S&P 500 was up 15.7% at 6 months and 13.3% at 12 months. The worst drop in the first 6 months was 17.7%. The policy scare faded by year-end, and the 12-month figure also spans the early-2020 pandemic crash, which I believe was a factor.
episodes.different: Yields were falling then (IEF +8.3%) with a Fed pivot ahead; today yields are rising. The valuation percentile was 39th then versus 67th now, so today's starting valuation is less forgiving.
episodes.lesson: A volatile path, with a deep drawdown before the recovery

reads.perf: The industry trails SPY by 17.6% over 1Y and 12.7% over 6M, and only 21% of names beat SPY over the year. The gap reflects de-rating more than earnings, since backlogs hit records.
reads.risk: Beta of 1.38, 34.1% volatility and a -27.8% max drawdown make the aggregate a high-risk asset, and a Sharpe of -0.06 shows it has not paid for that risk. The NY Fed corporate distress index sits at the 98th percentile, though high-yield distress is only 0.11 and broad HY spreads tightened over 3M.
reads.fund: TTM revenue growth of 12.6% and a 22.1% gross margin hide a split business. Engines and parts earn 28-46% margins and primes 10-14%, while SPCX's capex pushes the aggregate FCF margin to 1.0% (-0.5% after SBC).
reads.health: Aggregate D/E of 0.57 and 4.1x interest cover look adequate, but net debt/EBITDA improved mainly on SPCX IPO cash, and two-thirds of the cap sits on stretched balance sheets. The pressure points are BA's $45.9B of unchanged debt and SPCX's funding needs for $35-40B of quarterly capex.
reads.val: A trailing P/E of 72.5x (84th percentile, 45% above the 5Y median) and a 0.17% FCF yield imply 59.5% annual FCF growth, an SPCX cash-conversion bet. On NTM earnings the hurdle is a more modest 16.7%.
reads.earn: The beat rate is 78% with a 9.0% median surprise, and five of six large reporters raised guidance. Quality caveats are growing: RTX's $0.25 of one-off IEEPA recovery, LMT's Aero trim and BA's 777X-contingent cash path.
reads.cycle: Cycle: expansion, pricing power strong. Demand is broad. Defense primes posted record backlogs, led by RTX at $340B (+36% y/y, Q3 defense book-to-bill 4.57x on Tomahawk and AMRAAM multiyears), LMT at $292B (+$113B y/y) and NOC at $110B (+20%).

hist.read: The five episodes split: was a further slide, while,, and were positive at 12M. The base rates are mild: median 1M +0.5%, 3M +3.4%, 6M +3.9% and 12M +8.3%, with the industry beating the S&P 500 only about 35% of the time at 3M or longer. Expect volatility, with a real chance of a further 15-35% drawdown as in or, and modest relative edge. Today most resembles: yields rising, oil up, dollar up, a similar deep industry drawdown and weak relative strength. deserves the most weight, but it was a Fed-hiking regime, and the 0th-percentile P/E gives some cushion, so I would lean toward quality cash generators and not toward the broad group.

episodes.then: January 2022 brought a hawkish Fed pivot, rising yields, a growth-stock selloff and Russia-Ukraine tension just before the invasion. Aerospace & Defense had been weak through 2021, with supply-chain problems and a commercial aerospace recovery that was still stalling.
episodes.after: The industry kept falling: -6.6% after 1M, -18.5% at 3M, -27.3% at 6M and -25.7% at 12M, with a worst drawdown of -36.4% in the first 6 months. The S&P 500 also fell (-8.6% at 6M, -7.2% at 12M) as the Fed hiked and inflation persisted. I am not certain which specific industry shocks drove the gap beyond that macro and rate pressure.
episodes.different: Today the S&P 500 6M return is -2.6% rather than +3.3%, and the industry P/E is at the 0th percentile versus the 13th then. Cheaper starting valuations cut toward a better outcome, but a weaker equity tape and a higher VIX cut the other way.
episodes.lesson: Washed-out valuation did not stop a further 25% slide

episodes.then: In July 2012 the euro-crisis fear was peaking, just before Draghi's "whatever it takes" pledge, and US growth was soft. Defense stocks were weighed down by looming sequestration budget cuts and the fiscal-cliff debate.
episodes.after: The industry was calm and then rallied: -0.5% at 1M, +0.6% at 3M, +5.9% at 6M and +30% at 12M, with a worst drop of only -7.7%. The S&P 500 did better at 6M (+11.2%) and 12M (+26.9%) as central-bank support lifted markets. Budget worries faded as the fiscal outcome became clearer.
episodes.different: VIX was 19 then versus 28 now, oil was falling rather than up 14.8%, and yields were falling rather than rising. Today's backdrop is more stressed and carries more inflation risk, which cuts against a repeat.
episodes.lesson: Budget fear priced in, then relief rally

episodes.then: October 2020 saw the pandemic recovery, with the US election and a second COVID wave ahead, VIX at 38 and commercial aerospace still depressed. Defense names lagged the market's reopening trade.
episodes.after: The industry rebounded sharply: +14.8% at 1M, +39.8% at 3M, +23.4% at 6M and +16.5% at 12M, although the worst drawdown in the first 6 months was -22.3%. The S&P 500 did better still, at +42.9% over 12M, driven by vaccine news and stimulus. The industry beat the index in none of the 3M, 6M or 12M windows.
episodes.different: That was an externally shocked, liquidity-fueled recovery with credit spreads improving (+7.7pp), and today credit is flat (-0.1pp) and the dollar is rising. Today lacks the stimulus tailwind.
episodes.lesson: Crash rebounds need a liquidity or reopening catalyst

episodes.then: August 2010 was the "double-dip" recession scare, with weak data, Treasury yields falling and QE2 expectations building. Defense stocks were cheap and lagging as budget-restraint talk grew.
episodes.after: The industry rose: +9.5% at 1M, +10.4% at 3M, +19.1% at 6M and +4.8% at 12M, with a worst drop of only -6.8%. It lagged the S&P 500 (+25.9% at 6M, +17.9% at 12M), which rallied on QE2. That implies a cheap-stock bounce with relative underperformance.
episodes.different: Then, yields were falling (IEF +11.3%) and oil was weak, which supported easing. Today yields are rising and oil is up, so there is less monetary relief.
episodes.lesson: Cheap rebound, but lagged the market

episodes.then: August 2015 saw China's devaluation, a global growth scare and a sharp VIX spike, with oil falling. The industry had been pulling back from highs but was not deeply depressed.
episodes.after: The industry was choppy: -6.3% at 1M, +3.7% at 3M, -2.3% at 6M and +15.1% at 12M, with a worst drawdown of -15.2%. The S&P 500 was +1.8% at 6M and +12.7% at 12M, and the early 2016 selloff came in between. The path was volatile but ended higher.
episodes.different: The industry was only mildly weak then (12M -0.6%, P/E 53rd percentile), versus a deep drawdown and 0th percentile P/E now. Today is a more extreme setup and the oil tailwind is reversed.
episodes.lesson: Panic dips can be retested before recovery

hist.read: The episodes lean toward a rebound but with high dispersion. 3M was up in four of five (the medians in the base rates are +2.8% at 1M and +3.1% at 3M), 6M was a coin flip at 3 of 5 (median +1.3%), and 12M was up in four of five (median +4.1%). The base rates also show the industry beating the S&P 500 only 25% of the time at 6M and 15% at 12M, which argues against going overweight. Drawdowns of about -18% to -20% in the following 6 months occurred in, and, so a deeper dip is a real risk. looks closest today given the high VIX, oil strength and a deep drawdown, while is the bullish counterpoint, so the neutral stance fits and these analogues deserve only moderate weight.

episodes.then: March 2025 was the tariff-shock selloff: the S&P 500 was sliding toward its April low on 'Liberation Day' fears and growth worries. Machinery stocks were hit by tariff and capex uncertainty.
episodes.after: The industry rebounded: +3% in 1M, +11.7% in 3M, +12.3% in 6M and +16.7% in 12M, against the S&P 500's +18.5% over 12M. The worst drawdown in the next 6 months was only -7.9%, so the policy scare faded quickly and the group bounced, though it still trailed the index slightly.
episodes.different: Today the industry is far weaker (-29.6% from its 12-month high vs -19%, and -20.2% vs its 200-day average vs -7.6%) and credit spreads are no longer a tailwind. That makes today a deeper, more entrenched drawdown, which could cut either way: more rebound room or a more damaged trend.
episodes.lesson: Policy-scare drawdowns can reverse fast

episodes.then: October 2018 was the Q4 selloff, driven by Fed tightening worries, the US-China trade war and slowing global growth. Industrials were hit hard as the S&P 500 fell toward its December low.
episodes.after: The industry was up +4.3% in 1M but only +1.7% in 3M, with a worst drop of -18.2% in the next 6 months, which fits the December low. It then recovered to +11.8% in 6M and +11.8% in 12M, versus the S&P 500's +15.4% over 12M, so it was a painful path to a decent gain.
episodes.different: In 2018 the P/E percentile was low (39th) and the VIX was 21. Today valuation sits at the 71st percentile and the VIX is 28, so there is less valuation cushion and more fear than then.
episodes.lesson: Expect a deep dip before recovery

episodes.then: August 2015 saw China's yuan devaluation and a global growth scare, with a VIX spike and an oil and commodity slump that hurt industrial capex names. The industrial cycle was in a manufacturing recession.
episodes.after: The industry fell -8.6% in 1M and was -0.2% in 3M and -3.6% in 6M, with a worst drop of -18.3%, before recovering to +11.6% over 12M. The S&P 500 did better over 6M at +1.8% and rose +12.7% over 12M, so Machinery lagged for half a year and then caught up.
episodes.different: Then valuations were cheap (14th percentile) and oil was falling. Today valuation is high (71st percentile) and oil is up +14.8%, so there is less valuation support and more cost and inflation pressure.
episodes.lesson: Cheap multiples gave a floor; today's don't

episodes.then: April 2022 was the inflation and Fed-hiking bear market, with yields surging, oil spiking after Russia's invasion of Ukraine and a VIX of 33. Machinery was down sharply with the broad market.
episodes.after: The industry was roughly flat: -0.5% in 1M, +2.9% in 3M, +0.4% in 6M and +3.3% in 12M, with a worst drop of -19.8%. It beat the S&P 500's -4.8% over 6M, though the bear market kept both volatile.
episodes.different: In 2022 yields were surging (IEF -9.8% over 6M) and a hiking cycle drove the damage. Today yields are easing slightly (the 10Y at 4.84%) and the pressure comes from an AI-trade crash, which differs in source though the oil and VIX backdrop is similar.
episodes.lesson: Bear-market chop, with the industry holding up

episodes.then: September 2014 was the start of the dollar surge and oil collapse, with the S&P 500 near highs but industrials already lagging. Machinery had sold off about -10.6% over three months.
episodes.after: The industry rose +3.1% in 1M and +5.1% in 3M but gave back to -1.9% in 6M and fell -21.8% over 12M, with a worst drop of -10.5%. The S&P 500 was +5.5% over 6M, so the weak relative trend persisted as the oil bust hit energy-linked capex.
episodes.different: Then the S&P 500 was near its highs (-1.9%) with a calm VIX of 16. Today the market is also in a drawdown (-5.9%) and the VIX is 28, so the stress is broader, and today's setup is harsher.
episodes.lesson: Early bounces can fade into relative weakness

The deepest drawdowns of 17-26% came in the expensive-multiple analogs, and, while shows the upside if easy policy and credit return. Five episodes is a small sample and today's relative strength and VIX of 28 differ from them, so the weight is moderate, but it supports staying neutral on the group and not paying up. Today most resembles: a high valuation, higher oil, a stronger dollar and rising yields against a…

episodes.then: In January 2022 the Fed turned hawkish and signalled rate hikes, yields jumped, growth stocks sold off, and Russia-Ukraine tensions were building while oil climbed. Industrial distributors had run strongly through 2021 but were already 12.6% below their 12-month high.
episodes.after: The industry fell 4.4% in 1M, 11.1% in 3M, 12.4% in 6M and 7.4% in 12M, with a worst drop of 24% inside six months. The S&P 500 also fell (-8.6% at 6M, -7.2% at 12M) as rate hikes and the Ukraine invasion compressed multiples, and the industry fell more than the index at 6M.
episodes.different: Today's P/E percentile is 86th versus 55th then, so there is less valuation cushion, which cuts against today. The rise in yields has been milder (IEF -0.8% versus -3.9%) and the industry is only 4.9% off its high rather than 12.6%, which cuts in its favour.
episodes.lesson: Rising yields plus a stretched multiple hurt.

episodes.then: In June 2018 the Fed was hiking, the US-China tariff fight was escalating, the dollar was firming and oil was rising. Industrial distributors were richly valued (92nd percentile) and held up near their highs.
episodes.after: The industry gained 7% in 1M and 9.2% in 3M, then gave it all back, falling 14.5% at 6M and 6.7% at 12M, with a worst drop of 25.8%. The S&P 500 also fell 6.9% at 6M but was up 11.4% at 12M, so the market recovered from the late-2018 tightening and growth scare while the industry did not.
episodes.different: The VIX was 16 then and is 28 now, so some stress is already priced in, which cuts in today's favour. The industry's lead over the S&P 500 was only 0.2pp then versus 6.3pp now, so today's stock has more relative strength to lose.
episodes.lesson: Early gains can fade into a deep drawdown.

episodes.then: In April 2025 the tariff shock had just hit markets, the VIX was elevated and the S&P 500 was in a sharp drawdown. The industry was holding up better than the market.
episodes.after: The industry was roughly flat at first (+1.7% in 1M, +0.1% in 3M), slipped 1.6% at 6M, then gained 17.2% at 12M, with a worst drop of only 8%. The S&P 500 surged (+24.7% at 6M, +31.4% at 12M), so the industry lagged badly in the rebound. I am not certain of the exact drivers beyond the broad recovery from the tariff shock.
episodes.different: Then yields were falling (IEF +3.6%) and the dollar was weaker (-1.9%), while today yields are up and the dollar is up 4.6%, a tighter backdrop. The multiple is also higher now (86th versus 64th percentile). Both cut against today.
episodes.lesson: Defensive but lagging in a rebound.

episodes.then: In February 2021 reopening and stimulus were driving a cyclical rally, yields were rising and oil was surging. The industry was at an extreme valuation (99th percentile) after a strong run.
episodes.after: The industry rose 4.8% in 1M, 15.7% in 3M, 18.3% in 6M and 16% in 12M, in line with the S&P 500 (+18.1% at 6M, +16.6% at 12M). The worst drop was only 6%, as the reopening-driven earnings recovery outweighed higher yields.
episodes.different: Then credit was strongly supportive (high-yield +8.5pp) and the S&P 500 was up 9.8% over 6M, while today credit is flat (-0.1pp) and the S&P 500 is down 2.6%. That cuts against today.
episodes.lesson: Easy policy let rich valuations keep rising.

episodes.then: In June 2015 the dollar was strong, oil and commodities were weak, and industrial activity was soft ahead of the China devaluation scare that August. Distributors were expensive (98th percentile) and lagging the market.
episodes.after: The industry fell 3.2% in 1M, 14.2% in 3M, 13.6% at 6M and 11.5% at 12M, with a worst drop of 17.4%. The S&P 500 was roughly flat to slightly up (+1.9% at 6M, +2.6% at 12M), so the industry badly underperformed during the industrial slowdown.
episodes.different: The industry lagged the S&P 500 then (-5.7pp) while today it leads by 6.3pp, and oil was falling then but is up now. That cuts in today's favour, though the 86th percentile P/E is still rich.
episodes.lesson: Expensive cyclicals fell when the dollar rose.

hist.read: The five episodes are mixed: and rebounded strongly, and fell, and was modestly positive. The base rates are weak: 1M up 65% of the time, but 6M and 12M up only 55% and 50% (all months 62%), with the group beating the S&P 500 only 30% over 6M and 25% over 12M. That supports the team's market-weight view and a selective stance rather than an overweight, with a drawdown of 9-15% plausible over six months. Today most resembles, a tariff-style sell-off with a defensive group lagging, but the higher valuation (93rd percentile) and the 4.84% yield make the main risk; sample size is small, so the weight on these analogs should be modest.

episodes.then: In March 2025 markets were selling off on tariff fears and growth worries ahead of the April 'Liberation Day' announcement. Railroads were hit by tariff and trade-volume concerns and by the proposed Union Pacific–Norfolk Southern merger, which was not announced until July.
episodes.after: The industry rose 1.6% in 1M, 10.7% in 3M, 7.9% in 6M and 19.6% in 12M, while the S&P 500 returned 18.5% over 12M. The worst drop within 6 months was -9.1%, so the rebound came after a further dip. The market recovered once tariff fears eased, and railroads recovered with it.
episodes.different: Today the industry's P/E sits at the 93rd percentile versus the 79th then, and the 10-year yield is high at 4.84%, so there is less valuation cushion. The 12-month return was -16.6% then and is +7.5% now, so today's group has less depressed price to bounce from. This cuts against a repeat.
episodes.lesson: Washed-out sentiment rebounds, but valuation was lower

episodes.then: In January 2022 the Fed was turning hawkish, yields were rising and growth stocks were selling off, with oil rising and inflation high. Railroads were still strong on pricing power and had a high-multiple, 12-month-high-adjacent profile.
episodes.after: The industry fell 5.5% over 3M, 8.7% over 6M and 15% over 12M, against the S&P 500's 12M return of -7.2%. The worst drop in 6 months was -25.7%. The group de-rated as rates rose and the bear market ran through 2022, and it fell more than the market.
episodes.different: Then the industry was outperforming and above its 200-day average; today it is lagging and 4.6% below it. Today's credit spreads are calm (-0.1pp) rather than tightening, but the VIX is higher at 28 versus 25. This cuts both ways, though a high valuation is a shared risk.
episodes.lesson: High multiple plus rising yields meant de-rating

episodes.then: In March 2018 markets were hit by tariff and trade-war headlines and a spike in volatility after the February sell-off, with oil rising. Railroads had been lifted by tax cuts and strong earnings, but had slipped from highs.
episodes.after: The industry gained 1.3% in 1M, 5.8% in 3M, 19.8% in 6M and 16% in 12M, beating the S&P 500's 12M return of 10.7%. The worst drop in 6 months was only -5.7%. Strong earnings and tax-cut tailwinds carried the group through the correction.
episodes.different: Then the P/E percentile was 67 and the VIX was 20, calmer than today's 93 and 28. Today's dollar is rising rather than falling, which adds headwinds. This cuts against the same outcome.
episodes.lesson: Earnings strength can carry a pullback, at a lower valuation

episodes.then: In November 2022 the market was bouncing from the October low, with inflation peaking and the Fed still hiking. Railroads were down from highs, with labor and strike worries and a December contract fight.
episodes.after: The industry fell 6.1% in 1M, 6.6% in 3M and 10.5% in 6M, and was down 6.5% at 12M, while the S&P 500 returned 14.4% over 12M. The worst drop in 6 months was -15.2%. The group lagged as the rally was led elsewhere.
episodes.different: Then oil had fallen 17.8%; today it is up 14.8%, which adds cost pressure but also fuel-surcharge support. The S&P 500 was 13.7% below its high versus 5.9% now. The two are not directly comparable.
episodes.lesson: Defensive groups lag the rebound

episodes.then: In February 2021 vaccine rollout and stimulus drove a cyclical rally, with yields rising sharply and oil climbing. Railroads were richly valued, with the P/E near the 97th percentile, as freight volumes recovered.
episodes.after: The industry gained 6% in 1M, 6.5% in 3M, 1.5% in 6M and 8.9% in 12M, but trailed the S&P 500's 12M return of 16.6%. The worst drop in 6 months was -10.8%. The industry made modest gains while the market advanced more.
episodes.different: Then the industry was 8.6% above its 200-day average and the economy was reopening; now it is 4.6% below and the market is falling. Growth is slower than the reopening boom, which cuts against a repeat.
episodes.lesson: Rich valuation meant positive but lagging returns

Weight is limited because today's valuation (89th percentile) is far above most analogs, and the group's 30.9pp lag is group-specific rather than market-wide; the five episodes also show deep drawdowns of 14% to 26% even in the good outcomes. resembles today most closely: a similar 3M drop, VIX and dollar backdrop, and a stretched group, which suggests a bounce followed…

episodes.then: In November 2021 markets were near highs but jittery: Omicron emerged, the Fed was signaling faster tapering and inflation was surging. Ag machinery had rallied on strong farm incomes and then pulled back, so the group was down about 11.7% over 3 months.
episodes.after: The industry bounced 3% in 1M, was flat at 3M, then slipped 2.9% at 6M and was up 2.1% at 12M. The S&P 500 did worse at 3M, 6M and 12M (-3.5%, -9.5%, -9.2%) as the 2022 rate-hike bear market hit. The group held up better than the market over that year, but it saw a 22.9% drawdown within 6 months.
episodes.different: Today the group's P/E is at the 89th percentile versus the 57th then, and it sits 39.9% below its high versus 20%, so there is more valuation risk but also more washout. That cuts mixed.
episodes.lesson: Bounce, then a deep drawdown

episodes.then: In October 2018 US equities sold off sharply on rate fears and trade-war tensions, with the Fed still hiking. Ag machinery was hurt by tariffs, soybean trade disruption and weak farm sentiment, down about 16.1% over 3 months.
episodes.after: The industry rose 9.5% in 1M, 6.5% in 3M, 7.6% in 6M and 9.5% in 12M, after a 17% worst drop in the next 6 months. The S&P 500 recovered more slowly at first (+1.9% in 1M) but gained 15.4% over 12M. I am not sure of every driver, but the Fed pivot in early 2019 likely helped the rebound.
episodes.different: Then the P/E percentile was 30th, so valuation was cheap, while today it is 89th and the oil and dollar backdrop is firmer. That makes today's setup less supportive.
episodes.lesson: Cheap washouts rebounded

episodes.then: In August 2015 China's devaluation triggered a global equity selloff and a VIX spike, while oil and commodities were collapsing. Farm incomes were falling in the downturn and ag machinery was weak, down about 13.4% over 3 months.
episodes.after: The group fell another 14.3% in 1M, 7% at 3M and 11.7% at 6M, with a 24.1% worst drop. It was down only 2.6% at 12M, while the S&P 500 was up 12.7%. The farm downturn kept the group lagging even as the market recovered.
episodes.different: Then oil was falling and the group's P/E percentile was 25th, whereas today oil is up 14.8% and valuation is stretched. The stretched valuation cuts negative; the firmer oil is a mild offset.
episodes.lesson: Farm downcycle outlasts market recovery

episodes.then: In November 2011 the euro-area debt crisis and the US downgrade aftermath kept volatility high, and Treasuries were rallying. Ag machinery had held up relatively well through the commodity boom but was starting to weaken.
episodes.after: The industry fell 6.5% in 1M, rebounded 10.5% at 3M, then dropped to -14.6% at 6M and -10.6% at 12M, with a 25.5% worst drop. The S&P 500 gained 10.6% at 3M and 15.6% at 12M. Group gains faded as the market kept rising.
episodes.different: Then bonds were rallying (+9%) and credit was stressed (-11.8pp), whereas today yields are up and credit is calm. That cuts toward less panic-driven selling today.
episodes.lesson: 3M bounce faded by 6M

episodes.then: In August 2022 the Fed was hiking aggressively, the dollar was surging and Treasuries were falling hard. Ag machinery was down about 11.9% over 3 months in that bear market.
episodes.after: The industry fell another 11.6% in 1M but recovered 18.7% at 3M, 20.7% at 6M and 17% at 12M, with a 14.1% worst drop. The S&P 500 rose only 3.6% at 3M and 16% at 12M. The strong farm earnings cycle and peak-rate hopes likely drove it, though I am not certain of every detail.
episodes.different: Then the group was only 2.7pp behind the S&P 500 over 6 months, versus 30.9pp behind today, and the market was 16.7% off its high versus 5.9% now. Today's problem is group-specific, which cuts less favorably.
episodes.lesson: Forced selling can precede a rebound

They are driven by NVDA data center +117%, AVGO AI +221% and memory pricing. Margin dilution at NVDA (71-72% trough), AVGO (~73%) and TSM (2nm) is guided and modest.

reads.cycle: Cycle: expansion, pricing power strong. Semiconductors are in an AI-capex-driven expansion with an unusually sharp price and sentiment reset. TTM revenue is +62% and net income +151.5%, with a 50.6% operating margin and 47.1% ROIC (computed metrics).
reads.macro: RESTRICTIVE: Fundamentals are at record strength (TTM revenue +62%, NVDA Q3 guide $108B), but a hiking Fed (10Y 4.84%, December hike expected) and the 5 Nov midterm data-center-moratorium rout (SOX -31.8% in 1M, VIX 26.84) have turned the financing and valuation backdrop restrictive.

episodes.after: The industry rebounded sharply, +10.2% after 1M, +37.6% after 3M and +45.6% after 6M, and was still up +26.8% at 12M. The S&P 500 gained +10.7% over 3M and +19.8% over 6M, so the industry beat it by a wide margin. The worst drop in the following 6 months was only -7.3%, so the rebound began almost immediately.

episodes.lesson: Deep oversold semis can snap back fast

episodes.then: In July 2022 the Fed was raising rates aggressively against high inflation, and oil and the dollar were strong. Equities were in a bear-market bounce and semiconductors were weak after a post-pandemic demand peak.
episodes.after: The bounce failed: the industry fell -9.5% after 1M and -25.9% after 3M, with a worst drop of -33.5% in the next 6 months. It was still -8.6% at 6M, but recovered to +24.4% at 12M versus +12.6% for the S&P 500. The cause was ongoing rate hikes and a weakening chip cycle, and the recovery came once rate fears eased.
episodes.different: Today yields have fallen less (-0.8% vs -5.9% for IEF) and the S&P 500 is only 5.9% below its high versus 13.1% then, so the macro squeeze is milder. But the industry is already down more over 3M (-15.3% vs -5.5%), so some of the damage has already happened. That cuts mildly in favor of a smaller…
episodes.lesson: Oversold can get more oversold before it turns

episodes.then: In October 2018 equities sold off on Fed tightening and US-China trade-war worries. Semiconductors were also hit by a memory and inventory downturn.
episodes.after: The industry was flat for a while, -0.2% after 1M and -1% after 3M, with a worst drop of -17.1% in the next 6 months. It then recovered to +13.7% at 6M and +19.7% at 12M, beating the S&P 500's +9.3% and +15.4%. The December 2018 low and the Fed's later shift away from hikes are the likely explanation, though the returns here are from the code.
episodes.different: The valuation starting point was much lower then (21st percentile vs 69th today) and oil was flat instead of up. Today's starting point is less cheap, so there is less cushion, which cuts against the same recovery.
episodes.lesson: A cheap valuation helped; a pause came first

episodes.then: In August 2015 China's yuan devaluation triggered a global selloff and a volatility spike, with a VIX of 28 matching today's. Semiconductors were weak on slowing PC and China demand.
episodes.after: The industry slipped -1.4% after 1M, then gained +8.2% after 3M and +5.4% after 6M. It was +26.1% at 12M versus +12.7% for the S&P 500. The worst drop in the next 6 months was -15.8%, so the path was choppy before the rebound.
episodes.different: The industry then was cheap (16th percentile) and its 12-month high was only 20.4% away, compared with a 36% gap today. Today the damage is larger but the valuation is not cheap, which cuts against a quick, easy rebound.
episodes.lesson: Volatility spikes fade, but with a choppy retest

episodes.then: In October 2012 Europe's debt crisis was calmer after the ECB's promise to do whatever it takes, and the Fed had launched another round of QE. Semiconductors lagged the market because of weak PC demand.
episodes.after: This was the calmest outcome: +1.2% after 1M, +10.6% after 3M and +15.2% at 6M, with a worst drop of only -4.8%. At 12M the industry was +23% but trailed the S&P 500's +27.1%. A steady equity market with easy policy lifted the industry, though not above the market.
episodes.different: That setup was a cheap (5th percentile) industry in a calm market with falling oil. Today has a VIX of 28, oil up 14.8% and a 36% drawdown, so it is a far more stressed backdrop and this is the weakest analog.
episodes.lesson: Calm, cheap setups drift upward

verdict.summary: BIS rules set the regulatory balance for this industry. Leading-edge logic and HBM capacity stays outside China, which entrenches TSM, MU and SKHY and caps China upside for ASML, AMAT, LRCX and KLAC. Near-term diplomacy has lowered escalation risk: the $30B reciprocal tariff cut and new AI dialogue, plus a truce reported extended to January 2027.

most_material.rule: Advanced-computing / AI accelerator export controls (ECCN 3A090/4A090)
most_material.why: These controls touch the largest share of industry market cap (NVDA, AMD). Any licence relief from the new AI dialogue is an option, not a base case.

most_material.rule: SME/HBM controls, Entity List/FDP and the suspended Affiliates Rule
most_material.why: These rules permanently cap high-margin China system and service revenue for AMAT, LRCX, KLAC and ASML. HBM is caught too, but tight supply lets MU and SKHY redirect it.

most_material.rule: US–China trade truce and China's suspended critical-mineral and rare-earth controls
most_material.why: A lapse would hit toolmakers' supply chains and leading-edge fab ramps. China's EU carve-out signals that any reinstatement could be targeted at the US.

most_material.rule: Sec. 48D Advanced Manufacturing Investment Credit (35%) and CHIPS direct-funding awards
most_material.why: These lower net capex and cash taxes for US fab builders INTC, MU, TSM and TXN.

most_material.rule: EUV licence denial for China and national licensing of immersion DUV, metrology and servicing
most_material.why: This locks leading-edge capacity outside China and makes ASML's China DUV and installed-base revenue a policy variable. ASML's growing weight in the Dutch economy raises the domestic cost of further tightening.

winners.why: EUV licensing and the N-1 rule keep frontier wafers in Taiwan and under licensed control, protecting margins (Q4 GM guided 65-67%). US fabs are subsidised via CHIPS and 48D.
HBM is redirected to non-China AI buyers amid a memory shortage. CHIPS guardrails cap China bit growth, and 48D plus grants subsidise US fabs. Section 301 duties also help against Chinese memory.
Custom silicon for US hyperscalers is largely insulated from China licensing. It could gain modestly if SAMR interoperability remedies loosen NVDA's networking attach.
Direct-pay 48D credit, a federal equity stake and its position as the only uncapped US leading-edge option make it the relative structural beneficiary of onshoring policy.
The 50% Section 301 duty on Chinese-origin chips and a possible 2027 legacy-chip tariff protect its analog share. US fabs benefit from CHIPS awards and 48D.

losers.why: China data-center revenue is licence-contingent under 3A090/4A090. SAMR's open Mellanox-conditions probe gives Beijing a lever over its China access.
Has already absorbed an ~$800M MI308 charge. A rich valuation after the >$1T rerating leaves little room for another denial or threshold change.
China tool sales are capped by the SME rule and FDP reach. The Affiliates Rule snap-back carries an estimated ~$600M FY26 impact, and rare-earth licensing threatens consumables and tool builds.
High China mix is capped by the SME controls and indirectly by Dutch lithography limits on Chinese fabs. It is exposed to MOFCOM retaliation and mineral licensing if the truce lapses.
EUV is barred from China, and immersion DUV, metrology and servicing need case-by-case Dutch licences. That makes China non-EUV and installed-base revenue a policy variable.

debates.bull: Every major company raised guidance between calls: NVDA $108B for Q3, TSM ~44% growth in 2026, AVGO ~$115B FY27 AI, AMD >80% growth in 2027. Estimates are up 12.9% over 90 days, and the selling is specific to AI names while S&P ex-AI is…
debates.bear: The capex chain now depends on vendor financing and neocloud debt (NVDA DSO 60 days, $50B in frontier labs). Credit is widening, so the 2027 step-up to $1.3T is where any cut will land, and peak memory margins historically mean-revert.

debates.q: Will post-midterm politics actually curb US data-center construction?
debates.bull: Divided-government constraints, a January start and the absence of any enacted statute mean policy is more likely to channel into permitting and cost-sharing rules than bans. Hyperscalers can shift sites geographically.
debates.bear: Moratorium pledges in TX, OH and GA target the core build regions. Even delays shift 2027 revenue and justify a lasting political discount on the multiple.
debates.resolves: Texas legislative action and governor executive orders in Q1 2027; hyperscaler capex guides in late January

debates.q: Is memory (SKHY, MU) a cyclical top or a structural reset?
debates.bull: HBM4, server DDR5 and enterprise SSD demand exceed supply more than 2x. SKHY has >50% of 2027-28 capacity under long-term agreements and MU >75% of FY27 shipments committed, and both trade at ~3x forward earnings.
debates.bear: An 80% operating margin is historically unsustainable. CXMT is gaining, Goldman cut its KOSPI target 25%, and memory costs are already destroying PC demand.
debates.resolves: MU FQ1 results and pricing commentary on 2026-12-23; SKHY Q4 results on 2027-01-28

hist.read: The five episodes lean positive: the industry was up at 6M in 4 of 5 and at 12M in 3 of 5, in line with the base rates (75% up at 6M, median +10.8%). The path is rough, though: the worst drawdown in the next 6 months ranged from -8.9% to -29.8%, and the 1M and 3M outcomes are mixed, so do not expect a quick rebound. The high valuation, VIX of 28 and rising oil mean the weight on the benign cases should be tempered, and is the main warning of a de-rating. Today most resembles: a similar sell-off and valuation, but with weaker credit confirmation, which supports a patient, modestly overweight stance in quality names.

episodes.then: In March 2025 markets were selling off on tariff fears and growth worries, with the S&P 500 near correction territory and the dollar firm. Software had pulled back from its highs while still trading at a rich valuation.
episodes.after: The industry rebounded sharply once tariff tensions eased, with +8.3% at 1M and +27.6% at 3M, and +14.7% at 6M. By 12M it was -2.6% while the S&P 500 gained +18.5%, so the early rally faded and the industry lagged. The worst drop in the next 6 months was -14.4%.
episodes.different: Today credit spreads are not yet confirming a recovery (high-yield -0.1pp vs +2.1pp then) and oil is rising with the VIX higher at 28, so the backdrop is more stressed. The industry also holds above its 200-day average, which cuts mildly in its favour.
episodes.lesson: Sharp rebounds can come fast but fade

episodes.then: In January 2022 the Fed turned hawkish, yields were rising fast and oil was climbing ahead of Russia's invasion of Ukraine. High-multiple software was de-rating hard.
episodes.after: This was the worst outcome: the industry fell -5% at 1M, -14.3% at 3M, -20.3% at 6M and -29.7% at 12M, against -7.2% for the S&P 500 at 12M. Rate hikes compressed multiples, and the worst drop in the next 6 months was -29.8%.
episodes.different: Today yields have only edged up (-0.8% for IEF vs -3.9%) and the industry sits above its 200-day average, whereas it was below then; there is no sign of an aggressive Fed tightening cycle in this data. That cuts in favour of a milder outcome.
episodes.lesson: Rate shock de-rating hurts expensive software

episodes.then: In October 2018 equities sold off on Fed tightening and trade-war worries, with the dollar strong. Software had held up better than the market until then.
episodes.after: The industry was +1.8% at 1M and -0.9% at 3M as the December 2018 slump hit. It then recovered to +15.6% at 6M and +18.7% at 12M, versus +15.4% for the S&P 500 at 12M. The worst drop in the next 6 months was -17.7%.
episodes.different: Valuation today is much richer (85th percentile vs 63rd) and oil is up 14.8% rather than flat, so there is less cushion. The industry's 12M gain of +7.6% is also weaker than the +17.1% then.
episodes.lesson: Dip, then recovery, with a rough patch between

episodes.then: In August 2015 China's devaluation triggered a global growth scare and a VIX spike, while oil was collapsing. Software was down about 10% over three months.
episodes.after: The industry gained +1.9% at 1M, +16.9% at 3M, +8.7% at 6M and +20.2% at 12M, while the S&P 500 was +12.7% at 12M. The worst drop in the next 6 months was -17.2%, so there was a volatile retest before the recovery.
episodes.different: Oil is rising now, not collapsing, so inflation and yield pressure is a risk where then it was a tailwind. Credit stress was clearly visible then (-3.4pp) but is not today, which cuts in favour of today.
episodes.lesson: Panic lows can be bought, with volatility

episodes.then: In September 2023 yields were surging and oil was rallying on the 'higher for longer' Fed message. The S&P 500 was in a pullback, but software was already above its 200-day average.
episodes.after: The industry rallied strongly once yields peaked: +2.9% at 1M, +16.5% at 3M, +35% at 6M and +29.5% at 12M, against +34.8% for the S&P 500 at 12M. The worst drop in the next 6 months was only -8.9%.
episodes.different: Today's VIX is 28 against 18 and the valuation is richer, with a policy and credit overhang that was absent then. That cuts against a repeat of such a smooth rally.
episodes.lesson: Yield peak enables a strong software rally

moves.label: US 10Y Treasury yield

moves.situation: Warsh Fed on hold but leaning toward hikes; Treasury yields near two-decade highs

hist.read: The five episodes lean weak over the longer horizons. Three of five were up at 1M, 3M and 6M, but only one of five was up at 12M, and the base-rate 12M median is +7.4% with only 35% beating the S&P 500. For 1M expect noise, with a median of -1.5% and a middle half of -5.8% to +6.4%. The 3M and 6M medians are +3.5% and +4.7% with wide ranges, and drawdowns of roughly 10% to 40% inside six months were common. With only five episodes, and a P/E percentile higher than in any of them, the analogs deserve modest weight, but they are consistent with the team's modest underweight-to-neutral stance. Today most resembles on price setup, while is the closer match on stress and valuation.

episodes.then: March 2025 was a tariff-driven selloff, with the S&P 500 sliding toward a correction ahead of the April 'Liberation Day' tariffs and the dollar stronger over the prior six months. Apple and the consumer-hardware group were exposed to China tariff risk but had still outperformed the market over the prior year.
episodes.after: The industry rebounded after the April tariff shock: +14.3% at 1M, +11.9% at 3M and +20.7% at 6M, though the worst drop inside six months was -9.7%. By 12M the gain had faded to +12.5%, behind the S&P 500's +18.5%, so the industry led early and then gave up the lead.
episodes.different: Today's P/E percentile is 98th versus 82nd then, and the VIX is 28 versus 22. Today also has memory-cost margin pressure and falling estimates, and the 12-month gain is +20.4% versus +42.6% then. A clean policy-shock rebound looks less likely, which cuts bearish.
episodes.lesson: Shock rebounds fade from rich valuations

episodes.then: January 2022 was the start of the Fed's hawkish pivot, with yields rising, growth stocks selling off and oil climbing ahead of Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Apple was near its highs, having held up better than the market.
episodes.after: The industry fell hard: -5.1% at 1M, -12.3% at 3M, -15.1% at 6M and -28.7% at 12M, with a worst drop of -30.3% inside six months. The S&P 500 also fell (-8.6% at 6M, -7.2% at 12M), but the industry fell much more as rate hikes compressed multiples and tech sold off.
episodes.different: The P/E percentile was 73rd then versus 98th now, so valuation is more stretched today, which cuts bearish. Against that, today's Treasury move is smaller (-0.8% versus -3.9%), which cuts bullish. Whether a rate-hiking cycle is under way today is not something I can confirm from the data given.
episodes.lesson: Rich multiples fall hardest under stress

episodes.then: October 2018 was a sharp market drawdown driven by Fed tightening worries, US-China trade tension and a stronger dollar. Apple had peaked in early October, and its early-November results and guidance soon set off a steep fall.
episodes.after: The industry dropped -19.8% at 1M and -26.9% at 3M, with a worst drop of -39.6% inside six months. It recovered partly to -13.8% at 6M and -1.6% at 12M, while the S&P 500 gained +15.4% at 12M, so the industry badly lagged.
episodes.different: The P/E percentile was only 48th then versus 98th now, so there was far more valuation cushion then, which cuts bearish for today. The market drawdown today is a bit smaller (-5.9% versus -7.4%), which cuts slightly bullish.
episodes.lesson: Post-peak disappointments drop fast

episodes.then: May 2023 was the start of the AI-driven megacap rally, with the debt-ceiling standoff and regional-bank stress fading. Apple had rallied for months and traded near its highs on defensive-quality demand.
episodes.after: The industry gained +9.2% at 1M but only +4.1% at 3M and +3.4% at 6M, with a worst drop of -16.9%. It ended 12M at -1.6% while the S&P 500 rose +28%, so it lagged badly in a broad rally.
episodes.different: Today the market is under stress, with the VIX at 28 versus 18 and the S&P 500 5.9% off its high, whereas then it was only 1.5% below. Today's valuation is also higher and estimates are falling, which cuts bearish for the industry.
episodes.lesson: Megacap leadership can stall

episodes.then: September 2014 followed the iPhone 6 launch, with the dollar strengthening and oil starting its collapse. Apple was in a strong run and the market was near its highs.
episodes.after: The industry rose +5.5% at 1M, +8.7% at 3M and +16% at 6M, with a worst drop of -12.8%. By 12M it was -4% against -0.8% for the S&P 500, so the early gains reversed.

hist.read: The five episodes are split: and were large gains, a gain after a deep drawdown, and and 12-month losses. The 20-month base rates lean mildly positive: 65% up at 6M with a median of +9.4%, and 70% up at 12M with a median of +21.6%. The 1M and 3M odds are only modest, and the wide ranges, including's -25% drop, show path risk. The episodes beat the S&P 500 only about half the time, so they support neutral weight, not an overweight, and the team's negative scenario carries only modest weight. Today most resembles: a VIX in the 20s, a policy-driven selloff and software lagging its AI-fear de-rating, though's rising oil and dollar fit as well.

episodes.then: April 2025 followed the tariff shock, when the S&P 500 fell sharply, the VIX spiked and policy uncertainty dominated. Software had been weak, though it held up better than the broad market.
episodes.after: Over the next 12 months the industry returned -31.9% against +31.4% for the S&P 500. It was +1.5% at 1M and -1.9% at 3M, then -9.2% at 6M, with a worst drop of -15.4% inside the first six months. The market rebounded strongly while software lagged. I am not certain of the exact cause, but the AI-disruption worry over seat-based software seems the likely driver.
episodes.different: Then the industry was just recovering from a tariff-driven low, and yields had fallen. Today it sits 12.6% above its 200-day average, with oil and the dollar rising, so the setup is more extended and the macro mix is less supportive.
episodes.lesson: Rebounding indices can leave software behind

episodes.then: October 2016 came just before the US election, with a calm market (VIX 17) and yields starting to rise. Software was digesting a weak 12 months and sat well below its high.
episodes.after: The industry gained +42.4% over 12 months against +23.4% for the S&P 500, after -0.6% at 1M, +4% at 3M and +15.5% at 6M. The worst drop in the first six months was only -5.5%. The post-election reflation rally and strong earnings and cloud growth lifted the group.
episodes.different: Then the VIX was 17, high-yield spreads were improving and oil was falling. Today the VIX is 28 with oil rising and the dollar firm, so the stress is greater, though that can also mean cheaper entry points.
episodes.lesson: Calm, reflating backdrops favored software

episodes.then: June 2018 saw the US-China trade war escalate, a rising dollar, oil near multi-year highs and the Fed tightening. Software was a leader, outperforming the S&P 500 by 13.9pp over six months.
episodes.after: The industry returned +31.4% over 12 months versus +11.4% for the S&P 500. It was +1.4% at 1M and +13.9% at 3M, but -6.2% at 6M, with a worst drop of -25%. The Q4 2018 selloff hit software hard before a 2019 recovery.
episodes.different: Then the VIX was 16 and the industry was up 33.9% over 12 months. Today the VIX is 28 and 12-month gains are only +4.3%, so there is less froth but also less momentum.
episodes.lesson: Leadership can survive a deep drawdown

episodes.then: January 2014 was a time of Fed tapering and an emerging-market wobble. Software was strong, having outperformed the S&P 500 by 6.1pp over six months.
episodes.after: The industry returned -12.9% over 12 months against +15.5% for the S&P 500. It was +5.9% at 1M, -4.1% at 3M and -0.8% at 6M, with a worst drop of -13.4%. The spring 2014 growth and momentum selloff hurt richly valued software. I am not sure of every detail.
episodes.different: Then the P/E percentile was 19th and the VIX was 18, with stable oil. Today the P/E percentile is 32nd and the VIX is 28, with a macro backdrop that is more unsettled.
episodes.lesson: Momentum names can lag after strong runs

episodes.then: May 2012 saw the euro-zone crisis flare up again, Greek election worries, falling oil and falling yields. Software sat 22.9% below its high with a 9th-percentile P/E, so it was cheap.
episodes.after: The industry gained +58.7% over 12 months versus +27.2% for the S&P 500. It was -3.7% at 1M, then +25.6% at 3M and +51% at 6M, with a worst drop of -9.6%. Central-bank easing and a cheap starting valuation drove the rebound.
episodes.different: Then valuations were at the 9th percentile and yields were falling. Today the P/E percentile is 32nd and yields are rising, so there is less valuation cushion and no tailwind from lower rates.
episodes.lesson: Cheap valuations and easing support big rebounds

The base rates agree: 1M leans up (60% of the time, median +1.4%), 3M is weaker (45%, median -1.9%, 1 of 5 episodes up), 6M is a coin flip (median +0.2%, beat the S&P 500 only 15% of the time), and 12M is wide-ranging (median +7%, middle half -18% to +32.2%). The weight these deserve is modest because today differs from most of them: the drop is recent (12M still +12.6%) and the P/E is high for the industry's own history, even if the 9.3x forward multiple looks low. is the nearest by the code's ranking, but it…

episodes.then: March 2025 was a tariff-driven selloff, with growth worries and a sharp S&P 500 pullback ahead of the early-April tariff announcements. AI-hardware names had already been hit hard by earlier doubts about the AI spending trend, so the industry was far below its highs.
episodes.after: After a rough patch around the April tariff shock, the industry rebounded strongly: +11.3% at 1M, +44.9% at 3M, +80.7% at 6M and +64.4% at 12M, against +19.8% for the S&P 500 at 6M. The worst drop in the next 6 months was only -9.6%, so the panic low came quickly and AI-infrastructure demand then drove the recovery.
episodes.different: Then the industry was already down 30.8% over 12 months and the drop was a long grind. Today it is still up 12.6% over 12 months after a sudden crash, so there is less washed-out positioning and more to unwind, which cuts against a repeat.
episodes.lesson: Policy-shock lows can reverse violently upward

episodes.then: October 2018 brought a sharp equity selloff on Fed tightening, US-China trade-war worries and rising yields. Tech hardware was de-rating, and the market slide continued into the December low.
episodes.after: The industry fell 1.2% at 1M and 5.7% at 3M, and was flat at 6M (+0.1%) after a worst drop of -26.4% along the way. At 12M it was -16.1% while the S&P 500 was +15.4%, so the industry lagged the market even as the market recovered.
episodes.different: Then VIX was 21, and the industry was 20% below its 12-month high with a 88th percentile P/E. Today the drawdown is deeper (-34.9%) and VIX is higher at 28, so more fear is already priced, though the valuation still isn't cheap by its own history. That cuts mildly in favour of a bounce.
episodes.lesson: Expensive hardware can lag even as the market recovers

episodes.then: February 2022 saw Russia's invasion of Ukraine, an oil spike and an imminent start of Fed rate hikes. VIX was about 30, and bond yields were rising while growth stocks de-rated.
episodes.after: The industry gained 5.9% at 1M, then slid: -11.2% at 3M, -23% at 6M and -29% at 12M, with a worst drop of -31.6%. The S&P 500 also fell (-7.1% at 6M, -8.1% at 12M), so this was a broad bear market driven by inflation and rate hikes.
episodes.different: The macro looks similar, with oil up, a stronger dollar, rising yields and VIX near 28-30. But the industry was only 15.5% below its high then, versus 34.9% now, so today much of the damage is already done. That cuts toward less downside than HE3 delivered.
episodes.lesson: Rate-and-oil bear markets keep punishing multiples

episodes.then: June 2015 was a calm market with a Greek debt crisis in the background and China worries building toward August's devaluation and flash crash. Traditional hardware was in a long slump, with PC demand weak, and was already far behind the S&P 500.
episodes.after: The industry rose 1.5% at 1M but fell 19.3% at 3M and 21.7% at 6M, with a worst drop of -25.5%. At 12M it was -35.1% versus +2.6% for the S&P 500, so the weakness was industry-specific.
episodes.different: Then the P/E percentile was 36th, so the industry was cheap-ish and VIX was only 18. Today the multiple is in the 84th percentile of its own history and VIX is 28, so the setup is more stressed with less valuation cushion. That cuts toward more risk.
episodes.lesson: Relative-strength laggards can keep lagging

episodes.then: November 2022 was a post-midterm period in which the market was hoping for a peak in inflation and Fed hikes. The S&P 500 was still 13.7% below its high, and hardware was deeply de-rated. I am not certain of the industry-specific events that month.
episodes.after: The industry fell 10.3% at 1M and 2.6% at 3M, then recovered: +10.7% at 6M and +32.2% at 12M, with a worst drop of -12.9%. The S&P 500 was +14.4% at 12M, so the industry beat it only after a delayed rebound as rate fears eased and AI enthusiasm rose.
episodes.different: Then the industry had already fallen 35.3% over 12 months, with a mid-range P/E (62nd percentile). Today the multiple is higher relative to history and the fall has been quicker, which cuts against such a clean recovery.
episodes.lesson: Early pain, then recovery once rates stabilised

episodes.then: In February 2020 COVID-19 was spreading beyond China and equities were starting the fastest bear-market plunge on record. Communication equipment stocks were already weak and fell with the market.
episodes.after: The industry fell 13.1% in the first month and dropped as much as 26.2% within six months. It then recovered as the Fed cut rates to zero and stimulus arrived, with 3M -0.5%, 6M -2.8% and 12M +10.6%. The S&P 500 rebounded much harder, with 6M +18.8% and 12M +34%.
episodes.different: In 2020 the shock was an outside event (a pandemic) that policy erased within weeks, and the VIX was 40 versus 28 today. Today the market is under much less stress, and the industry's P/E sits at the 88th percentile versus the 73rd then, with no obvious rescue in sight. That cuts toward a weaker…
episodes.lesson: Shock-driven crashes can recover fast, but only with a policy backstop

episodes.then: In November 2013 the market was near record highs on QE and the Fed's taper debate, with a calm VIX of 14. Communication equipment had badly lagged the market.
episodes.after: The industry went nowhere over the next year, with 1M +2.6%, 3M +4.3%, 6M +1.7% and 12M +1.3%, though it fell as much as 19.1% along the way within six months. The S&P 500 kept climbing, with 12M +15.9%. The group stayed a laggard while the broad market rose.
episodes.different: The market was calm then, with the S&P 500 only 0.1% below its high and a VIX of 14. Today the S&P 500 is 5.9% below its high and the VIX is 28, so stress is much higher. That cuts toward a more volatile path today.
episodes.lesson: Cheap laggards can stay laggards for a year

episodes.then: In July 2012 the euro-area crisis was easing after Draghi's 'whatever it takes' pledge. Communication equipment was deeply depressed and its valuation was at the 8th percentile of its own history.
episodes.after: The industry rebounded 11.7% in the first month and gained 24.9% over six months, though 12M was only +6.9% and the worst drop within six months was 11.8%. The S&P 500 rose 26.9% over 12 months. The bounce came from a washed-out starting valuation and a central-bank backstop.
episodes.different: Valuation was at the 8th percentile then and is at the 88th percentile now. Today lacks the cheap-multiple cushion that helped drive that rebound, which cuts against a similar bounce.
episodes.lesson: Rebounds are easier from a cheap starting valuation

episodes.then: In July 2022 the Fed was hiking aggressively against 40-year-high inflation. The S&P 500 was in a bear market, and the dollar and oil were strong, much like today.
episodes.after: The industry slipped over the following year, with 1M -1.2%, 3M -6.5%, 6M -2.6% and 12M -3.2%, and a worst drop of 19.8% within six months. The S&P 500 fell more at first, with 3M -7.4%, then recovered to 12M +12.6%. The industry did not share the later market recovery.
episodes.different: In 2022 the pain came from a broad rate shock (IEF -5.9% over six months versus -0.8% today) and the S&P 500 was 13.1% below its high. Today the industry's own rout is far deeper (3M -23.4% versus -5.3%) while the broad market is holding up better. That cuts both ways: the group is more washed out…
episodes.lesson: Macro tightening drags the group, and gains lag the market

episodes.then: In July 2011 the US debt-ceiling fight, the S&P downgrade and the euro crisis sparked a sharp selloff, with a VIX of 25. Communication equipment was already weak and cheap, at the 10th percentile of its own valuation history.
episodes.after: The industry fell 8.3% in the first month and was roughly flat at 3M (+0.4%), then drifted lower, with 6M -7% and 12M -26.5% and a worst drop of 18% within six months. The S&P 500 steadied, with 12M +9.5%. I am not certain of the exact fundamental drivers, but the group clearly did not rebound with the market.
episodes.different: The industry was cheap then, at the 10th percentile, and is expensive now, at the 88th. Starting from a higher valuation cuts toward more downside risk today.
episodes.lesson: A stressed market can keep dragging a weak group

episodes.then: In September 2023 Treasury yields were surging toward 5% on 'higher for longer' Fed messaging, oil was rallying and the S&P 500 was in a late-summer pullback. Tech hardware had sold off hard over the prior three months, and I am not sure of the exact industry drivers beyond the rate shock.
episodes.after: The industry fell 9.8% in the first month, then recovered to +13.6% at 3M and +18.8% at 6M, ending +9.2% at 12M. That was a solid rebound, but it lagged the S&P 500's +34.8% over the same 12 months. The worst drop within six months was -12.6%, so the rebound was bumpy. The recovery is consistent with yields peaking and rate-cut hopes returning late in 2023.
episodes.different: Today's industry is far more stretched: it sits 32.3% below its 200-day average versus 13.9% then, and lags the S&P 500 by 40.6pp versus 20pp. The P/E percentile is also higher (80th vs 60th), and VIX is 28 vs 18, so today's setup is more extreme and the valuation cushion is thinner. Credit was…
episodes.lesson: Rate-shock selloffs can reverse sharply, but only after another leg down

episodes.then: In August 2015 China's devaluation shock triggered a global equity selloff and a VIX spike, while oil was collapsing and the dollar was strong. Tech hardware was already weak after a long slide.
episodes.after: The industry slipped 3.3% in one month, gained 5.1% at 3M, was -2.8% at 6M and ended +7.3% at 12M. The S&P 500 was also choppy (+1.8% at 6M, +12.7% at 12M). The worst drop within six months was -19.4%, as the market retested its lows in early 2016 before recovering.
episodes.different: Valuation then was cheap (27th percentile) versus 80th percentile today, so there was less de-rating risk. Today's oil is rising (+14.8%) rather than collapsing, which adds an inflation pressure that wasn't there. Both cut against the mild recovery then.
episodes.lesson: A volatile retest can come before the recovery

episodes.then: In February 2022 Russia invaded Ukraine just as the Fed was preparing its first hikes. Oil surged, yields were rising and growth and tech stocks were in a bear phase.
episodes.after: The industry gained 2.3% in the first month but then fell, to -9.7% at 3M and -11.5% at 6M, finishing -27.4% at 12M. The S&P 500 fell 8.1% at 12M. The worst drop within six months was -23.8%. Aggressive rate hikes and de-rating of high-multiple tech drove the decline.
episodes.different: That valuation (76th percentile) is the closest match to today's, which matters. But in 2022 the Fed was starting an aggressive hiking cycle, whereas today's stress comes from funding, AI credit and policy worries. The industry is also already much deeper in drawdown now (-47.6% vs -16.2%), so more…
episodes.lesson: A high multiple plus a macro shock meant a long grind lower

episodes.then: In November 2022 inflation was starting to cool, but the Fed was still hiking and the 2022 bear market was in its late stages. Tech hardware was down sharply over the year.
episodes.after: The industry fell 14.5% in the first month, was -9.8% at 3M and -14.8% at 6M, and ended -23% at 12M. The S&P 500 rose 14.4% over the same 12 months. The worst drop within six months was -22.4%. I am unsure of the exact industry-specific drivers, but it was a clear case of the industry lagging while the broad market recovered.
episodes.different: Then the S&P 500 was 13.7% below its high, whereas today it is only 5.9% below, so today's weakness is more concentrated in the industry. The industry's drawdown is also deeper now, which could mean more washout, though a narrower problem is not necessarily an easier one.
episodes.lesson: The industry can keep falling even when the broad market recovers

episodes.then: In October 2018 equities sold off sharply on Fed tightening and US-China trade-war fears, and the dollar was strong. The industry was down about 12% over the prior year.
episodes.after: The industry gained 1.8% in the first month, 3.4% at 3M, 12.6% at 6M and 13.3% at 12M. The S&P 500 gained 15.4% at 12M. The worst drop within six months was -17.6%, which fits the December 2018 low before the Fed's pivot and the 2019 rally.
episodes.different: Valuation then was mid-range (52nd percentile) and the industry was much less stretched below its 200-day average (-10.7% vs -32.3%). Today there is no clear Fed pivot on the horizon, and the AI funding and policy risk is more specific. That makes the quick rebound less likely.
episodes.lesson: A policy pivot rescued the rebound

Four of the five episodes were flat to down at 3 months, and every one had a 6-month drawdown of at least 4%, four of them deeper than 7%. That supports the team's neutral stance and argues against chasing the refuge rally after a +31.5pp lead over the market. The weight is moderate, because today's VIX of 28, rising yields and a hawkish Fed are not matched by most analogues (only had comparable stress, and it was a cheap early-cycle rebound). Today most resembles: a…

episodes.then: In July 2019 the Fed was about to cut rates for the first time since 2008, and the US-China trade war was still escalating. IT services had rallied hard and traded well above their 200-day average.
episodes.after: The industry fell 4.6% in the first month and 4.7% by 3 months, then recovered to +5% at 6 months. It slid to -9.8% at 12 months, a window that includes the 2020 pandemic crash, while the S&P 500 gained 11.1%. The worst drop inside the first 6 months was -7.8%.
episodes.different: In 2019 yields had been falling (IEF +6%) and VIX was 16, so the backdrop was calm and easing. Today yields are rising, VIX is 28 and the Fed leans toward hikes, which cuts against the industry.
episodes.lesson: Stretched leaders fade even in calm markets

episodes.then: In January 2010 markets were wobbling after the 2009 rebound, on Greek debt worries and fears about bank regulation. IT services were recovering from the financial crisis and were still well below their prior high.
episodes.after: The industry rose 15.3% in 1 month and 17.6% by 3 months, then eased to +8% at 6 months and +21% at 12 months. The S&P 500 matched it at 12 months (+21.3%), but the industry had a -14.5% drawdown along the way. The rebound looks driven by early-cycle recovery and cheap valuations (28th percentile).
episodes.different: In 2010 the industry was cheap and coming out of a recession, and high-yield bonds were beating Treasuries by 5.4pp. Today it is mid-valuation, 5% below its high after a big run, and the Fed leans hawkish, so there is less room for a rebound.
episodes.lesson: Cheap early-cycle rebound is not today's setup

episodes.then: In May 2025 markets were recovering from the April tariff shock and the Fed was on hold. IT services were richly valued (90th percentile), and AI disruption worries were starting to weigh on services names, though I am not certain how much that drove the group that month.
episodes.after: The industry gained 3.1% in 1 month but fell 6.2% by 3 months, -2.6% at 6 months and -19.4% at 12 months. The S&P 500 rose 30.4% over the same 12 months. The worst drop within 6 months was -15.4%, as the market favored other leaders over services providers.
episodes.different: Today's valuation is mid-range (50th percentile) rather than the 90th, and the industry has acted as a refuge in a sell-off, which is a stronger relative position. VIX is also much higher now, at 28 versus 19.
episodes.lesson: Rich valuations plus a lagging group hurt

episodes.then: In March 2018 the S&P 500 was correcting after the February volatility spike, and tariff headlines and Fed hikes were weighing on markets. Oil was rising strongly and IT services were modestly above trend.
episodes.after: The industry fell 2.2% in 1 month and 0.1% by 3 months, then gained 6% at 6 months and 2.6% at 12 months. The S&P 500 outperformed, up 11.5% at 6 months and 10.7% at 12 months. The worst 6-month drop was only -4.2%.
episodes.different: In 2018 the industry was only slightly ahead of the market (+2.2pp), whereas today it leads by 31.5pp. That stretched lead leaves more room to mean-revert.
episodes.lesson: Mild correction, industry lags the recovery

episodes.then: In January 2024 the market was pricing in Fed cuts and the AI rally was lifting equities. IT services had jumped 20.4% in 3 months, and VIX was low at 14.
episodes.after: The industry gained 7.4% in 1 month, then fell 7.1% by 3 months, -4.2% at 6 months and -4.1% at 12 months. The S&P 500 rose 25.4% over 12 months, and the industry's worst 6-month drop was -17.8%. Early gains faded as the group lagged the broader market.
episodes.different: In 2024 conditions were calm and easing, with VIX at 14. Today VIX is 28, tech is in correction and rates are not falling, so this is a stress period where defensive behavior has been rewarded.
episodes.lesson: Early pops fade; the group lags the market

hist.read: The five episodes and base rates lean positive: 5 of 5 up at 1M, 4 of 5 at 3M, 6M and 12M, with 20-month medians of +2.4% (1M), +5.5% (3M), +7.8% (6M) and +12.3% (12M). Beating the S&P 500 is only a coin flip at best (30% at 12M), so the case is for absolute gains, not relative outperformance, and shows the downside when equities rally and yields stay high. Drawdowns of -6% to -11% inside six months occurred in every episode, which supports adding on pullbacks rather than chasing at RSI 66. Only five episodes with real differences in valuation, VIX and oil deserve modest weight; today most resembles, because of the stressed VIX, the falling S&P 500 and the haven bid, with a close second.

episodes.then: In June 2015 markets were focused on the Greek debt crisis and the approaching first Fed hike, and the dollar was strong. Utilities were sliding as rate-hike fears hit yield-sensitive sectors.
episodes.after: The industry rose 4.8% in 1M, 2.8% in 3M, 6.1% in 6M and 23.2% in 12M. The S&P 500 was +2.4% at 1M but -8.1% at 3M, so utilities worked as a haven; the worst drawdown within 6 months was still -11.1%. I am not certain of every driver, but the measured path fits a defensive rotation.
episodes.different: Today's valuation is richer (68th percentile vs 32nd) and VIX is higher (28 vs 18). Oil is up 14.8% rather than falling, and the AI-linked selloff is a different shock. This cuts against a repeat of the strong 12M gain.
episodes.lesson: Defensive rotation rewarded patient holders despite deep drawdowns

episodes.then: In February 2023 the Fed was still hiking and yields were rising again after a January rally. Utilities lagged a resilient equity market and sat about 19% off their high.
episodes.after: The industry gained 3.7% in 1M but fell 0.8% in 3M, 2.6% in 6M and 8.4% in 12M, with a worst 6M drop of -11.3%. The S&P 500 rose 6.4% in 3M, 14.2% in 6M and 30.2% in 12M, so the group badly lagged a risk-on market. Rates staying high plausibly explains this.
episodes.different: Today the S&P 500 is falling (6M -2.6%) rather than rallying, and the group has acted as a haven. Yields are not clearly pressuring it now (IEF -0.8% vs -4%). This cuts in favor of relative resilience, though the AI-capex story is a new factor.
episodes.lesson: Bounce faded when equities ran and yields stayed high

episodes.then: In March 2018 markets had a volatility hangover from February, with trade-war tariff fears and rising rates. Utilities were weak relative to the market.
episodes.after: The industry gained 2.1% in 1M, 1% in 3M, 0.7% in 6M and 13.7% in 12M. The S&P 500 gained 3.4% in 3M, 11.5% in 6M and 10.7% in 12M, so utilities lagged for six months before catching up. The worst 6M drop was -7.2%.
episodes.different: Today's VIX (28 vs 20) and the sector's 12M decline (-13.8% vs -3.3%) are both much worse. The setup is more stressed and the sector more oversold. This cuts toward a bigger rebound but also more volatility.
episodes.lesson: Slow six months, then a decent 12M gain

episodes.then: In February 2021 vaccine-driven reflation sent yields and oil sharply higher. Utilities, richly valued, sold off as growth and cyclicals led.
episodes.after: The industry gained 9.8% in 1M, 10.9% in 3M, 15.5% in 6M and 13.9% in 12M, with a worst 6M drop of only -6.2%. The S&P 500 gained 10.6% in 3M, 18.1% in 6M and 16.6% in 12M, so the industry kept pace at first and trailed over 6M and 12M. Falling yields after the spring plausibly helped.
episodes.different: Then the P/E percentile was 97th, credit was easing and the economy was reopening. Today the P/E percentile is 68th, the S&P 500 is weak and credit is flat. The cheaper starting point cuts mildly in favor; the weaker growth backdrop is less clear.
episodes.lesson: Oversold utilities rebounded when yields stabilized

episodes.then: In November 2021 the Fed signaled tapering, inflation was rising and the Omicron variant emerged late in the month. VIX was 27 and utilities were expensive but still near highs.
episodes.after: The industry gained 7.7% in 1M, 2.4% in 3M, 9.2% in 6M and 0.2% in 12M, with a worst 6M drop of -8.9%. The S&P 500 gained 4.9% in 1M but lost 3.5% in 3M, 9.5% in 6M and 9.2% in 12M as the 2022 rate-hike bear market hit. Utilities held up far better, though the 12M gain faded to almost nothing.
episodes.different: Then the industry was only 5.3% off its high and above its 200-day average (+0.2%). Today it is 17.9% off its high and 9.9% below its 200-day average. That cuts toward more rebound room, but it also signals a broken trend.
episodes.lesson: Haven bid worked in a falling market, then faded
